SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Title VII of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (“Dodd-Frank Act”) established a comprehensive regulatory framework for swaps.
[
2
]
Section 712(d)(1) of the Dodd-Frank Act provides that the Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”), in consultation with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the “Federal Reserve Board”), shall jointly further define, among other terms, the term “swap.”
[
3
]
Pursuant to this requirement, in 2012, the Commission and the SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, issued a final rule further defining the term “swap” and other terms.
[
4
]
This Proposal seeks to clarify that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps within the CFTC's jurisdiction. The CFTC has historically recognized that many event contracts are covered by the Commodity Exchange Act's (the “CEA”) swap definition.
[
5
]
Under section 1a(47)(A) of the CEA, the term swap is defined “broadly.”
[
6
]
As discussed further in this section below, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(ii) defines “swap” to include “any agreement, contract, or transaction . . . that provides for any purchase, sale, payment, or delivery (other than a dividend on an equity security) that is dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
[
7
]
The broad nature of clause (ii) of the swap definition is in keeping with the broad definition of the term “commodity” in the CEA. The 1974 amendments to the CEA expanded the definition of the term “commodity” to encompass “all services, rights, and interests in which contracts for future delivery are presently or in the future dealt in.”
[
8
]
In 2000, Congress reaffirmed the broad scope of the commodity definition in adding the term “excluded commodity” to the CEA—which, despite the name,
is
a commodity.
[
9
]
This term includes, among other indices and measures, any “occurrence, extent of an occurrence, or contingency” of financial, commercial, or economic consequence that is beyond the control of any party to the relevant derivatives contract and is not based on a change in the price, rate, value, or level of a physical commodity.
[
10
]
Derivatives
(
printed page 66024)
contracts based on these “ excluded commodities” are subject to the Commission's jurisdiction just as derivatives based on other commodities are.
The definition of “excluded commodity” makes clear that events that fall within the definition, including those related to sports, politics, culture, and weather, are themselves commodities.
[
11
]
The CFTC has a long history of regulating event contracts. “Since 1992, Commission-regulated exchanges have listed for trading a variety of commodity futures and options contracts with payout terms based on” events “as diverse as regional insured property losses, the count of bankruptcies, temperature volatilities, corporate mergers, and corporate credit events,” and in subsequent years, event contracts encompassed “the accomplishment of certain scientific advances, world population levels, the adoption of particular pieces of legislation,” and even “the length of celebrity marriages.”
[
12
]
In 1993, the Commission issued a no-action letter to Iowa Electronic Markets, allowing the facility to list event contracts tied to U.S. and Canadian elections.
[
13
]
In 2004, the CFTC designated the first contract market (“DCM”) dedicated to listing contracts based on events that are excluded commodities.
[
14
]
Initially, these contracts were structured as commodity options known as “binary options,” the cash settlement of which was based on whether a specified event had occurred.
[
15
]
Under the plain language of the CEA, event contracts are implicated by four clauses of the “swap” definition.
First, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(ii) defines “swap” to include “any agreement, contract, or transaction . . . that provides for any purchase, sale, payment, or delivery (other than a dividend on an equity security) that is dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
[
16
]
Second, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(i) includes binary options and other commodity options in the “swap” definition by including “any agreement, contract, or transaction . . . that is a put, call, cap, floor, collar, or similar option of any kind that is for the purchase or sale, or based on the value, of 1 or more interest or other rates, currencies, commodities, securities, instruments of indebtedness, indices, quantitative measures, or other financial or economic interests or property of any kind.”
[
17
]
Third, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(iv) includes in the “swap” definition “an agreement, contract, or transaction that is, or in the future becomes, commonly known to the trade as a swap.”
[
18
]
Finally, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(vi) makes clear that the “swap” definition includes “any combination or permutation of, or option on, any agreement, contract, or transaction described in any of clauses (i) through (v)” of CEA section 1a(47)(A).
[
19
]
In addition to the “swap” definitions provided by the statute, the Dodd-Frank Act included several provisions that give the Commission authority to further define “swap.” First, Dodd-Frank Act section 712(d)(2),
15 U.S.C. 8302(d)(1)
, directs the CFTC and SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, to “further define” the term “swap.”
[
20
]
Second, Dodd-Frank Act section 721(b),
15 U.S.C. 8321(a)(2)
, permits the CFTC to define any term included in an amendment to the CEA in Subtitle A of the Wall Street Transparency and Accountability Act of 2010, which includes the term “swap.” Third, Dodd-Frank Act section 721(b),
15 U.S.C. 8321(b)
, directs the CFTC to further define “swap” to include transactions and entities that have been structured to evade Subtitle A.
In recent months, States have taken actions and courts have issued rulings that undermine the CFTC's jurisdiction over event contracts. The State of Minnesota enacted a criminal prohibition on the operation or facilitation of a “prediction market,” which purports to make it a felony to offer event contracts on athletic events, elections, policymaking decisions, and a variety of other events.
[
21
]
The State of Arizona filed a “twenty-count criminal information” against a DCM in Arizona Superior Court for offering event contracts on sports and elections in the State.
[
22
]
The State of New York sought a temporary restraining order in State court that would prohibit a DCM from offering event “contracts relating to sports, culture, elections, and other events” “within or from New York or to persons in New York.”
[
23
]
Because that DCM is headquartered in New York, that relief threatens to prohibit it from offering event contracts nationwide. That same DCM has also been ordered by State trial courts to geofence its offering of sports-related event contracts in the States of Michigan, Washington, and Nevada.
[
24
]
(
printed page 66025)
To date, three Federal courts of appeals have issued rulings concerning whether an event contract whose underlying is related to an outcome of a sporting event is a swap under CEA section 1a(47)(A)(ii). In April 2026, a divided panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit held in
KalshiEX, LLC
v.
Flaherty
that because “sports-related event contracts are traded on a CFTC-licensed DCM and depend on event outcomes associated with economic consequences, they fit within the Act's definition of `swaps' subject to the CFTC's jurisdiction.”
[
25
]
The dissenting judge also agreed that a “plain reading of the Act's text suggests that [ ] sports-event contracts fit comfortably within the statutory definition.”
[
26
]
In August 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit adopted the opposite interpretation of CEA section 1a(47)(A)(ii).
[
27
]
After acknowledging that “the CEA expressly preempts state law regulating swaps `traded or executed on' a DCM,” the court rejected the “dictionary definitions” and “plain-language appeal” of the Third Circuit's interpretation and concluded that, as used in the CEA, “event” means something different from “a thing that happens or takes place.”
[
28
]
The court stated that the “substance” of the sports event contracts at issue was “sports gambling, regardless of whether [the DCM] calls them swaps” (and, by inference, regardless of whether the CFTC regulates them as swaps).
[
29
]
It expressed concern that the plain-text interpretation of the definition swap would subject bingo games and ping-pong matches to the CFTC's jurisdiction.
[
30
]
For these and other reasons involving the court's understanding of the CEA's “context” and “history,”
[
31
]
the court ultimately “conclude[d] that these sports event contracts are likely not swaps under the CEA.”
[
32
]
The Ninth Circuit did not address whether sports event contracts could qualify as swaps under other prongs of the CEA swap definition, including sections 1a(47)(A)(i) and (iv). A petition for rehearing and rehearing en banc has been filed in that case.
[
33
]
In September 2026, a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit also held that sports-related event contracts are not “swaps,” albeit for somewhat different reasons than the Ninth Circuit panel.
[
34
]
Unlike the Ninth Circuit, the Sixth Circuit acknowledged that “[d]ictionaries commonly define an `event' to include an ‘outcome,’ ” and “nothing in the statutory text provides a clear indication that the event must be defined to exclude outcomes.”
[
35
]
Thus, “it would be reasonable to describe the Giants winning the Super Bowl” as an “event,” even if it is also “the outcome of the game.”
[
36
]
However, the court held that sports events are not “associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence,” explaining that the relevant event must be “
inherently
associated with a ‘financial, economic, or commercial consequence.’ ”
[
37
]
As the above discussion demonstrates, there is widespread confusion and disuniformity about the definition of swap. The Commission therefore proposes to exercise its statutory authority to “further define” swap and expressly clarify that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps.
Statutory Authority
Section 712(d)(1) of the Dodd-Frank Act provides that the Commission and the SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, shall jointly further define, among other terms, the term “swap.”
[
38
]
Section 712(d)(2)(A) further empowers the Commission and the SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, to “jointly adopt such other rules regarding such definitions as the [CFTC and SEC] determine are necessary and appropriate, in the public interest, and for the protection of investors.”
[
39
]
II. Proposed Rule
The Commission is proposing to further define the term swap in the context of event contracts. Specifically, the Commission proposes to add new paragraph (2)(i)(G) to the definition of “swap” in § 1.3 of the Commission's regulations.
[
40
]
This proposed addition identifies as swaps event contracts, including, in a non-exhaustive list, those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events.
[
41
]
As discussed in more detail below, event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are financial instruments that are commonly known to the trade as swaps, structured as binary options, and/or structured to make payment dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence. It is the Commission's view that the best reading of the statute is that event contracts based on sports-, political-, cultural-, or weather-related events qualify as swaps under each of these statutory prongs. In addition, the Commission's exercise of its express statutory authority to “further define” the term “swap” provides an independent legal basis to deem these contracts as swaps.
[
42
]
First, the Commission believes that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events are “commonly known to the trade as a swap” within the meaning of prong (iv) of the swap definition.
[
43
]
The Commission
(
printed page 66026)
understands the phrase “commonly known to the trade as a swap” as a residual, catch-all prong intended to cover instruments that, in the market's view, are swaps.
[
44
]
The Commission further understands “the trade” in this context to mean those who participate in the derivatives markets, including the CFTC, its registrants, and traders, rather than some broader group, such as the general public.
[
45
]
Furthermore, the Commission notes that this standard does not require universal recognition—“commonly known” is not the same as “universally known.” In this regard, the scope of prong (iv) should be informed by the actual practice of market participants and the longstanding regulatory treatment of instruments by the CFTC.
For decades, the CFTC's position has been that event contracts are derivatives subject to its jurisdiction, whether as “swaps” or as “binary options” (which are themselves swaps).
[
46
]
The CFTC's 1993 no-action letter to Iowa Electronic Markets allowed the facility to list event contracts tied to U.S. and Canadian elections.
[
47
]
The CFTC issued a concept release in 2008 acknowledging its regulatory-oversight responsibility for event contracts.
[
48
]
It approved event contracts on box-office receipts in 2010.
[
49
]
The Commission also issued an order penalizing Blockratize, Inc. (d/b/a
Polymarket.com
) for offering event contracts on various economic, political, and sports events without registering with the Commission, explaining that the event contracts “constitute swaps under the CFTC's jurisdiction.”
[
50
]
Furthermore, the CFTC has filed civil-enforcement actions and obtained civil penalties against persons that engage in insider trading or manipulative activity around event contracts.
[
51
]
The United States has also brought commodity-fraud charges for insider trading of event contracts on the theory that event contracts are swaps under the CEA.
[
52
]
Market participants have also overwhelmingly recognized that event contracts are swaps by complying with the CFTC's swap regulatory regime just as they do when listing, clearing, or trading other swaps. For example, over the past several years, DCMs have self-certified thousands of event contracts based on sports, politics, cultural events, and weather to the Commission.
[
53
]
This includes both new entrants into the market and longstanding exchanges like CME Group (“CME”), which has self-certified numerous event contracts based on sports and elections as swaps.
[
54
]
And in comments to the CFTC, CME has recognized that “event contracts and swaps are not new and have been subject to the existing regulatory scheme for years without issue,” and that the CEA's “Core Principles[ ] provide[ ] the proper structure to regulate these products.”
[
55
]
Cboe Global Markets has likewise stated in comments that event contracts “generally fall within the CEA's broad definition of `swap,' ” absent a statutory exception.
[
56
]
Consistent with this commonly held market view, such Commission registrants have not sought to register at the State level or offer products under State gambling laws. Instead, they offer event contracts for multilateral trading on a national, competitive market, just like other derivatives.
Other market participants likewise treat event contracts as swaps and trade them as they do other derivatives products. For example, institutional traders act as market makers on prediction markets—earning revenue by capturing the bid-ask spread directly from peer-to-peer trading volume, unlike traditional sports betting where centralized sportsbooks extract a static “vig” from fixed odds. Similar to how such firms provide liquidity in other financial markets, these participants support price discovery based on shifting supply and demand rather than odds manually adjusted by a bookmaker.
[
57
]
And a wide array of market participants
[
58
]
have looked to prediction markets to hedge various risks, including those related to sports, weather, and legislative outcomes.
[
59
]
Together, the Commission preliminarily concludes that this market practice provides compelling evidence that such event contracts are, in fact, commonly known to the trade as swaps, satisfying prong (iv).
[
60
]
(
printed page 66027)
Second, the Commission believes that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, fall within prong (ii) of the swap definition, which encompasses any agreement, contract, or transaction whose underlying is an occurrence or contingency “associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
[
61
]
The Third Circuit's
Flaherty
decision adopted this conclusion in the context of sports-related event contracts, and the reasoning applies more generally as well. Applying the plain text of the statute, the court held that “[t]he outcome of a sports event certainly can be associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence,” and that sports-related event contracts traded on a CFTC-licensed DCM “fit within the Act's definition of `swaps' subject to the CFTC's jurisdiction.”
[
62
]
In reaching that conclusion, the court expressly endorsed the district court's identification of the broad range of economic stakeholders—including sponsors, advertisers, television networks, sports franchises, and local and national communities—whose financial interests are directly affected by sporting event outcomes, finding that identification of such stakeholders was sufficient to satisfy the “associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence” standard.
[
63
]
Even the dissent conceded that a plain reading of the Act's text suggests that sports-related event contracts fit comfortably within the statutory definition.
[
64
]
And the court confirmed that the Commission's statutory authority to further define “swap” would be valuable in this area.
While the Sixth and Ninth Circuit panels took a different view of section 1a(47)(A)(ii) of the CEA, their reasoning was substantially based on the concern that treating sports event contracts as swaps would also subject casino-style gambling to the CFTC's jurisdiction.
[
65
]
As the Commission explains in a separate Interim Final Rule, the swap definition does not encompass casino-style gambling wagers, sports or otherwise.
[
66
]
Additionally, the Ninth Circuit relied on CFTC Rule 40.11 to conclude that “gaming-related contracts” are “bar[red]” from “being listed on a DCM.”
[
67
]
Even assuming that premise, the Commission notes that CFTC Rule 40.11 does not provide a basis to conclude that event contracts are not swaps or that event contracts could be subject to State gambling law. Indeed, as the concurrence and other courts have recognized, the statutory provision that undergirds CFTC Rule 40.11 affirmatively contemplates that event contracts are swaps subject to the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction.
[
68
]
Regardless, to the extent that the Ninth Circuit panel's reasoning was based on a CFTC regulation, this Proposal would serve to clarify by federal regulation that event contracts are swaps. Accordingly, there would no longer be a valid basis to interpret CFTC regulations to conclude that event contracts are not swaps.
Third, the Commission believes that event contracts may independently satisfy the first prong of the swap definition. The Commission's preliminary reasoning is based on a plain reading of section 1a(47)(A)(i) of the CEA. Section 1a(47)(A)(i) explicitly defines a swap to include any agreement, contract, or transaction that is a “put, call, cap, floor, collar, or similar option of any kind” that is “based on the value[ ] of 1 or more . . . commodities . . . or other financial or economic interests or property of any kind.”
[
69
]
In this regard, the Commission notes that many event contracts are structured as binary options, meaning that the contract's payout is a predetermined fixed amount (typically, one dollar) if the underlying condition is satisfied, and zero if it is not. Courts
[
70
]
and the CFTC
[
71
]
have repeatedly affirmed that binary option event contracts are a type of swap subject to the Commission's jurisdiction. Because, as described above, an event (such as a sports-, politics-, cultural-, or weather-related event) is an excluded commodity, a binary option event contract referencing such an event is a swap within the Commission's jurisdiction.
The term “excluded commodity,” including “an occurrence, extent of an occurrence, or contingency . . . that is—(I) beyond the control of the parties to the relevant contract, agreement, or transaction; and (II) associated with a financial, commercial, or economic consequence,” has long been interpreted broadly. This definition was added to the CEA by the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 (“CFMA”).
[
72
]
The CFMA provided for a near-complete exemption from the exchange trading requirement for swaps in an “excluded commodity” between institutional traders.
[
73
]
In other words, these commodities are defined as “excluded” because the CFMA exempted swaps involving them from the exchange trading requirement.
However, swaps in excluded commodities remained within the jurisdiction of the CFTC. The CEA, as amended by the CFMA in 2000, provided that off-exchange swaps in “excluded commodities” between institutional traders would remain subject to CEA sections 5b and 12(e)(2).
[
74
]
Notably, CEA section 12(e)(2) provided at that time that the CEA “shall supersede and preempt the application of any State or local law that prohibits or regulates gaming or the operation of bucket shops (other than antifraud provisions of general applicability) in the case of . . . (B) an agreement, contract, or transaction that is excluded from this chapter under section . . . 2(d) . . . of this title . . . (regardless of whether any such agreement, contract, or transaction is otherwise subject to this chapter).”
[
75
]
Thus, in 2000, Congress clarified that the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction
(
printed page 66028)
preempted State law—even as to off-exchange transactions—by explicitly providing that State gaming laws would not apply to off-exchange swaps in excluded commodities between institutional traders.
The CFMA was driven by the November 1999 report of the President's Working Group on Financial Markets, which was composed of the Secretary of the Treasury, and the Chairs of the CFTC, the SEC, and the Federal Reserve Board (“PWG Report”).
[
76
]
The PWG Report concluded, among other things, that off-exchange swaps between institutional traders should be excluded from the CEA, unless the swap involves a non-financial commodity with a finite supply.
[
77
]
The “excluded commodity” definition enacted in the CFMA was therefore intended to encompass all types of swaps except for those based on non-financial commodities with a finite supply.
In 2010, the Dodd-Frank Act created a framework within the CEA for the on-exchange execution, clearing and reporting of the previously over-the-counter (“OTC”) swap markets. Among other things, the Dodd-Frank Act repealed the exclusion that had been added by the CFMA to CEA section 2(d),
[
78
]
and required retail swap transactions (
i.e.,
transactions not between eligible contract participants (“ECPs”)) to be entered into on a DCM.
[
79
]
Finally, the Special Rule added by Dodd-Frank to the CEA clarifies that the CFTC has jurisdiction over “[e]vent contracts,” including event contracts based on non-financial commodities. The Special Rule provides that “[i]n connection with the listing of agreements, contracts, transactions, or
swaps
in
excluded commodities
that are based upon the occurrence, extent of an occurrence, or contingency (other than a change in the price, rate, value, or levels of a commodity described in section 1a(2)(i) of this title), by a designated contract market or swap execution facility, the Commission may determine that such agreements, contracts, or transactions are contrary to the public interest if the agreements, contracts, or transactions involve—(I) activity that is unlawful under any Federal or State law; (II) terrorism; (III) assassination; (IV) war; (V) gaming; or (VI) other similar activity determined by the Commission, by rule or regulation, to be contrary to the public interest.
[
80
]
This rule confirms that the term “excluded commodities” includes “occurrence[s]” that “involve” various non-financial events, including but not limited to terrorism, assassination, war, and gaming. It also confirms that “swaps” can be “based upon” such non-financial activities. Thus, the notion that the “event” referred to in the second prong of the “swap” definition must “be one inherently associated with a financial, economic, or commercial consequence” is incompatible with the text of the Special Rule.
[
81
]
The Special Rule has particular significance for sports-related event contracts. Applying the plain text of the statute, sports are a type of “gam[e].”
[
82
]
Accordingly, sports-related event contracts are “based upon” an “occurrence, extent of an occurrence, or contingency” that “involve[s]” “gaming.” Far from exempting sports-related contracts from the CFTC's jurisdiction, this provision confirms that such instruments can be “swaps” in “excluded commodities” and that they are within the CFTC's jurisdiction.
[
83
]
Some courts and States have expressed the view that some, but not all, event contracts are swaps on the theory that certain underlying sports, political, cultural, or weather events are not associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.
[
84
]
This argument would at most affect the applicability of the first and second prongs of the “swap” definition, but it would not affect the fourth prong,
i.e.,
that the contracts are commonly known to the trade as a “swap.” Furthermore, to the extent there is uncertainty about whether particular underlying sports, political, cultural, or weather events have potential financial consequences, the Commission's exercise of its power to further define “swap” confers on the Commission the authority to determine which contracts qualify as “swaps.”
The Commission also notes that it retains authority under the Special Rule to prohibit event contracts involving “gaming” that are contrary to the public interest, and that the Commission has proposed to consider whether a contract has utility for price discovery, hedging, and economic decisions in making public-interest determinations.
[
85
]
Indeed, that proposal distinguishes between sports event contracts “depend[ing] on the aggregate performance over an extended period of play”—which “may serve price discovery functions and provide meaningful information”—from “event contracts settling on the type of a specific play called for or executed by a specific player or team, the type or outcome of a specific pitch thrown by a specific pitcher, the outcome of a specific shot taken by a specific player, or whether a specific player or team commits a specific foul or penalty”—which, among other things, “do not provide meaningful information.”
[
86
]
The Commission also preliminarily believes there typically are potential financial, economic, or commercial consequences associated with underlying sports, political, cultural, and weather events that are the subject of event contracts. Importantly, the statute uses the word “potential,” which is broad.
[
87
]
So even if the financial consequences of a particular event are not felt right away—indeed, even if they never
actually
occur—an event contract remains a swap so long as there is potential for commercial ramifications.
[
88
]
For example, it may be difficult to empirically verify that there are financial consequences associated with a particular city reaching a temperature of 97 to 98 degrees on a given day, as opposed to 95 to 96 degrees. By inserting the word “potential” into the swap definition, Congress signaled that it did not wish
(
printed page 66029)
for the Commission to engage in this exercise. Temperature has the potential to cause financial consequences for agriculture, energy usage, participation in outdoor activity, and more—event contracts based on temperature therefore satisfy the “potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence” requirement.
Sports events likewise can be associated with potential economic consequences. Most obviously, when a team succeeds in the postseason, that team is able to play more home games, which generates additional ticketing revenue for the franchise and economic opportunity for nearby businesses like restaurants and hotels.
[
89
]
For example, the New York Knicks' 2026 championship-winning postseason run generated around $380 million for New York City's economy.
[
90
]
Similarly, after the Milwaukee Bucks won the 2021 NBA Finals, the City of Milwaukee estimated that the team's postseason performance generated $2.7 million in economic impact to the city in the first round, $12.8 million in the second round, $14.1 million in the third round, and $28 million in the final round—thus, each time the Bucks won a round of the playoffs, there were concrete economic consequences for Milwaukee.
[
91
]
Postseason success also affects a sports team's valuation. Madison Square Garden Sports, the Knicks' parent company, doubled in market value over the course of a year because of the team's championship-winning performance.
[
92
]
At least at some level of generality, it is inescapably true that sports events are associated with potential economic consequences.
The result of single regular-season games are associated with potential economic consequences, too. Studies have verified that a single win in a college football game can result in millions of dollars in additional revenue to the program.
[
93
]
And when a team wins a game, that has direct commercial consequences for businesses around the stadium, as fans are more likely to spend money at those establishments in celebration.
In-game events and contingencies are also associated with potential economic consequences. For example, a close game is more likely to have higher television viewership than a blowout, and thus, the spread of a game is associated with potential economic consequences.
[
94
]
Player contracts often have bonuses associated with specific statistical results, like the number of touchdowns scored or receptions made, so player performance within a game has potential economic consequences.
[
95
]
Business promotions can amplify these economic consequences. For example, a furniture store in Houston, Texas, runs a regular promotion in which customers who spend a minimum amount will get their purchases refunded if the Houston Astros win the World Series, creating a direct link between the outcome of the World Series and financial consequences for numerous furniture purchasers in Houston.
[
96
]
Similarly, a New York bar promised free drinks to patrons if the Knicks won the first NBA Finals game, which also linked the outcome of the game to an economic consequence.
[
97
]
Businesses also structure promotions around whether particular events occur within a game. For example, when the Cincinnati Reds hit a home run in the 4th inning, ticketholders get a reward from Chick-fil-A,
[
98
]
when the Minnesota Vikings intercept a pass, Caribou Coffee offers a buy-one-get-one drink deal,
[
99
]
and Delta Air Lines' loyalty program customers earn one mile for each Seattle Seahawks passing yard in a season.
[
100
]
The list of examples could extend indefinitely. The salient point is that many sports-, politics-, cultural, and weather-related events are associated with potential economic consequences, and thus event contracts that are predicated on those events are swaps subject to the Commission's exclusive jurisdiction. To the extent a sports-, politics-, cultural-, or weather-related event is not associated with a potential economic consequence and does not satisfy any other prong of the swap definition, the Commission retains authority to stay the listing of that contract.
[
101
]
For these reasons, the Commission is proposing to amend the “swap” definition to explicitly identify event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, as swaps within the Commission's jurisdiction. Specifically, the Commission proposes to add paragraph (2)(i)(G) to § 1.3's definition of “swap”
[
102
]
to provide that the term swap includes “[e]vent contracts, including those based o\n sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events.” And, as set forth in a separate Interim Final Rule,
[
103
]
the Commission does not intrude upon existing regulation of in-person and online casino-style gambling by doing so. Rather, the Commission proposes, consistent with its clear statutory mandate, to regulate only event contracts, including those based on
(
printed page 66030)
sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events.
The classifications proposed here are for purposes of the Commodity Exchange Act. Federal tax treatment and associated information reporting, withholding, registration, and payment obligations are determined under the Internal Revenue Code and applicable Treasury regulations and Internal Revenue Service guidance.

C. Consideration of Benefits and Costs
1. Introduction
The Commission is mindful of the economic effects, including the benefits and costs, of the Proposal. Section 15(a) of the CEA requires the Commission to consider the benefits and costs of its actions before promulgating a regulation under the CEA or issuing certain orders.
[
117
]
As required by section 15(a), the Commission evaluates these benefits and costs evaluated in light of five broad areas of market and public concern: (1) protection of market participants and the public; (2) efficiency, competitiveness, and financial integrity of futures markets; (3) price discovery; (4) sound risk management practices; and (5) other public interest considerations.
The Proposal further defines the term “swap” under CEA section 1a(47) to include event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events.
[
118
]
It is the
(
printed page 66031)
Commission's preliminary belief that the Proposal would not change the legal rights or obligations of market participants under the CEA because the Commission already treats event contracts as swaps under existing law. Instead, the Commission preliminarily believes that the Proposal will reduce interpretive uncertainty and facilitate uniform nationwide treatment of event contracts under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Commission.
The Commission qualitatively discusses the benefits and costs of the Proposal below because it is not practicable to quantify the effect of greater regulatory certainty on market participant behavior.
2. Baseline
The baseline against which the benefits and costs of the Proposal are measured consists of the current regulatory framework and the current state of the event contracts market.
a. Regulatory Baseline
The Commission has exclusive jurisdiction to regulate transactions involving swaps (other than security-based swaps, which the SEC regulates, and mixed swaps, over which it shares jurisdiction with the SEC).
[
119
]
The Commission preliminary believes that under the plain language of the CEA, event contracts, including event contracts based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps.
[
120
]
For example, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(ii) defines “swap” to include “any agreement, contract, or transaction . . . that provides for any purchase, sale, payment, or delivery (other than a dividend on an equity security) that is dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
[
121
]
It is the Commission's preliminary belief that this comprehensive definition captures many event contracts, which are a type of swap where payment is triggered by “the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence,” such as a political election or a sporting event.
[
122
]
Accordingly, it is the Commission's preliminary belief that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are subject to Federal law concerning swaps, including that retail participants may only trade swaps on a DCM.
[
123
]
DCMs listing event contracts must comply with the substantive and procedural requirements that apply to a DCM's listing of derivative contracts for trading.
[
124
]
In particular, these requirements include adherence to the Core Principles for DCMs, including listing only contracts that are not readily susceptible to manipulation, preventing market disruption, and protecting of markets and market participants.
[
125
]
However, certain State regulators have asserted that certain event contracts—particularly those based on sports-related events—are subject to their laws regulating gaming and other matters. These other legal regimes have various, sometimes conflicting, requirements that states have purported to apply to event contracts.
[
126
]
b. Current Event Contract Markets
The number of DCMs listing event contracts and the volume of trading in such contracts have increased significantly in recent years. For example, as of September 1, 2026, at least seven DCMs registered with the CFTC offer contracts that include event contracts based on sports-related events to U.S. persons. More than fifteen pending DCM applications have been filed since 2025. Many of these newly designated DCMs and platforms with pending applications have stated they intend to offer contracts that could be considered event contracts. In August 2026, average monthly trading volume in event contracts was about $1.5 billion across all DCMs reporting to the Commission.
[
127
]
Of that volume, approximately $1.2 billion was in event contracts based on sports-related events; approximately $11 million was in event contracts based on politics-related events, including elections-related event contracts; and approximately $4 million was in event contracts based on weather-related events.
[
128
]
3. Benefits
Because the Commission does not expect the Proposal to change the legal rights or obligations of market participants under the CEA, it is the Commission's preliminary belief that the primary benefit of this Proposal would be added certainty that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps that are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the CFTC. Although the extent of the benefit may be limited by the ongoing efforts of certain state regulators to assert their jurisdiction over certain event contracts, market participants—including DCMs listing event contracts— may benefit by spending less time and fewer resources determining which regulatory regime applies and by saving the costs of complying with various State regulatory regimes.
4. Costs
It is the Commission's preliminary belief that there should be negligible costs from codifying that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps subject to the Commission's exclusive jurisdiction, as there would be no expected changes required of market participants under the CEA or the Commission's regulations.
However, the Proposal may result in indirect costs to the extent that market participants respond to the added certainty by shifting activity toward the CFTC swaps framework. For example, States might receive less fee and other revenue if entities choose to structure their business operations as DCMs instead of structuring their operations within State regulatory frameworks. It is also possible that costs could also result from the potential transition, generating short-term frictions. For example, market participants could incur reconciling costs where Federal and State regulatory regimes overlap during the transition, such as unwinding or
(
printed page 66032)
maintaining State licenses in parallel with CFTC-regulated obligations during the transition.
5. Section 15(a) Factors
a. Protection of Market Participants and the Public
The Commission preliminarily believes that classification certainty provided by the Proposal may allow market participants to more readily operate within the Federal swaps framework and its attendant protections. Insofar as this certainty leads to an increase in the number of event contracts listed on DCMs, the protection of market participants and the public may be advanced by application of the Core Principles to the market. However, certainty provided by the Proposal could be perceived as a safety signal by retail participants. This may raise risk appetite for certain categories of event contracts as retail market participants may update their beliefs about oversight of these products and under-weigh their inherent risk and increase their exposure to these products without parallel improvements in disclosure or education that could improve comprehension of risks related to event contracts based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, or weather-related events.
b. Efficiency, Competitiveness, and Financial Integrity of Futures Markets
The Commission preliminarily believes that the Proposal is unlikely to affect the efficiency or financial integrity of the futures markets, but there could be effects on the swaps market. To the extent that firms restructure their operations from State regimes to the Federal swaps regime, the Proposal could facilitate direct competition between CFTC-regulated DCMs and State-regulated businesses. However, because the Federal swaps regime requires infrastructure with fixed costs, certainty provided by the Proposal might favor incumbent DCMs with established infrastructure and customer bases. Furthermore, the Commission preliminarily believes that clarifying that event contracts are swaps may advantage exchanges already configured for Federal compliance relative to state-licensed platforms, shifting costs unevenly where new entrants may face higher fixed costs to reach swaps compliance scale, potentially reducing competitive pressure on fees, service quality, and innovation diversity at the margin.
c. Price Discovery
The Commission preliminarily believes that price discovery for event contracts will not be materially affected because the Proposal does not alter trading rules, exchange requirements, or information-dissemination obligations for the contracts it covers, which the Commission already expects to trade on DCMs subject to existing Core Principles.
d. Sound Risk Management Practices
The Commission preliminarily believes that risk management practices will not be materially affected because the Proposal does not alter the application of Commission requirements regarding risk management, including DCM risk-management Core Principles.
e. Other Public Interest Considerations
Codification of the Commission's understanding that event contracts, including those based on sports-, politics-, cultural-, and weather-related events, are swaps may improve legal predictability and administrability, consistent with the CEA's purpose of encouraging effective self-regulation of trading facilities, clearing systems, and market participants. The Commission preliminarily believes that the Proposal may reduce the resources market participants devote to complying with various, sometimes-contradictory State regulatory regimes.
But, insofar as the certainty provided by the Proposal increases the volume of event contracts listed on DCMs, the Commission preliminarily believes that retail market participants could be harmed because some event contract trading characteristics (such as outcomes occurring at unpredictable intervals, perception of skill-based decision making, near-miss experiences, and potential for loss-chasing behavior) can be associated with addictive potential. It is possible that these characteristics can lead to financial harm to participants who accumulate losses through high-frequency trading, allocate disproportionate resources to trading activity, and have trouble disengaging voluntarily.
6. Regulatory Alternatives
Given the Proposal seeks to articulate the Commission's existing jurisdiction over swaps, the Commission has not identified any viable regulatory alternatives.

129

Commodity Futures Trading Commission
17 CFR Part 1
RIN 3038-AF81
AGENCY:
Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
ACTION:
Interim final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“Commission” or “CFTC”) is adopting an interim final rule (“Interim Final Rule”) to codify its longstanding position that casino-style gambling products, including wagers placed on sportsbooks and casino games, are excluded from the “swap” definition.
DATES:
Effective Date:
This interim final rule is effective October 19, 2026.
Request for comment:
Comments must be received by November 18, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments, specifically referencing “Further Definition of `Swap' to Exclude Casino-Style Gambling Products” and RIN 3038-AF81, by any of the following methods:
Regulations.gov:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and press the “Search” button, then proceed as follows:
1. Under Refine Documents Results—check the box to “Only show documents open for comment”;
2. Under Agency—select “See More” and check the box for “Commodity Futures Trading Commission,” then press the Apply button;
3. Identify this proposal in the list of CFTC documents open for comment, press the “Comment” button to open the submission form, and follow the instructions on the form.
Alternatively, if you are viewing this proposal on
www.federalregister.gov
,
click the “Submit A Public Comment” button at the top of the page to open the comment form. Follow the instructions on the form to submit your comment to
Regulations.gov
.
Mail:
Send to—Christopher Kirkpatrick, Secretary of the Commission, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Three Lafayette Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581.
Hand Delivery/Courier:
Address to—CFTC Comment Submission, Attn: Christopher Kirkpatrick, Secretary of the Commission, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Three Lafayette Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581.
Please submit your comments using only one of these methods. To avoid possible delays with mail or in-person deliveries, submissions through
Regulations.gov
are encouraged.
All comments must be submitted in English or, if not, accompanied by an English translation. Do not include in your comment text or attachments any personal identifying information or business information that you do not want published online. Comments (regardless of submission method) will be published without review for, and without removal of, any personal identifying information or information your business may consider confidential.
