The CFTC reserves the right, but shall have no obligation, to review, pre-screen, filter, or redact all or any part of your comment submission. The CFTC also reserves the right, without further notification, to refuse to publish or to remove from public view all or any part of your submission to the extent it contains content inappropriate for publication in a comment file, such as—without limitation—obscene language, threats of violence, solicitations for commercial sales or illegal activity, or obvious spam. If a submission that is refused for or withdrawn from publication because of inappropriate content also contains comments on the merits of this proposal, such submission will be retained in the record for the matter and will be considered as required under the Administrative Procedure Act and other applicable laws, and may be accessible under the FOIA.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Tyler S. Badgley, General Counsel; Aaron M. Levine, Deputy General Counsel for Regulation,
rulemaking@cftc.gov
,
202-418-5000, Office of the General Counsel, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Three Lafayette Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Title VII of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (“Dodd-Frank Act”) established a comprehensive regulatory framework for swaps.
[
1
]
Section 712(d)(1) of the Dodd-Frank Act provides that the Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”), in consultation with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the “Federal Reserve Board”), shall jointly further define, among other terms, the term “swap.”
[
2
]
Pursuant to this requirement, in 2012, the Commission and the SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, issued a final rule further defining the term “swap” and other terms.
[
3
]
That rule addressed, among other topics, the treatment of certain traditional, non-derivatives products, agreements, contracts, and transactions that they concluded Congress did not intend to be regulated as swaps or security-based swaps, including insurance contracts and certain commercial and consumer transactions.
This Interim Final Rule arises in the context of the ongoing debate regarding the scope of the Commission's jurisdiction under the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”), particularly as it relates to event contracts. The CFTC generally has found that many event contracts, including those based on sports-related events, are covered by the CEA's swap definition.
[
4
]
The CEA contains six definitions of “swap,” at least four of which are applicable to event contracts.
First, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(i) includes binary options and other commodity options in the “swap” definition by including “any agreement, contract, or transaction . . . that is a put, call, cap, floor, collar, or similar option of any kind that is for the purchase or sale, or based on the value, of 1 or more interest or other rates, currencies, commodities, securities, instruments of indebtedness, indices, quantitative measures, or other financial or economic interests or property of any kind.”
[
5
]
Second, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(ii) defines “swap” to include “any agreement, contract, or transaction . . . that provides for any purchase, sale, payment, or delivery (other than a dividend on an equity security) that is dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
[
6
]
Third, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(iv) includes in the “swap” definition “an agreement, contract, or transaction that is, or in the future becomes, commonly known to the trade as a swap.”
[
7
]
Fourth, CEA section 1a(47)(A)(vi) makes clear that the “swap” definition includes “any combination or permutation of, or option on, any agreement, contract, or transaction described in any of clauses (i) through (v)” of CEA section 1a(47)(A).
[
8
]
In addition to the “swap” definitions provided by the statute, the Dodd-Frank Act included several provisions that give the Commission authority to further define “swap.” First, Dodd-Frank Act section 712(d)(2),
15 U.S.C. 8302(d)(1)
, directs the CFTC and SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, to “further define” the term “swap.”
[
9
]
Second, Dodd-Frank Act section 721(b),
15 U.S.C. 8321(a)(2)
, permits the CFTC to define any term included in an amendment to the CEA in Subtitle A of the Wall Street Transparency and Accountability Act of 2010, which includes the term “swap.” Third, Dodd-Frank Act section 721(b),
15 U.S.C. 8321(b)
, directs the CFTC to
(
printed page 65971)
further define “swap” to include transactions and entities that have been structured to evade Subtitle A.
In recent months, many have expressed concern that a natural, plain-text interpretation of the “swap” definition would necessarily encompass casino-style gambling products and, finding that consequence untenable, have diverged from the plain text of the statute. For example, the Sixth Circuit in
KalshiEX LLC
v.
Schuler
viewed sports event contracts as legally indistinguishable from casino-style sports wagers; and thus it expressed concern that, if sports event contracts are swaps,
any
sports wager—including “every sports wager placed in a casino, on an online sports book, or between two friends at a bar”—would need to “take place on federal markets.”
[
10
]
Indeed, the Sixth Circuit explained, a person would commit a felony by engaging in gambling off a designated contract market (“DCM”).
[
11
]
Thus, the Sixth Circuit believed that its atextual interpretation of the “swap” definition would avoid “attach[ing] criminal penalties to a breathtaking amount of commonplace gambling activity.”
[
12
]
The Ninth Circuit similarly reasoned in
KalshiEX, LLC
v.
Assad
that sports event contracts and casino-style sports wagering are indistinguishable, finding that the “substance” of the sports event contracts at issue was “sports gambling, regardless of whether [the DCM] calls them swaps” (and, by inference, regardless of whether the CFTC regulates them as swaps).
[
13
]
And because “there is not a difference under the CEA's swap definition between sports betting on Kalshi and sports betting in Caesar's Sportsbook, then every person placing a sports bet at Caesar's Sportsbook (or anywhere else for that matter) is violating the CEA.”
[
14
]
The court also expressed concern that “bingo games and pingpong matches” would fall under CFTC jurisdiction.
[
15
]
For these and other reasons involving the court's understanding of the CEA's “context” and “history,”
[
16
]
the court ultimately “conclude[d] that these sports event contracts are likely not swaps under the CEA.”
[
17
]
Exploiting this lack of clarity, certain States have asserted that event contracts traded or executed on a DCM should be State regulated (rather than federally regulated under the CEA). These States argue that if the Commission has jurisdiction over event contracts, that would necessarily subject casino-style sports wagers—traditionally regulated by the States—to the Commission's jurisdiction as well. For example, in response to a Commission proposed rulemaking, 40 States and the District of Columbia submitted a comment, arguing that sports event contracts are “indistinguishable from traditional sports betting.”
[
18
]
The State of New Jersey recently argued to the United States Supreme Court that “[n]othing in the [CEA] gives the CFTC unprecedented authority to become the sole regulator of sports gambling in this country.”
[
19
]
And the Commonwealth of Kentucky has claimed that determining that event contracts are swaps under the CEA amounts to “[t]ransferring every ounce of authority over sports wagering from the States to the CFTC.”
[
20
]
There also appears to be confusion within the gaming industry. The American Gaming Association has argued that if “sports wagers qualify as `swaps,' the CEA would require
all
sports bets—including those placed on the Las Vegas Strip—to be traded on DCMs.”
[
21
]
In its view, there is “no plausible statutory basis to distinguish retail sports bets from identical wagers placed on [a DCM]—if the latter are swaps, the former must be as well.”
[
22
]
As the above discussion demonstrates, there is widespread confusion regarding whether the definition of a swap includes casino-style gambling products, including wagers placed on sportsbooks and casino games, traditionally regulated at the State level. In this regard, many courts, States, and private businesses are currently operating under the erroneous premise that if event contracts are swaps, then casino-style gambling products must also be swaps subject to CFTC jurisdiction. That premise has led courts and States to deviate from the plain text of the “swap” definition and impose atextual limitations on the concept of an “event” that is “associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
[
23
]
To address this misunderstanding, this Interim Final Rule affirms and codifies the Commission's longstanding position that casino-style gambling products, including sports-wagering contracts entered into on a sportsbook and casino games, are not swaps and do not fall within the CFTC's jurisdiction. This action is intended to remove regulatory ambiguity and clarify the boundaries between the Commission's jurisdiction over the derivatives markets and State and Tribal jurisdiction over casino-style gambling.
The Commission notes that this approach is supported by a decision of the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit in
KalshiEX, LLC
v.
Flaherty,
which held that “sports-related event contracts are traded on a CFTC-licensed DCM and depend on event outcomes associated with economic consequences” and therefore “fit within the Act's definition of `swaps' subject to the CFTC's jurisdiction.”
[
24
]
In response to the State's concern that “anything from bingo games to pingpong matches will fall under the CFTC's jurisdiction,” the court observed that ”[i]n such far-fetched scenarios, Congress's express delegation to the CTFC and the Securities and Exchange Commission to `further define' swaps would prove useful,” and it cited the Commission's 2012 rulemaking excluding insurance contracts and consumer transactions.
[
25
]
Other courts have similarly recognized that the CEA applies to sports event contracts that “take[ ] the form of swaps,” even while the CEA “does not federalize all gambling, or even all sports gambling.”
[
26
]
This Interim Final Rule implements the Third Circuit's suggested approach.
Statutory Authority
Section 712(d)(1) of the Dodd-Frank Act provides that the Commission and the SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, “shall further define,” among other terms, the term
(
printed page 65972)
“swap.”
[
27
]
Section 712(d)(2)(A) further empowers the Commission and the SEC, in consultation with the Federal Reserve Board, to “jointly adopt such other rules regarding such definitions as the [CFTC and SEC] determine are necessary and appropriate, in the public interest, and for the protection of investors.”
[
28
]
II. Interim Final Rule
The Commission is issuing this Interim Final Rule to further define the term “swap” to explicitly exclude casino-style gambling products, including sports-wagering contracts entered into on a sportsbook, from the swap definition. By enacting this Interim Final Rule, the Commission seeks to reiterate its longstanding position that its oversight of federally regulated derivatives markets does not intrude upon the traditional State and Tribal regulation of casino-style gambling products.
Though Congress deliberately drafted a broad definition of a swap,
[
29
]
the CFTC's jurisdiction is not boundless. The Commission has always acknowledged that certain instruments may, on their face, plausibly fit within the definition of “swap” in CEA section 1a(47), but that the swap definition is best read to exclude that instrument in light of statutory context and a longstanding tradition of regulation by another regulator. Gambling products offered by State or Tribe-licensed casino operators and sportsbooks fit this mold.
Insurance serves as a prime precedent.
[
30
]
On its face, prong (ii) of the “swap” definition could plausibly be read to encompass insurance contracts, because they make “payment” “dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
[
31
]
Given that potential ambiguity, when the Commission and the SEC jointly further defined the term “swap” in 2012, the agencies explicitly noted that they did not interpret prong (ii) of the swap definition
[
32
]
“to mean that products historically regulated as insurance products should be included.”
[
33
]
The Commission and the SEC further emphasized that nothing in the Dodd-Frank Act “suggest[ed] that Congress intended for traditional insurance products to be regulated as swaps.”
[
34
]
Consequently, the Commission and the SEC specifically carved out traditional insurance products from the swap definition by relying on core factual and structural differences to distinguish them from derivatives. A foundational distinction was whether the instrument is traded: the Commission and the SEC noted that “insurance products traditionally have not been entered into on or subject to the rules of an organized exchange nor traded in secondary market transactions (
i.e.,
they are not traded on an organized market or over the counter),” whereas swaps are routinely traded on such venues.
[
35
]
Furthermore, the Commission and SEC emphasized that “all or part of swaps and security-based swaps are novated or assigned to third parties, usually pursuant to industry standard terms and documents.” In other words, swaps can be centrally cleared, unlike insurance contracts.
[
36
]
The Commission and the SEC also relied on the fact that insurance products are “provided by a person that is subject to supervision by the insurance commissioner (or similar official or agency) of any state or by the United States” and are “regulated as insurance under applicable state law or the laws of the United States.”
[
37
]
The agencies clarified, however, that other instruments providing substantially similar economic exposure to an insurance contract—such as certain credit default swaps—remain within the swap definition and subject to the CFTC's jurisdiction.
[
38
]
The Commission and the SEC took a similar approach to “consumer and commercial agreements that historically have not been considered swaps or security-based swaps” but nonetheless “may have attributes that could be viewed as falling within the swap or security-based swap definition.”
[
39
]
Examples included “acquisitions or sales of property (tangible and intangible), provisions of services, employment of individuals, and other matters that could be viewed as falling within the definitions.”
[
40
]
The Commission and the SEC excluded these contracts on the ground that they did “not believe Congress intended to include these types of customary consumer and commercial agreements, contracts, or transactions in the swap or security-based swap definition,” again highlighting the “key” point that such transactions are “not traded on an organized market or over-the-counter.”
[
41
]
The Commissions adopted this interpretation to address, among other concerns, the possibility that customary consumer and commercial agreements, contracts, or transactions could be subject to the restriction in section 2(e) of the CEA on entering into swaps with persons who are not eligible contract participants (“ECPs”) other than on, or subject to the rules of, a DCM.
As explained in Part I, similar concerns have recently arisen in connection with traditional gambling products offered by State-regulated gambling companies and tribes. To address this concern, the Commission seeks to further clarify through this Interim Final Rule that casino-style gambling products are not within Commission's jurisdiction. As explained below, the same concerns that led the Commission to exclude insurance contracts and consumer and commercial agreements from the “swap” definition are equally applicable to gambling products.
First, and most fundamentally, gambling products do not bear the structural characteristics of a CEA-regulated derivative. Gambling products are typically conducted as bilateral transactions between a casino or bookkeeper (a “house”) and its customer rather than on an organized market.
[
42
]
Prices are not set by market forces and are not subject to negotiation; rather, customers must accept the price
(
printed page 65973)
set by the house. Because of these dynamics, gambling products are not inherently
tradable,
which is a strong indicator that these products are not swaps or any other kind of derivative within the Commission's jurisdiction.
[
43
]
Tradability is a material consideration in determining whether a financial instrument has the legal status of a derivative, as the Commission and SEC emphasized with respect to insurance contracts and consumer transactions. Although the CEA's “swap” definition does not itself contain a tradability requirement, interpreters of statutory text nonetheless must be guided by “[t]he broader context provided by other sections of the statute.”
[
44
]
The CEA's broader context repeatedly reinforces tradability as an important consideration in whether a particular contract qualifies as a swap.
[
45
]
For example, CEA section 2(e) makes it unlawful for any person, other than an ECP, to enter into a swap unless executed on, or subject to the rules of, a DCM.
[
46
]
Likewise, section 2(a)(1) of the CEA confers exclusive jurisdiction on the CFTC with respect to “accounts, agreements . . . , and transactions involving swaps or contracts of sale of a commodity for future delivery,” to the extent they are “traded or executed on a [DCM] or a swap execution facility.”
[
47
]
Furthermore, the CEA provides that the transactions subject to the Commission's exclusive jurisdiction serve a “national public interest by providing a means for managing and assuming price risks, discovering prices, or disseminating pricing information through trading in liquid, fair and financially secure trading facilities.”
[
48
]
Only tradable instruments—
i.e.,
those that are executed multilaterally or at least subject to negotiation—can serve those purposes.
The CEA's Core Principles also presuppose that derivatives are tradable instruments. Core Principle 9 for DCMs requires exchanges to provide “a competitive, open, and efficient market and mechanism for executing transactions that protects the price discovery process of trading in the centralized market.”
[
49
]
Gambling products are not offered through “trading” on “centralized market[s],” and prices for gambling products are not set by “a competitive, open, and efficient market”—they are unilaterally dictated by the casino or sportsbook. Other Core Principles for DCMs and swap execution facilities (“SEFs”) likewise presuppose the competitive trading of derivatives, which cannot be said of gambling products.
[
50
]
For these reasons, gambling products are not derivatives subject to its jurisdiction.
Second, the CEA contemplates that a swap can be cleared. Section 2(h) of the CEA provides that “[i]t shall be unlawful for any person to engage in a swap unless that person submits such swap for clearing to a derivatives clearing organization that is registered under this chapter or a derivatives clearing organization that is exempt from registration under this chapter if the swap is required to be cleared.”
[
51
]
Like insurance contracts, gambling products are not “cleared,” in that the wager obligation is not routinely transferred to a third party to eliminate counterparty credit risk and ensure contract fulfillment.
Third, there is no indication that “Congress intended to include [gambling products] in the swap . . . definition.”
[
52
]
To the contrary, Congress has long recognized a distinction between gambling products and derivatives contracts.
[
53
]
Furthermore, when Congress adopted the “swap” definition, it did so against a background of other federal statutory provisions regulating sports gambling, and the Commission does not presume Congress to have impliedly repealed those provisions.
[
54
]
Fourth, just as insurance products and consumer transactions have traditionally been subject to a distinct regulatory framework governed by State law, casino-style gambling products have historically been, and are, offered by State-licensed gambling venues or Tribes, and subject to a gambling-specific regulatory regime. Absent a more specific indication in the statutory text, the Commission does not presume that Congress intended to disrupt that federal-state balance.
[
55
]
Fifth, the “swap” definition also encompasses any “agreement, contract, or transaction that is, or in the future becomes, commonly known to the trade as a swap.”
[
56
]
The Commission is unaware of any trade usage or market belief that gambling products are considered swaps in the derivatives industry. To the contrary, DCMs and industry groups have repeatedly emphasized to federal courts that gambling contracts are
not
swaps.
[
57
]
Event contracts differ from gambling products in all five respects. First, unlike gambling products, event contracts have the essential structural characteristics of a derivatives contract. By design, they are traded on CFTC-registered national exchanges at market-set prices through the interaction of bids or offers placed on a central orderbook, not at prices unilaterally dictated by a “house.” The exchanges are neutral;
(
printed page 65974)
they do not profit when the event contract settles one way versus another. Rather, they earn profit by charging transaction fees when a trade occurs, similar to any other derivatives trade.
[
58
]
Such contracts are subject to the comprehensive DCM and derivatives clearing organization (“DCO”) Core Principles that serve to, among other things, protect customers who are trading and clearing such contracts. The structure of gambling wagers and event contracts is materially different, and therefore subject to different regulatory regimes.
[
59
]
Second, event contracts traded on a DCM are centrally cleared by CFTC-registered clearinghouses to eliminate counterparty credit risk, just like other derivatives transactions. Thus, when a bid and offer match on a DCM's central orderbook, the parties enter into a contract with one another, but that contract is then novated such that each party has a contractual relationship with a neutral, creditworthy clearinghouse.
Third, there is strong textual evidence that Congress intended for event contracts to be considered “swaps” under the CEA and to give the Commission authority to regulate them. The second prong of the “swap” definition is the most obvious illustration, as it specifically covers “contract[s]” based on “event[s].”
[
60
]
Additionally, when Congress created the “swap” definition, it also enacted a “Special rule for review and approval of
event contracts and swaps contracts.”
[
61
]
The Special Rule recognizes that “swaps in excluded commodities” can be “based upon the occurrence, extent of an occurrence, or contingency” that “involve[s],” among other things, “gaming.”
[
62
]
The word “ `gaming,' as used in the special rule, refers to playing games,” so “event contracts related to . . . sporting events . . . could implicate the gaming category.”
[
63
]
Congress expressly gave the Commission jurisdiction over those contracts, confirming their status as derivatives contracts.
[
64
]
Notably, Congress did
not
give the Commission authority over “gaming” products themselves, further confirming that gaming products like wagers fall outside the Commission's jurisdiction but event contracts that involve games are within the Commission's jurisdiction.
[
65
]
The Sixth Circuit expressed the view that “just because the CFTC may prohibit gaming-related event contracts does not mean [a DCM's] sports-event contracts are
necessarily
swaps,” since event contracts can also be “agreements, contracts, [or] transactions” under the Special Rule.
[
66
]
But apart from “gaming,” the Special Rule only applies to event contracts that “involve” “activity that is unlawful under any Federal or State law,” “terrorism,” “assassination,” “war”, or “other similar activity determined by the Commission, by rule or regulation, to be contrary to the public interest.”
[
67
]
It must be the case that a “swap” can “involve” at least one of these categories of activity, or else the word “swap” in the Special Rule is surplusage. Furthermore, even if a “gaming” contract is considered an “agreement,” “contract,” or “transaction,” the Special Rule still classifies that contract as being “in excluded commodities.”
[
68
]
And the swap definition covers binary options in excluded commodities which, as discussed below, includes event contracts.
[
69
]
In short, the Special Rule contemplates that “gam[es]” are “excluded commodities,” which reinforces that event contracts based on games are derivatives.
Fourth, event contracts have traditionally been regulated by the Commission, not the States. “Since 1992, Commission-regulated exchanges have listed for trading a variety of commodity futures and options contracts with payout terms based on” events “as diverse as regional insured property losses, the count of bankruptcies, temperature volatilities, corporate mergers, and corporate credit events”; and, in subsequent years, event contracts encompassed “the accomplishment of certain scientific advances, world population levels, the adoption of particular pieces of legislation,” and even “the length of celebrity marriages.”
[
70
]
In 1993, the Commission issued a no-action letter to Iowa Electronic Markets, allowing the facility to list event contracts tied to U.S. and Canadian elections.
[
71
]
In 2004, the CFTC designated the first DCM dedicated to listing contracts based on events that are excluded commodities.
[
72
]
Initially, these contracts were structured as commodity options known as “binary options,” the cash settlement of which was based on whether a specified event had occurred.
[
73
]
Thus, while gambling is traditionally State-regulated, event contracts are traditionally federally regulated.
Fifth, as set forth in the separate Notice of Proposed Rulemaking published on the same day as this Interim Final Rule proposing to further define “swap” to include event contracts, the Commission preliminarily believes that event contracts are known to the trade as “swaps.” Therefore, if certain event contracts do not qualify as swaps under the first or second prongs of the swap definition, they do qualify under the fourth prong. The same cannot be said of gambling products, for the reasons noted above.
In sum, the “swap” definition generally should not apply where a product has a longstanding history of being subject to a distinct regulatory framework and structurally does not lend itself to the requirements of the CEA, including its exchange-trading requirement and the Core Principles. As the Commission and SEC recognized in 2012, insurance contracts and consumer and commercial agreements are such examples. Today, the Commission clarifies that casino-style gambling
(
printed page 65975)
products offered by casinos or sportsbooks likewise fit the exclusion.
The Commission acknowledges that a person can achieve similar economic exposure by either entering into a gambling wager or purchasing an event contract. However, that does not make the two products one and the same, nor does it require that the two be subject to identical regulatory frameworks. Indeed, there are many instances in which a person can achieve the same (or similar) economic exposure via structurally different products subject to distinct regulatory regimes. For example, as noted, insurance and credit default swaps can provide similar risk mitigation, but that does not mean the two are or must be regulated the same way. Likewise, a person can gain exposure to a crypto asset by purchasing the crypto asset itself, purchasing shares in a firm that holds the crypto asset, or by purchasing crypto asset futures, each of which has distinct regulatory consequences. The same is true in the context of event contracts and casino-style gambling products.
Based on this interpretation and to address the concerns referenced in Part I above, the Commission is adopting this Interim Final Rule to establish an exclusion confirming that traditional gambling products do not qualify as swaps under the CEA. Nothing herein implies or presumes that an agreement, contract, or transaction that does not meet any of the requirements of this exclusion is a swap. Such an agreement, contract, or transaction will require further analysis of the applicable facts and circumstances, including the form and substance of such agreement, contract, or transaction, to determine whether it is a gambling product, and thus not a swap.
Similar to the exclusions for insurance contracts and consumer transactions, the exclusion has two components: a test relating to the status of the party offering the agreement, contract, or transaction (the “Provider Test”) and a test relating to the terms of the agreement, contract, or transaction (the “Product Test”).
To satisfy the Provider Test, the relevant agreement, contract, or transaction must be provided by a person that is subject to supervision by the gaming commissioner (or similar official or agency) of any State or by a Tribe, and such agreement, contract, or transaction is regulated as gaming or gambling under applicable State or Tribal law.
[
74
]
This requirement ensures that the Commission does not have jurisdiction over persons or products that have traditionally been the subject of State or Tribal regulation, particularly given the absence of an indication in Dodd-Frank that Congress intended the Commission to regulate these persons and transactions.
To satisfy the Product Test, the agreement, contract, or transaction must not be traded on a board of trade, an organized exchange, a swap execution facility, or any other market in which trades are executed multilaterally or subject to individual negotiation. For example, bets or wagers offered by a sports book or casino as principal to its customers, where the material terms of those bets or wagers are governed by standard “house rules” or similar standard terms, would satisfy the Product Test. In contrast, an agreement, contract, or transaction entered into on a trading facility,
[
75
]
including a DCM, or a SEF,
[
76
]
would not satisfy the Product Test because its price and other economic terms would be determined through the competitive interaction of multiple buyers and sellers on a multilateral basis, even though the other material terms of the agreement, contract, or transaction would be governed by standardized rules adopted by the facility.
[
77
]
Although there is not currently a practical overlap between the casino-style gambling products offered by State and Tribe-regulated entities (
i.e.,
bilateral and non-tradable) and swaps offered by CFTC-registered entities (
i.e.,
multilateral and tradable), the Product Test is designed to nonetheless acknowledge the functional distinction between the types of products and relationships that traditionally fall within the scope of derivatives regulation under the CEA from those traditionally addressed by State or Tribal gaming regulation.
[
78
]
By distinguishing agreements, contracts, or transactions entered into on a bilateral basis from those entered into on a multilateral basis, the Product Test recognizes that a principal purpose of the CEA is to establish a regulatory framework for price discovery on “liquid, fair and financially secure trading facilities”
[
79
]
—that is, trading on multilateral execution venues such as DCMs and SEFs—whereas State and Tribal gaming regulation typically concerns bets or wagers in which the odds or “line” are set by a licensed gaming operator acting as principal with its customers on a bilateral basis. The Product Test thereby ensures that State and Tribal-regulated entities do not, in the future, begin offering products properly within the Commission's jurisdiction, unless they do so consistent with the CEA and the Commission's regulations.
Therefore, the Commission is adding a new paragraph (7) to the definition of “swap” in
17 CFR 1.3
to further define the term swap to not include any agreement, contract, or transaction that: (A) is offered or entered into by a person that is licensed or otherwise authorized to offer gambling or gaming products, or accept wagers, under the law of a State or the law of a federally recognized Indian Tribe pursuant to the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act,
[
80
]
if that person is acting within the scope of that license or authorization, and such agreement, contract, or transaction is regulated as gaming or gambling under applicable state or Tribal law; and (B) is not traded on a board of trade, an organized exchange, a swap execution facility, or any other market in which trades are executed multilaterally or subject to individual negotiation. Paragraph (7) also explicitly identifies sports wagers, casino games, and other licensed games of chance as products that are not swaps subject to the Commission's jurisdiction.
Finally, the Commission reiterates that this Interim Final Rule does not further define the term “security-based
(
printed page 65976)
swap” and that nothing in the Interim Final Rule should be read to imply or presume that an agreement, contract, or transaction that does not meet any of the requirements of this exclusion is necessarily a swap. Also as previously noted, there may be other types of unlicensed gambling transactions that do not meet this Interim Final Rule's exclusion but nonetheless are still not swaps subject to the Commission's jurisdiction.
[
81
]
The classifications adopted in this Interim Final Rule are for purposes of the Commodity Exchange Act. Federal tax treatment and associated information reporting, withholding, registration, and payment obligations are determined under the Internal Revenue Code, applicable Treasury regulations, and IRS guidance.
III. Request for Comment
The Commission welcomes public comments from interested persons regarding any aspect of the Interim Final Rule. The Commission also seeks comment on the following specific questions. The Commission will take into consideration comments received and may modify the Interim Final Rule if warranted.
(1) This Interim Final Rule limits the exclusion to agreements, contracts, and transactions offered by a person that satisfies the Provider Test. Are there additional categories of providers that the Provider Test should cover beyond State-regulated gaming companies and Tribes, such as those discussed in note 43? If so, please explain the basis for including each additional category of qualifying provider.
(2) The Provider Test requires that the agreement, contract, or transaction be regulated as gaming or gambling under applicable State or Tribal law. Is it clear which agreements, contracts, or transactions are subject to these regulations? Are there better ways to define how State or Tribal gaming regulation should apply to agreements, contracts, or transactions covered by the exclusion? If so, please explain.
(3) The Product Test turns on whether the agreement, contract, or transaction is traded on a board of trade, an organized exchange, a SEF, or any other market in which trades are either executed multilaterally or subject to individual negotiation. Are there better ways to draw an objective, functional distinction between swaps, on the one hand, and traditional gambling products, on the other hand? If so, please explain, including how any alternative or additional basis for a distinction would be consistent with the CEA, including the definitions of “swap,” “commodity,” and “excluded commodity” and the Special Rule.
IV. Related Matters
A. Administrative Procedure Act
1. Legal Standard
Under section 533(b)(B) of the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”), agencies need not engage in notice-and-comment rulemaking “when the agency for good cause finds” that such “notice and public procedure . . . are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.”
[
82
]
In interpreting this “good cause” standard, courts have looked to APA Senate Report, which explains that “ `[i]mpracticable' means a situation in which the due and required execution of the agency functions would be unavoidably prevented by its undertaking public rulemaking proceedings . . . . `Public interest' supplements the term[ ] `impracticable' . . .; it requires that public rule-making procedures shall not prevent an agency from operating.”
[
83
]
“[T]here is a general consensus among the circuit courts that an agency's invocation of the good cause exception [to notice-and-comment rulemaking] should . . . be upheld . . . where following the regular rulemaking procedure would result in serious or real harm.”
[
84
]
Absent traditional emergencies, courts have found good cause where notice-and-comment rulemaking would create “possible fiscal harm,” where “the agency's prior regulations or guidelines had been invalidated by a court order, and thus, immediate promulgation of a new regulation was needed to prevent harm to the public in the interim,”
[
85
]
and/or where such rulemakings are not intended to be permanent.
[
86
]
2. Rationale for Interim Final Rule
Recent developments require the Commission to exercise its statutory authority to further define the term “swap” to explicitly exclude casino-style gambling products, including sports-wagering contracts entered into on a sportsbook, from the swap definition. As a group of 39 States and the District of Columbia recently observed, “[f]ederal and state courts are hopelessly confused and divided over an issue of immense importance”—whether, among other things, the swap definition is broad enough to encompass casino-style gambling products, which would threaten, among other things, State regulatory authority and Tribal revenue.
[
87
]
For example, and as described above in Part I, the Commonwealth of Kentucky has claimed that determining that event contracts are swaps under the CEA amounts to “[t]ransferring every ounce of authority over sports wagering from the States to the CFTC.”
[
88
]
And the State of New Jersey recently argued to the United States Supreme Court that “[n]othing in the [CEA] gives the CFTC unprecedented authority to become the sole regulator of sports gambling in this country.”
[
89
]
One result of this confusion has been State actions and court decisions that threaten to expose large areas of hitherto uncontroversial CFTC jurisdiction to incursion by certain of the States.
[
90
]
This lack of nuance has already led to overreach that risks indiscriminate disruption—or the outright dismantling—of federally regulated event contract markets, whether they purportedly offer casino-style gambling products or not.
In particular, the Ninth Circuit panel's interpretation of the “swap” definition in section 1a(47)(A)(ii)—which would deprive the CFTC of exclusive
(
printed page 65977)
jurisdiction over most event contracts—threatens to wreak havoc on the operations of DCMs nationwide. That is particularly true in Arizona, where the State's pending criminal case against a DCM—for offering event contracts of any kind—may be permitted to move forward.
[
91
]
Arizona does not stand alone. The State of Minnesota has attempted to enact a criminal statutory ban on prediction markets; the State of New York has sought emergency injunctive relief that would prohibit a DCM from offering event contracts anywhere; and many more enforcement actions remain pending.
[
92
]
These State-level actions imperil a nascent industry that Congress has entrusted to the “exclusive jurisdiction” of a federal agency, the CFTC.
[
93
]
The economic consequences of the shuttering of prediction markets on a State-by-State basis due to a lack of clear guidance are of a type and magnitude well in excess of prior cases recognizing good cause to skip notice-and-comment rulemaking due to “possible fiscal harm.”
[
94
]
In one instance, “actuarial disarray [that] might have posed a serious threat to the financial stability of a [federal employee] benefit program” constituted “good cause” to dispense with notice-and-comment.
[
95
]
In another, market “confusion” and “economic harm and disruption” that would have resulted if the agency had been forced to use “antiquated [poultry processing] guidelines” rather than its interim rule constituted “good cause.”
[
96

Here, in contrast to the relatively limited economic harm envisioned in those cases, entire markets on which various individuals and businesses rely for hedging and/or financial, economic, or commercial planning purposes—with tens of billions of dollars of transactions—are at stake.
[
97

“A massive rush to . . . conduct `actual transactions'—
or avoid them,”
as would occur if any states succeeded in closing prediction markets, similarly constituted “good cause” where the Temporary Emergency Court of Appeals found that section 553(b)(B) was satisfied by price control regulations adopted without notice-and-comment.
[
98

“Good cause” is further demonstrated by the circumstances that gave rise to this Interim Final Rule. This is not a case where the CFTC seeks to circumvent the APA's notice-and-comment requirement. Rather, like in cases where an “agency's prior regulations or guidelines had been invalidated by a court order, . . . immediate promulgation of a new regulation [is] needed [here] to prevent harm to the public” while the judiciary adjudicates the outer contours of one prong of the “swap” definition.
[
99

Just as a regulatory gap—leading to possible “confusion” and “irremedi[able] financial consequences”—would have resulted following a prior rule invalidation in
Mid-Tex Elec. Coop., Inv.
v.
FERC,
[

so too do
Flaherty, Assad,
and other judicial decisions justify this Interim Final Rule. The “promulgation of emergency regulations by [an agency is] a reasonable and perhaps inevitable response to [some adverse] injunctive court order[s],” like certain of those at issue here.

D. Consideration of Benefits and Costs
1. Introduction
The Commission is mindful of the economic effects, including the benefits and costs, of the Interim Final Rule. Section 15(a) of the CEA requires the Commission to consider the benefits and costs of its actions before promulgating a regulation under the CEA or issuing certain orders.
[
113
]
As required by section 15(a), the Commission evaluates these benefits and costs evaluated in light of five broad areas of market and public concern: (1) protection of market participants and the public; (2) efficiency, competitiveness, and financial integrity of futures markets; (3) price discovery; (4) sound risk management practices; and (5) other public interest considerations.
The Interim Final Rule excludes casino-style gambling products from the definition of swaps. In promulgating the Interim Final Rule, the Commission would not change the legal rights or obligations of market participants under the CEA because the Commission already treats casino-style gambling products as outside its jurisdiction. Instead, consistent with the CEA, the Interim Final Rule will reduce interpretive uncertainty by codifying the Commission's understanding that regulation of casino-style gambling products is outside of the Commission's jurisdiction, affirming the long-standing regulatory authority of States and Tribes.
The Commission qualitatively discusses the benefits and costs of the Interim Final Rule below because it is not practicable to quantify the effect of greater regulatory certainty on market participant behavior.
2. Baseline
The baseline against which the benefits and costs of the Interim Final Rule are measured consists of the current regulatory framework and the current state of Commission-regulated markets.
The Commission has exclusive jurisdiction to regulate transactions involving swaps (other than security-based swaps).
[
114
]
Under the plain language of the CEA, casino-style gambling products are not swaps or any other instrument that the Commission regulates and therefore, outside the scope of the Commission's jurisdiction. The Commission is not aware of any casino-style gambling products that are treated as Commission-regulated instruments or otherwise traded on Commission-licensed DCMs or SEFs.
However, as discussed above, recent court decisions regarding whether sports-related event contracts are swaps and the breadth of the swaps definition under the CEA, including casino-style gambling products, has created legal uncertainty.
[
115
]
3. Benefits
Because the Interim Final Rule does not change the legal rights or obligations of market participants under the CEA, the primary benefit of the Interim Final Rule is the immediate mitigation of regulatory and interpretive uncertainty triggered by recent, conflicting federal appellate court interpretations of the CEA's swap definition.
By expressly stating that traditional casino-style gambling products and sportsbook wagers do not constitute swaps, the Interim Final Rule could benefit gambling industry participants, State gaming commissions, and Tribal authorities. Insofar as industry participants and others are less likely to misapprehend the scope of the Commission's regulatory authority, they may benefit by allocating less capital to challenge or defend against Federal derivatives oversight, or to unnecessarily re-engineer their localized wagering infrastructures to meet incompatible Federal frameworks.
4. Costs
Because the Interim Final Rule codifies the Commission's long-standing operational baseline—that traditional casino-style gambling products reside outside its jurisdiction—it does not directly impose any new or incremental compliance costs under the CEA or the Commissions' regulations on derivatives market participants or retail gaming operators.
Codification of the exclusion of casino-style gambling products might slightly increase the incentive for certain entities to attempt to structure certain derivatives contracts as locally regulated gambling wagers to evade Commission jurisdiction. However, because the alternative to Federal regulation is compliance with a patchwork of State and Tribal regulatory frameworks (including outright prohibition in some jurisdictions), the risk of increased regulatory arbitrage is likely minimal. If entities nevertheless seek to evade Commission jurisdiction, the Commission understands that State and Tribal regulatory frameworks—although different than the Federal regulatory framework—would also offer some protection to industry participants and the public.
5. Section 15(a) Factors
Because the Interim Final Rule is consistent with existing law and market
(
printed page 65979)
practice, it will have limited impact on protecting market participants and the public; efficiency, competitiveness, and financial integrity of the futures markets; price discovery; sound risk management practices; and other public interest considerations.
6. Regulatory Alternatives
Given the Interim Final Rule seeks only to clarify that casino-style gambling products are outside of the Commission's jurisdiction, the Commission has not identified any viable regulatory alternatives.

116
]

The Commission also has not identified any less anticompetitive means of achieving the purposes of the CEA.

G. Congressional Review Act
Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, also known as the Congressional Review Act (“CRA”), generally provides for congressional review of agency rules. CFTC must submit a report to Congress and the Comptroller General when it issues a final rule, as defined in the CRA. An agency rule, in addition to being subject to congressional oversight, may also be subject to a delayed effective date if the rule is a “major rule.” OIRA has determined that this rule is not a “major rule” within the meaning of the relevant sections of the CRA. CFTC will also file appropriate reports with Congress and the Comptroller General so this rule may be reviewed.

§ 1.3
Definitions.
*

Swap.
* * *
(7)
Casino-style gambling products.
(i) The term
swap
as used in section 1a(47) of the Commodity Exchange Act does not include an agreement, contract, or transaction that:
(A) Is offered or entered into by a person that is licensed or otherwise authorized to offer gambling or gaming products, or accept wagers, under the law of a State or the law of a federally recognized Indian tribe pursuant to the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (
25 U.S.C. 2701
et seq.
), is acting within the scope of that license or authorization, and such agreement, contract, or transaction is regulated as gaming or gambling under applicable State or Tribal law; and
(B) Is not traded on a board of trade, an organized exchange, a swap execution facility, or any other market in which trades are executed multilaterally or subject to individual negotiation.
(ii) Provided that the requirements of paragraph (7)(i) of this definition are met, and without limiting the generality of paragraph (7)(i) of this definition, the following agreements, contracts, and transactions are excluded from the term
swap:
(A)
Sports wagers.
Any agreement, contract, or transaction in which a licensed sportsbook or sports wagering operator accepts a wager on the outcome of one or more sporting events;
(B)
Casino games.
Any agreement, contract, or transaction in which a licensed casino operator accepts a wager in connection with a casino table game, slot machine, or other electronic gaming device; and
(C)
Other licensed games of chance.
Any agreement, contract, or transaction in which a licensed operator accepts a wager in connection with any other game of chance (such as bingo, pool wagering, lotteries, and raffles).

Background
OPM is collecting information from tribal employers applying to participate in the FEHB Program under
25 U.S.C. 1647b
and subpart N of
5 CFR part 890
. OPM defines “tribal employer” in
5 CFR 890.1402
to include an Indian tribe or tribal organization carrying out at least one program under the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act or the Tribally Controlled Schools Act; or an urban Indian organization carrying out at least one program under title V of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act. A tribal employer must be entitled to purchase coverage, rights, and benefits under the FEHB Program for their tribal employees. AGENCY:
Fish and Wildlife Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), in response to a request under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) of 1972 from the Alaska Oil and Gas Association (AOGA), finalize regulations facilitating the authorization of incidental, unintentional take of small numbers of polar bears (
Ursus maritimus
) and Pacific walruses (
Odobenus rosmarus divergens
) during year-round oil and gas industry activities in the Beaufort Sea (Alaska and the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS)) and adjacent northern coast of Alaska. Take may result from oil and gas exploration, development, production, and transportation activities occurring for a period of 5 years. Oil and gas industry operations include similar types of activities covered by the previous 5-year Beaufort Sea incidental take regulations effective from August 6, 2021, through August 5, 2026. We will issue letters of authorization, upon request, for specific activities in accordance with these regulations.
DATES:
This rule is effective October 19, 2026 and remains effective through October 19, 2031.
ADDRESSES:
Document availability:
You may view this rule, the associated final environmental assessment (EA), and other supporting material at
https://www.regulations.gov
under Docket No. FWS-R7-ES-2026-0694, or these documents may be requested as described in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section below.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Madonna Baucum, Chief of Regulations, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, by email at
Info_Coll@fws.gov
,
or by telephone at (703) 468-8211. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Immediate Promulgation
In accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA;
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
), we find that we have good cause to make this rule effective less than 30 days after publication. Immediate promulgation of the rule will ensure that the requester will implement mitigation measures, monitoring, and reporting requirements that reduce potential impacts on polar bears (
Ursus maritimus
) and Pacific walruses (
Odobenus rosmarus divergens
), will allow the applicant to receive coverage under the MMPA (
16 U.S.C. 1371(a)(5)(A)
) for potential take of polar bears and Pacific walruses, increase our understanding of impacts that result from the requester's activities, and thus further our conservation objectives. Finally, this rule recognizes an exemption that is afforded the requester under the MMPA.
Executive Summary
In accordance with the MMPA and its implementing regulations, we, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (hereafter “FWS” or we), finalize incidental take regulations (ITRs) that facilitate the authorization of the incidental, unintentional take of small numbers of polar bears and Pacific walruses during oil and gas exploration, development, production, and transportation activities in the Beaufort Sea (Alaska and the OCS) and adjacent northern coast of Alaska, not including lands within the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR), for a 5-year period. Oil and gas activities include similar types of activities covered by the previous 5-year Beaufort Sea ITRs effective from August 5, 2021, through August 5, 2026 (
86 FR 42982
, August 5, 2021; revised
90 FR 27398
, June 26, 2025).
This final rule is based on our findings that the total takings of polar bears and Pacific walruses during specified activities will impact small numbers of animals, will have a negligible impact on the species or stocks, and will not have an unmitigable adverse impact on the availability of these species or stocks for subsistence use by Alaska Natives. We base our findings on data from monitoring the encounters and interactions between these species and the oil and gas industry; research on these species; oil spill risk assessments; potential and documented effects on these species from similar activities; information regarding the natural history and conservation status of polar bears and Pacific walruses; data reported from Alaska Native subsistence hunters; and predictive modeling. In conjunction with this rulemaking, the FWS has prepared an EA and associated FONSI.
These regulations include permissible methods of taking; mitigation measures to ensure that AOGA activities will have the least practicable adverse impact on these species or stocks, their habitat, and the availability of these species for subsistence uses; and requirements for monitoring and reporting.
Background
Section 101(a)(5)(A) of the MMPA gives the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary) the authority to allow the incidental, but not intentional, taking of small numbers of marine mammals, in response to requests by U.S. citizens (as defined in
title 50 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) in part 18 (at
50 CFR 18.27(c)
) engaged in a specified activity, other than commercial fishing, within a specified geographic region. The Secretary has delegated authority for implementation of the MMPA to the FWS. According to the MMPA, the FWS shall allow this incidental taking for a period of up to 5 consecutive years if we find that the total of such taking:
(1) Will affect only small numbers of individuals of the species or stock;
(2) Will have no more than a negligible impact on the species or stock;
(3) Will not have an unmitigable adverse impact on the availability of the species or stock for taking for subsistence use by Alaska Natives; and
(4) We issue regulations that set forth:
(a) Permissible methods of taking,
(b) Means of effecting the least practicable adverse impact on the species or stock and its habitat and the availability of the species or stock for subsistence uses, and
(c) Requirements for monitoring and reporting of such taking.
If final regulations allowing such incidental take are issued, we may then subsequently issue letters of authorization (LOAs), upon request, to authorize incidental take during the specified activities.
The term “take” means to harass, hunt, capture, or kill, or attempt to harass, hunt, capture, or kill any marine mammal. Harassment for activities other than military readiness activities or scientific research conducted by or on behalf of the Federal Government means “any act of pursuit, torment, or annoyance which (i) has the potential to injure a marine mammal or marine mammal stock in the wild” (the MMPA defines this as “Level A harassment”),
(
printed page 66205)
or “(ii) has the potential to disturb a marine mammal or marine mammal stock in the wild by causing disruption of behavioral patterns, including, but not limited to, migration, breathing, nursing, breeding, feeding, or sheltering” (the MMPA defines this as “Level B harassment”).
The terms “negligible impact” and “unmitigable adverse impact” are defined in
50 CFR 18.27
(
i.e.,
regulations governing small takes of marine mammals incidental to specified activities) as follows: “Negligible impact” is an impact resulting from the specified activity that cannot be reasonably expected to, and is not reasonably likely to, adversely affect the species or stock through effects on annual rates of recruitment or survival. “Unmitigable adverse impact” means an impact resulting from the specified activity: (1) that is likely to reduce the availability of the species to a level insufficient for a harvest to meet subsistence needs by (i) causing the marine mammals to abandon or avoid hunting areas, (ii) directly displacing subsistence users, or (iii) placing physical barriers between the marine mammals and the subsistence hunters; and (2) that cannot be sufficiently mitigated by other measures to increase the availability of marine mammals to allow subsistence needs to be met.
The term “small numbers” is also defined in
50 CFR 18.27
. However, we do not rely on that definition here as it conflates “small numbers” with “negligible impact.” We recognize “small numbers” and “negligible impact” as two separate and distinct requirements for promulgating ITRs under the MMPA (see
Ctr. for Biological Diversity
v.
Salazar,
695 F.3d 893, 904 (9th Cir. 2012)). Instead, for our small numbers determination, we evaluate if the number of marine mammals estimated to be incidentally taken is small relative to the size of the species or stock.
The term “least practicable adverse impact” is not defined in the MMPA or its implementing regulations. In promulgating ITRs, we ensure the least practicable adverse impact by requiring mitigation measures that are effective in reducing the impact of specified activities, but not so restrictive as to make specified activities unduly burdensome or impossible to undertake and complete.
In this rule, the term “Industry” includes individuals, companies, and organizations involved in exploration, development, production, and transportation activities of the petroleum industry. Industry activities may result in the incidental taking of Southern Beaufort Sea (SBS) polar bears and Pacific walruses (hereafter “walruses”). The MMPA does not require any party to obtain an incidental take authorization; however, any incidental taking that occurs without authorization is a violation of the MMPA. Since 1993, the oil and gas industry operating in the Beaufort Sea and the adjacent northern coast of Alaska has requested and we have issued ITRs for the incidental take of polar bears and walruses within a specified geographic region during specified activities. For a detailed history of our current and past Beaufort Sea ITRs, refer to the
Federal Register
at
90 FR 27398
, June 26, 2025;
86 FR 42982
, August 5, 2021;
81 FR 52276
, August 5, 2016;
76 FR 47010
, August 3, 2011;
71 FR 43926
, August 2, 2006; and
68 FR 66744
, November 28, 2003.
Summary of Request
On September 30, 2025, the FWS received a request from AOGA on behalf of its members and 8 Star Alaska, LLC to promulgate regulations for incidental take of small numbers of polar bears and walruses during oil and gas exploration, development, production, and transportation activities in the Beaufort Sea and adjacent northern coast of Alaska for a period of 5 years (2026-2031) (hereafter referred to as the “Request”). The FWS deemed AOGA's Request as adequate and complete on January 12, 2026.
The AOGA requested regulations that will be applicable to the oil and gas exploration, development, production, and transportation activities of multiple companies specified in the Request. This includes AOGA member companies and 8 Star Alaska, LLC that have applied for these regulations. The companies represented in the Request (as modified via subsequent communication from AOGA concerning membership changes) include: Alyeska Pipeline Service Company; APA Corporation; BlueCrest Energy, Inc.; Chevron Corporation; ConocoPhillips Alaska, Inc. (CPAI); ExxonMobil Alaska Production, Inc. (ExxonMobil); Hex Operating, LLC; Glacier Oil and Gas Corporation (Glacier); Hilcorp Alaska, LLC and Hilcorp North Slope, LLC (Hilcorp); Marathon Petroleum Corporation; Petro Star, Inc.; Repsol; Santos; Shell Exploration and Production Company (Shell); and 8 Star Alaska, LLC (a non-member company).
The activities within the scope of the Request are consistent with the nature of oil and gas activities that have occurred on the Alaska North Slope for decades. Those activities have occurred in parallel with monitoring and reporting that has provided a record of polar bear interactions in connection with such activities. To date, we have not made any determination of an effect on more than small numbers, a more than negligible impact, or an unmitigatable adverse impact on the availability for taking for subsistence use by Alaska Natives for polar bears or Pacific walruses in the Alaska North Slope from oil and gas activities. AOGA has indicated that not all activities described in the Request will actually occur during the ITR period, noting the broad scope of activities in the Request was included to support a comprehensive analysis and account for variability.
Summary of Changes From the Proposed Regulations
In preparing the final rule for the incidental take of polar bears and walruses, we reviewed and considered comments and information from the public on our proposed ITR published in the
Federal Register
on March 9, 2026 (
91 FR 11240
). We also reviewed and considered comments and information from the public on our draft EA. Based on public comment on these and other issues in the proposed ITR and draft EA, the final rule reflects the following changes:
The requester asked FWS to clarify the LOA process; specifically requesting FWS issue LOAs for activities within the scope and type of activities described in the Petition without detailed data requirements or new model runs. We have clarified the LOA process in the regulatory text at
50 CFR 18.123
.
The requester asked FWS to revisit our predictive estimates for vessel impacts, as they felt some routes were being double counted. Some routes were found to be counted in both the vessel analysis and the surface analysis. We have accordingly updated these estimates.
The requester noted several small editorial errors. These errors did not substantially affect the content of the preamble. They have been corrected.
The requester asked for several small points of clarification in the description of their specified activities. These included clarifying the following: helicopters will not knowingly hover over polar bear dens, ice roads may be used to access wells for plugging and abandonment, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) may be used for environmental studies, geophones may not necessarily be placed in the ground, airborne gravity and airborne magnetic surveys may use rotary or fixed-wing aircraft, and aerial pipeline surveys may be
(
printed page 66206)
conducted with fixed-wing aircraft in addition to rotary aircraft. None of these impact any take estimates.
The requester stated the mitigation measure requiring vessels to maintain the “maximum distance possible” from polar bears and walruses was too vague. In response, FWS has changed the language to “maximum distance practicable (805 m (0.5 mi) or greater).” This change does not affect any take estimates. FWS take estimates were calculated under the assumption that polar bears may be harassed within a 1.6 kilometer (km) (1 mile (mi)) impact area surrounding vessels.
The requester stated skirting around facilities is not current practice, is not necessary, and is not operationally possible. We have removed discussion of this mitigation measure. This change does not affect any take estimates.
The requester stated that conducting a required third aerial infrared (AIR) survey of polar bear included in the proposed ITR as an additional mitigation measure is not practicable due to logistical, human safety, and economic factors. As explained below, the FWS concluded that a third AIR survey is not practicable and has removed this additional mitigation measure.
Commenters noted a discrepancy in the title of Subpart J which has been corrected.
The requester and other commentors also noted the substantial differences between the historical data and the results from the predictive model and questioned whether the use of the model accurately estimates “take” of the species under the MMPA. We recognize the limitations of the predictive model and take estimates that significantly exceed historical data and AOGA take estimates. For that reason, the Service affirmatively considers other information and does not give its predictive models more weight than those other sources of information. FWS is clarifying that it considered all information before it, namely: monitoring encounters and interactions between the at-issue species and the oil and gas industry; research on these species; oil spill risk assessments; potential and documented effects on these species from similar activities; information regarding the natural history and conservation status of polar bears and Pacific walruses; and data reported from Alaska Native subsistence hunters; the FWS model; and AOGA's take estimates. FWS considers all these inputs in line with Executive Order (E.O.) 14303, “Restoring Gold Standard Science.” We recognize that, if it considered the model absent considering qualitative factors and AOGA's take estimates, it would not be considering the “best available science.” In other words, considering all these inputs ensures the “best available scientific evidence” is used to support the determinations in this ITR.
We also present in the preamble of this final ITR revised estimates from the FWS predictive modeling efforts, specifically the estimates of impacts to denning bears. Through the process of further streamlining the code for the predictive denning model, we discovered two errors causing inaccurate model outputs. In the first error, dens that had zero cubs naturally (a roughly 7 percent chance in the model) but were simulated to receive lethal or level A harassment were being counted when we summarized the number of dens impacted in those categories. While the simulated den was impacted in terms of the sow, there could not be any harassment of cubs because they did not exist. In the second error, a line of code was identified that was causing an error in the counting of a single category of disturbance events.
The model relies on a simulation of polar bear dens across the landscape, followed by simulated exposure to project activities, and finally simulated disturbance (for some of the dens). We iterate this 10,000 times so that we can account for variation in different aspects of polar bear denning biology (
e.g.,
date of entry, birthdate, number of cubs, emergence date) as well as the random element of whether disturbance occurred based on empirical probabilities. We then calculate summary statistics for each kind of take, such as the probability of occurrence, mean, median, and upper and lower confidence intervals.
One line of code led to a single unaccounted category of dens. These dens were previously undisturbed in early and late denning but disturbed in the post-emergence period. That line of code has been fixed, the remaining code has been reviewed to ensure it does not have similar issues, and a series of auto-check functions have been written to ensure a similar issue doesn't present during future code updates.
To describe the change plainly, instead of coding to “count all the dens specifically marked undisturbed” we changed the code to “count all dens except for those that were marked disturbed.” This change is necessary because the latter statement also selects those dens with a “missing” value where the former does not. Missing values in the code were present because the den was not labeled “disturbed” at the previous denning stages.
As a result of the code repairs, some FWS take estimates have changed. The estimated probability of lethal take has decreased slightly because we were using a den count to calculate the probability, and a small number of zero-cub dens were included in the calculation. Level A and Level B harassment estimates have increased as they now account for impacts to previously undisturbed dens that are simulated to exhibit a disturbance response in the post emergence period. The probabilities of such dens experiencing Level B (applicable to the sow) and Level A harassment (applicable to any cubs) is 28 percent and 72 percent respectively. This is a change from the faulty output, which did not count any take for these dens (
i.e.,
0 percent take).
Description of the Regulations
These regulations facilitate the authorization of the incidental, unintentional take of small numbers of polar bears and walruses that may result from the specified activities. They do not authorize or “permit” the specified activities themselves. The regulations include:
(1) Permissible methods of taking;
(2) Measures designed to ensure the least practicable adverse impact on polar bears and walruses, their habitat, and on the availability of these species or stocks for subsistence uses; and
(3) Requirements for monitoring and reporting.
Description of Letters of Authorization (LOAs)
An LOA is required to conduct activities pursuant to ITRs. Under these ITRs, eligible parties may request LOAs that would authorize incidental take of polar bears and walruses resulting from the specified activities described in these ITRs. Eligible parties are the member companies and 8 Star Alaska, LLC as specified in AOGA's Request, and their corporate affiliates, respective contractors, subcontractors, partners, owners, co-lessees, designees, or successors-in-interest. Requests for LOAs must be consistent with the activity descriptions and mitigation and monitoring requirements of the ITRs and be received in writing at least 90 days before the activity is to begin. Requests must include (1) an operational plan for the activity, including the timing of work and the nature of work to be conducted; (2) an interaction plan for polar bears and walruses; (3) a site-specific marine mammal monitoring and mitigation plan that specifies the procedures to monitor and mitigate the effects of the
(
printed page 66207)
activities on polar bears and walruses; and (4) plans of cooperation (if required as described in Mitigation Measures, below). Once this information has been received, we will evaluate whether the level of activity identified in the LOA request exceeds that analyzed by us in considering the findings made for the total taking allowable under these ITRs. If the level of activity exceeds that analyzed, the FWS may request additional information. For more information on requesting and receiving an LOA, refer to
50 CFR 18.27(f)
.
Description of Specified Geographic Region and Specified Activities
The specified geographic region covered by the requested ITRs (Beaufort Sea ITR region, see figure 1, below) encompasses all Beaufort Sea waters (including State waters and OCS waters as defined by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management) east of a north-south line extending from Point Barrow (latitude 71.39139° N, longitude 156.475° W; Board on Geographic Names (BGN) 1944) to the Canadian border, except for marine waters located within the ANWR. The offshore boundary extends 80.5 km (50 mi) offshore. The onshore boundary includes land on the North Slope of Alaska from Point Barrow to the western boundary of ANWR. The onshore boundary is 40 km (25 mi) inland. No lands or waters within the exterior boundaries of ANWR are included in the Beaufort Sea ITR region. The geographical extent of the proposed Beaufort Sea ITR region (approximately 7.9 million hectares (ha) (approximately 19.8 million acres (ac))) is the same region covered in previous regulations set forth in the final rule that published at
86 FR 42982
, August 5, 2021 and revised at
90 FR 27398
, June 26, 2025. The specified geographic region includes but is not limited to the following oil and gas development areas on the North Slope of Alaska: Nikaitchuq, Oooguruk, Badami, Northstar, Endicott (Duck Island), Liberty, Milne Point, Point Thomson, Prudhoe Bay, Pikka, Quokka, Southern Miluveach, Kuparuk River, Greater Mooses Tooth, Colville River, Horseshoe, and Bear Tooth.
The specified activities include oil and gas exploration, development, production, and transportation activities within the specified geographic region. This section summarizes the type and scale of Industry activities anticipated to
(
printed page 66208)
occur in the Beaufort Sea ITR region from 2026 to 2031. Year-round onshore and offshore Industry activities are anticipated. During the 5-year ITR period, Industry activities are expected to be generally similar in type, timing, and effect to activities evaluated under the prior ITRs. Additional information is available in the Request at
https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. FWS-R7-ES-2026-0694.
Transportation and Staging
Transportation activities will include aircraft operations; vehicle and equipment operations on gravel roads, gravel pads, ice roads, and ice pads; vehicle operations on tundra; and vessel transit and barging operations.
Aircraft operations will consist of personnel and cargo transport flights to support operations, aerial pipeline inspections, and environmental monitoring surveys. Personnel and cargo flights will be conducted routinely throughout the Beaufort Sea ITR region to support operations, and the frequency of these flights may vary depending on the location and type of operation. Fixed-wing aircraft will generally be used to transport personnel and cargo across development areas. Helicopters will be used to transport personnel and cargo to coastal or offshore facilities and to access remote areas. Flight altitude for personnel and cargo transport flights will generally be above 305 meters (m) (1,000 feet (ft)) above ground level unless inclement weather requires a lower flight altitude for personnel safety. Aerial pipeline inspections will be conducted frequently year-round using helicopters, UAVs, or fixed-wing aircraft. Environmental monitoring surveys will be conducted using helicopters, UAVs, or fixed-wing aircraft depending on the type of survey and the frequency of these environmental monitoring surveys will vary across location and time of year during the ITR period.
Vehicle and equipment operations will occur on the existing gravel road system and gravel pads within the ITR region to support operations. Expansion of existing gravel roads and gravel pads as well as construction of new gravel roads and gravel pads will be conducted to support operations as needed throughout the ITR period. Gravel roads and pads typically will be constructed or expanded during the winter, although new gravel placement on the tundra may occur during any season. Equipment that will be used to construct or expand gravel roads and pads includes all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), graders, loaders, excavators, rollers, dump trucks, tractors, bulldozers, vehicles, and other heavy equipment. Gravel road and pad maintenance will occur as needed to support transportation and operations throughout the ITR period. Gravel will be obtained from existing gravel mine sites and new gravel mine sites that may be developed within the ITR region.
During the winter, ice roads and ice pads will be constructed both onshore and offshore to support vehicle and equipment transportation and operations. The number, size, and personnel occupancy of ice roads and pads will vary each winter depending on the operations. Some ice roads will be constructed annually in the same location and other ice roads will be constructed in different locations based on operation requirements that vary during the ITR period. Offshore ice roads, trails, and pads will be constructed on floating sea ice or grounded ice in shallow water (less than 2 m (7 ft)). Offshore ice roads, trails, and pads may be constructed as early as December and be used until May during each winter. Equipment that will be used to construct ice roads, trails, and pads includes tracked vehicles, tractors, snowplows, pump trucks, ATVs, graders, and loaders.
Vehicle operations will occur on the tundra to support surveys, scout transportation routes, conduct environmental monitoring studies, and support infrastructure inspections and maintenance activities. Tundra travel will occur year-round throughout the ITR period. Equipment that will be used for tundra travel includes tracked vehicles, ATVs, snowmachines, Tucker Sno-Cat vehicles, and Rolligons.
Vessel transit and barging operations will support transportation of personnel, equipment, and supplies for operations. There are several marine dock facilities that will be used to support vessel transit and barging operations in the ITR region including West Dock, Oliktok Dock, and other private dock facilities in development areas. West Dock is located on the northwestern shore of Prudhoe Bay east of Point McIntyre. Oliktok Dock is located on the eastern side of West Harrison Bay at Oliktok Point. Maintenance dredging or screeding will be conducted as needed at the marine dock facilities. The majority of the vessel transit and barging operations will occur during the open-water season (July through October). Vessels of various sizes will be used to support transportation activities and may include crew boats, hovercrafts, zodiac vessels, and catamarans. Hovercrafts will also be used to transport personnel and cargo during both the ice-covered season and open-water season.
