Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to all Airbus SAS Model A330-
(

243, A330-243F, A330-341, A330-342, A330-343, A330-841, and A330-941 airplanes; and Model A340-211, A340-212, A340-213, A340-311, A340-312, A340-313, A340-541, and A340-642 airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on August 13, 2026 (
91 FR 52269
). The NPRM was prompted by EASA AD 2026-0060R1, dated June 9, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0060R1) (also referred to as the MCAI), issued by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. The MCAI states that occurrences of leaks on closed fuel LPSOVs were reported due to the LPSOV failing to seal. Depending on its amount, a fuel leak from an LPSOV could sustain a fire. This condition, if not detected and corrected, could lead to the inability to extinguish a fire and result in significant damage to airplane structure or systems.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require repetitive leak checks of certain fuel LPSOVs and replacement of an affected part if any discrepancy is detected, as specified in EASA AD 2026-0060R1. The NPRM also proposed to allow the installation of an affected part under certain conditions, as specified in EASA AD 2026-0060R1. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-8780.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received a comment from the Air Line Pilots Association, International (ALPA) who supported the NPRM without change.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.

2026-21-03 Airbus SAS:
Amendment 39-23492; Docket No. FAA-2026-8780; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00262-T.
(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective November 23, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
None.
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to all Airbus SAS airplanes specified in paragraphs (c)(1) and (2) of this AD, certificated in any category.
(1) Model A330-243, A330-243F, A330-341, A330-342, A330-343, A330-841, and A330-941 airplanes.
(2) Model A340-211, A340-212, A340-213, A340-311, A340-312, A340-313, A340-541, and A340-642 airplanes.
(d) Subject
Air Transport Association (ATA) of America Code 28, Fuel.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by reports of leaks on closed fuel low pressure shut-off valves (LPSOVs) due to the LPSOV failing to seal. The FAA is issuing this AD to address such leaks, which, depending on the amount of the leak, could sustain a fire. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could lead to the inability to extinguish a fire and result in significant damage to airplane structure or systems.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Requirements
Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD: Comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with, European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2026-0060R1, dated June 9, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0060R1).
(h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2026-0060R1
(1) Where Table 1 of EASA AD 2026-0060R1 specifies a compliance time of between November 12, 2025, and March 3, 2029, this AD requires accomplishing the initial leak check within 35 months after the effective date of this AD.
(2) Where EASA AD 2026-0060R1 refers to April 3, 2026 (the effective date of the original issue of EASA AD 2026-0060), this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(3) Where EASA AD 2026-0060R1 defines a serviceable part as “Any fuel LPSOV eligible for installation in accordance with Airbus instructions”, for this AD, replace that text with “Any fuel LPSOV eligible for installation”.
(4) Where paragraph (4) of EASA AD 2026-0060R1 specifies “any discrepancy of an affected part, as specified in the SB, is detected”, for this AD, replace that text with “any discrepancy of an affected part is detected”.
(5) This AD does not adopt the “Remarks” section of EASA AD 2026-0060R1.
(i) No Reporting and No Return of Parts
Although the material referenced in EASA AD 2026-0060R1 specifies to submit certain information to the manufacturer and to send removed parts to the manufacturer, this AD does not include those requirements.
(j) Additional AD Provisions
The following provisions also apply to this AD:
(1)
Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs):
The Manager, AIR-520, Continued Operational Safety Branch, FAA, has the authority to approve AMOCs for this AD, if requested using the procedures found in
14 CFR 39.19
. In accordance with

AMOC@faa.gov
.
Before using any approved AMOC, notify your appropriate principal inspector, or lacking a principal inspector, the manager of the responsible Flight Standards Office.
(2)
Contacting the Manufacturer:
For any requirement in this AD to obtain instructions from a manufacturer, the instructions must be accomplished using a method approved by the Manager, AIR-520, Continued Operational Safety Branch, FAA; or EASA; or Airbus SAS's EASA Design Organization Approval (DOA). If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.
(3)
Required for Compliance (RC):
Except as required by paragraph (j)(2) of this AD, if any material contains procedures or tests that are identified as RC, those procedures and tests must be done to comply with this AD; any procedures or tests that are not identified as RC are recommended. Those procedures and tests that are not identified as RC may be deviated from using accepted methods in accordance with the operator's maintenance or inspection program without obtaining approval of an AMOC, provided the procedures and tests identified as RC can be done and the airplane can be put back in an airworthy condition. Any substitutions or changes to procedures or tests identified as RC require approval of an AMOC.

Needs and Uses
On July 22, 2026, in furtherance of the goal of releasing more mid-band spectrum into the market to support and enable next-generation wireless networks, the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) adopted a Report and Order, FCC 26-46,
91 FR 48700
(
Upper C-band R&O
), in which it reformed the use of the 4.0-4.2 GHz portion of the C-Band. The 4.0-4.2 GHz band currently is allocated in the United States exclusively for non-Federal use on a primary basis for Fixed Satellite Service (FSS) and Fixed Service.
Domestically, space station operators use the 4.0-4.2 GHz band to provide downlink signals of various bandwidths to licensed transmit-receive, registered receive-only, and unregistered receive-only earth stations throughout the United States. The
Upper C-band R&O
calls for the relocation of existing FSS operations in the C-band, making 160 megahertz (3.98-4.14 GHz) available for flexible-use terrestrial wireless service throughout the contiguous United States through a Commission-administered public auction of licenses that must be completed by July 4, 2027, pursuant to a statutory mandate in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act,
Public Law 119-21
, section 40002(b)(2).
The Commission adopted a robust transition schedule to achieve an expeditious clearing and relocation of FSS operations and ensure that a significant amount of spectrum is made available quickly for next-generation wireless deployments, while also ensuring effective accommodation of relocated incumbent users. Pursuant to the
Upper C-band R&O,
all incumbent FSS operations in the contiguous United States must clear the 4.0-4.16 GHz portion of the C-band by December 30, 2030, or June 30, 2031, to ensure a timely transition process. The December 30 deadline applies to the top 75 Partial Economic Areas (PEAs) and aligns with the Federal Aviation Administration's first deadline to retrofit aircraft radio altimeters. The June 30 deadline applies to all other areas.
The Commission concluded in the
Upper C-band R&O
that, before the public auction of new licenses commences, it is appropriate for potential bidders to: (1) know when they will get access to the spectrum in the 3.98-4.14 GHz portion of the C-band that is currently occupied by incumbent FSS space station operators and earth stations; and (2) have an estimate of how much they may be required to pay for incumbent relocation costs and incentive payments should they become Upper C-band wireless licensees. New Upper C-band wireless licensees are required to pay for the reasonable and necessary relocation costs of incumbent space station and incumbent earth station operators that are required to clear the 4.0-4.16 GHz portion of the C-band.
To facilitate the provision of this information to potential auction bidders, the Commission is seeking approval for a modified information collection to permit it to collect the following information from incumbents as adopted in the
Upper C-band R&O:
Transition Plans
The
Upper C-band R&O
requires each eligible space station operator to submit to the Commission by November 5, 2026, and make available for public review, a detailed transition plan describing the necessary steps and estimated costs for the eligible space station operator to clear its existing operations in the 4.0-4.16 GHz portion of the C-band in the contiguous United States and its individual timeline for doing so. An eligible space station operator may make changes to its transition plan to update certain information or cure any defects that may be identified by the Commission or by relevant stakeholders during a public comment window.
Incumbent Earth Station Lump Sum Payment Elections
The
Upper C-band R&O
provides an incumbent earth station operator with the option of: (1) accepting reimbursement payments for its reasonable and necessary relocation costs for the transition; or (2) in lieu of actual relocation costs, opting out of the formal relocation process and accepting a lump sum reimbursement payment for its incumbent earth stations on a per-site basis based on the average, estimated cost of relocating such incumbent earth stations. The
Upper C-band R&O
directs the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau to announce the lump sum that will be available per incumbent earth station as well as the process for electing lump sum payments and requires that, no later than 60 days after the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau announces the lump sum payment amounts, an incumbent earth station operator that wishes to receive a lump sum payment make an irrevocable lump sum payment election that will apply to such earth stations in the contiguous United States.
This information collection will serve as the starting point for planning and managing the process of efficiently and expeditiously clearing the 4.0-4.16 GHz portion of the C-band, so that this spectrum can be auctioned for flexible-use service licenses.

Needs and Uses:
Pursuant to Congress' directive in
Public Law 119-21
, 40002(b)(2), 139 Stat. 72 (2025), that it grant licenses for spectrum in the 3.98-4.2 GHz band (Upper C-band) through a system of competitive bidding no later than July 4, 2027, on July 22, 2026, the Commission adopted the Upper C-band Report and Order, FCC 26-46, in which it reconfigured 160 megahertz of spectrum in the 3.98-4.14 GHz portion of the Upper C-band in order to make new flexible-use licenses in that band available in a Commission auction that is tentatively scheduled to begin in April 2027.
Prior to the Commission's adoption of the Upper C-Band Report and Order, the 4.0-4.2 GHz portion of the Upper C-
(
printed page 66137)
band was allocated for non-Federal use on a primary basis for Fixed Satellite Service (FSS) and Fixed Service (FS) links throughout the United States, although FS operations were sunset in the contiguous United States across the entire C-band as part of the Lower C-band transition. Space station operators use 4.0-4.2 GHz nationwide to provide space-to-Earth (
i.e.,
downlink) signals of various bandwidths to licensed transmit-receive, registered receive-only, and unregistered receive-only earth stations throughout the United States. In addition, the 3.98-4.0 GHz portion of the Upper C-band in the contiguous United States was reserved as a guard band to protect operations in the Upper C-band from potential harmful interference. In the Upper C-band Report and Order, the Commission modified the licenses and market access authorizations of incumbent FSS operators to clear the Upper C-band for new flexible-use terrestrial wireless operations in the contiguous United States.
The Commission established a framework in the Upper C-band Report and Order for relocating impacted incumbent FSS operations within the contiguous United States and for requiring that new Upper C-band licensees reimburse eligible FSS incumbents' reasonable and necessary transition costs. To facilitate a rapid and predictable transition of incumbent FSS services in the Upper C-band, the Upper C-band Report and Order establishes a Primary Transition Deadline of December 30, 2030 for the relocation of all incumbent FSS operations in the top 75 Partial Economic Areas (PEAs) in the contiguous United States, and a Final Transition Deadline of June 30, 2031 for the entire 160 megahertz in all remaining PEAs in the contiguous United States. Terrestrial wireless operations may begin in PEAs subject to the Final Transition Deadline as of July 1, 2031 or once all eligible space station operators have had their Certifications of Completion for those PEAs validated and the associated incentive payments have been made by the new Upper C-band wireless licensees.
In keeping with the approach used to relocate incumbents in the Lower C-band, the Commission concluded in the Upper C-band Report and Order that an independent third-party clearinghouse (Upper C-band Clearinghouse) should be used to oversee the cost-related aspects of the FSS transition, and that the logistics of clearing FSS operations from 4.0-4.16 GHz should be structured around an eligible space station operator-led process facilitated by a Relocation Coordinator (RC) that will use its expertise to track and supplement transition efforts across all eligible space station operators to ensure a timely and coordinated relocation process.
To protect the fair and level playing field for applicants to participate in the Commission's auction for licenses in the Upper C-band, the Upper C-band Clearinghouse and the RC are each required to make real-time disclosures of the content and timing of and the parties to communications, if any, from or to such applicants, as applicants are defined by the Commission's rule prohibiting certain auction-related communications,
47 CFR 1.2105(c)(5)(i)
, whenever the prohibition in
47 CFR 1.2105(c)
applies to competitive bidding for licenses in the in the Upper C-band. See
47 CFR 27.1413(c)(10)
and
27.1414(c)(4)(i)
(as adopted in the Upper C-band Report and Order). The Commission is seeking approval for a new information collection to permit the Upper C-band Clearinghouse and the RC to make the required real-time disclosure of any such communications, as necessary.

e.g.,
.doc, .xml, .ppt, searchable .pdf). Participants in this proceeding should familiarize themselves with the Commission's
ex parte
rules (
47 CFR 1.1200
et seq.
).
Synopsis
With this
Public Notice,
the Bureau invites interested parties to comment on the Cost Catalog contained in Attachment A. In the
Upper C-band R&O
(
91 FR 55281
(Aug. 27, 2026)), the Commission adopted rules to make 160 megahertz of mid-band spectrum available for flexible use throughout the contiguous United States by transitioning incumbent Fixed Satellite Service (FSS) operations out of 4.0-4.16 GHz. The
Upper C-band R&O
established that new Upper C-band wireless licensees in the 3.7 GHz Service will reimburse the reasonable and necessary transition costs of incumbents to transition out of the reconfigured portion of the band. The
Upper C-band R&O
further gives incumbent earth station operators the option to elect on a per-site basis a lump sum payment in lieu of actual cost reimbursement. The lump sum election is irrevocable, and any incumbent earth station operators that select the lump sum will have opted out of the formal transition process, will be responsible for their own transition work for the relevant sites from that point forward, and must comply with the relevant Transition Deadline for the partial economic area (PEA) where they are located.
Actual Cost Reimbursement.
To provide additional guidance on compensable costs in connection with actual cost reimbursements, the Commission directed the Bureau to develop a Cost Catalog and instructed the Upper C-band Clearinghouse, which will administer the financial aspects of the transition, to presume as reasonable all reimbursement claims that fall within the estimated range of costs that the Cost Catalog identifies. To this end, the Commission engaged a contractor, Teltrium, Inc. (Teltrium), to assist with developing the Preliminary Cost Catalog in Attachment A, which contains draft categories for the most common anticipated transition tasks and related ranges of presumptively reasonable expenses that incumbents may incur as they clear operations out of 4.0-4.16 GHz. This Preliminary Cost Catalog is based in part upon the Final Cost Catalog that was developed in 2020 for the Lower C-band transition (
85 FR 47209
), with adjustments for inflation, but it also includes proposed new categories tailored to the different anticipated transition steps implicated by the Upper C-band transition. To compile the information needed for the Preliminary Cost Catalog, Teltrium considered comments and filings in the underlying record in GN Docket No. 25-59, publicly available pricing and technical information, and information obtained from confidential interviews with vendors and other targeted stakeholders, including satellite
(
printed page 66141)
operators and earth station operators, about their anticipated transition work.
We seek comment on the Preliminary Cost Catalog, including whether the draft categories and estimated range of expenses for each category are reasonable. As mentioned, this Preliminary Cost Catalog is based in part on the Lower C-band Final Cost Catalog, and we seek comment whether additional updates are necessary to better suit the specific circumstances of the Upper C-band transition. If so, what additional transition tasks and categories should we include? We note that the Cost Catalog is only intended to cover the most common anticipated transition tasks and is not a comprehensive list of every possible relocation action whose costs may ultimately be deemed reimbursable. Claimants may still submit claims for items not included in the final Cost Catalog, and those claims will be subject to review and disposition by the Upper C-band Clearinghouse as part of its remit to prevent fraud, waste, and abuse. Further, in formulating this list as a guidance resource, we do not intend for it to constrain the Upper C-band Clearinghouse from exercising its independent judgment on what claims or elements thereof constitute optional upgrades or non-compensable costs as it assesses the specific merits of individual claims. For the initial categories set forth in the Preliminary Cost Catalog, and for any additions that commenters may suggest, commenters seeking adjustments are encouraged to provide specific pricing information for individual items as well as more general information on the costs that incumbents expect to incur.
Incumbent Earth Station Lump Sum Payments.
The Preliminary Cost Catalog sets forth specific lump sum categories and amounts for incumbent earth station operators seeking to opt out of the formal transition process led by the eligible space station operators. This mechanism will afford lump sum electees the option to: (1) perform their own transition work to maintain FSS service; (2) migrate to an alternative distribution technology, such as an IP-delivered service; or (3) discontinue service altogether. While the decision to opt for the lump sum payment in lieu of actual cost reimbursement is irrevocable, incumbent earth station operators may elect lump sum payments on a per-site basis to enable operators with a mix of facilities in urban and rural areas to opt for the type of transition that best meets their long-term needs. We reiterate that any incumbent earth station operators electing the lump sum will be responsible for their own transition work for the relevant sites from that point forward and must comply with the relevant Transition Deadline for the PEA where they are located.
We seek comment on the preliminary lump sum categories and amounts provided in Appendix A, which, as directed by the Commission in the
Upper C-band R&O,
are based upon the average estimated, reasonable costs of transitioning those facilities out of 4.0-4.16 GHz, including costs related to the potential migration of service or links to the Ku-band. We also seek comment on the proposed lump sum amount for each category and the methodology used to arrive at those amounts. Does the methodology described in Appendix A and these amounts reflect the appropriate lump-sum inputs for each class of earth station? Should we make any adjustments to account for other factors? We also seek comment on the specific filing and certification procedures used in connection with the Lower C-band transition and whether to repurpose them here or adjust them, given the shift to a per-site lump sum approach in the instant transition.

Office of Personnel Management
5 CFR Parts 351, 630, and 715
[Docket ID: OPM-2026-0397]
RIN: 3206-AP07
AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final rule to amend its regulations governing administrative leave for workforce realignment and other purposes. This final rule more fully addresses the appropriate uses of administrative leave, including use in connection with deferred resignation programs and other workforce realignment initiatives, and for other purposes. The final rule also clarifies when an agency may provide administrative leave during a reduction-in-force notice period and accept or deny an employee's request to withdraw a resignation in the context of a deferred resignation program.
DATES:
This rule is effective November 18, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Bryce Baker by telephone at (202) 606-2858 or by email at
leavepolicy@opm.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
OPM is issuing a final rule to amend its regulations on administrative leave in
5 CFR part 630, subpart N
, and related regulations on reductions in force in
5 CFR 351.806
and on resignations in
5 CFR 715.202
. OPM issued a proposed rule on June 29, 2026 (
91 FR 39032
).
I. Digest of Public Comments
In response to the proposed rule, OPM received 30 comments during the 30-day public comment period from multiple individuals, one agency (0027), two unions (0022 and 0030), and three employee advocacy groups (0025, 0026, and 0029). All comments were posted and made available to the public in the docket at
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​OPM-2026-0397
.
A reference to a comment provides the location of the item in the public record (
i.e.,
comments filed in response to the proposed rule are available at
https://www.regulations.gov/​comment/​OPM-2026-0397-nnnn
where “nnnn” is the comment number).
At the conclusion of the public comment period, OPM reviewed and analyzed the comments. In general, the comments on the proposed regulation changes were mixed. The comments are summarized below, including suggestions for revisions that OPM considered and either adopted, adopted in part, or declined to adopt, along with OPM's supporting rationale. Section II of this preamble provides background information. Section III responds to the comments. Section IV provides a section-by-section analysis of the regulatory changes, section V sets forth the regulatory analysis, and section VI addresses regulatory compliance requirements.
II. Background
On December 17, 2024, OPM issued final regulations on administrative leave that added a new subpart N in
5 CFR part 630
(
89 FR 102256
). The regulations in subpart N govern use of administrative leave authorized for Federal employees under
5 U.S.C. 6329a
, which was enacted as part of the Administrative Leave Act of 2016 (section 1138 of
Pub. L. 114-328
, December 23, 2016). OPM subsequently
(
printed page 65925)
identified the need to clarify certain matters in subpart N. On June 29, 2026, OPM issued a proposed rule (
91 FR 39032
) pursuant to its regulatory authority at
5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)
. The proposed rule addressed acceptable and unacceptable uses of administrative leave. In particular, OPM proposed to add a list of specific examples of acceptable uses, including use in connection with deferred resignation programs
[
1
]
and other workforce restructuring initiatives. These final regulations codify existing OPM policies on administrative leave. The primary OPM policy documents are a “Fact Sheet: Administrative Leave” and an OPM memorandum to agency Chief Human Capital Officers entitled “Template for Agency Administrative Leave Policies” (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025) (“Agency Policy Template”).
[
2
]
In addition, the proposed rule included proposed changes to related regulations. It proposed to amend OPM's reduction-in-force (RIF) regulations at
5 CFR 351.806
to clarify the conditions under which an agency may provide administrative leave during a RIF notice period. It also proposed to amend OPM's resignation regulations at
5 CFR 715.202
to (1) provide that an agency has sole and exclusive discretion in deciding whether to accept or deny an employee's request to withdraw a resignation before the resignation has become effective and (2) specifically address that an employee's receipt of benefits provided under a deferred resignation agreement, such as paid administrative leave, is a valid reason to deny an employee's request to withdraw a resignation.
III. Responses to Comments
A. Use of Administrative Leave in Connection With a Deferred Resignation Program
A number of comments, including 0004, 0006, 0016, 0019, 0025, 0026, and 0029, opposed codifying use of administrative leave in connection with deferred resignation programs (DRP) as an acceptable use, arguing that use of administrative leave for workforce restructuring circumvents RIF procedures in
5 CFR part 351
, which includes legal safeguards to ensure that, when necessary, employees are released from employment in an orderly manner. Commenters argued that voluntary early retirement authority (VERA) and voluntary separation incentive payments (VSIP) already provide bounded, accountable mechanisms with statutory caps, and that open-ended administrative leave is designed to escape those limits. Comment 0004 stated that OPM should reject any regulatory framework that treats administrative leave as a preferred alternative to lawful RIF procedures. Comment 0006 objected that administrative leave, traditionally a short-duration tool, is being expanded into a workforce reduction mechanism that departs from established civil service procedures.
Comment 0025 argued that deferred resignation programs require a statutory foundation separate from section 6329a, noting that Congress has separately authorized the VSIP and VERA programs and asserting that section 6329a cannot be used to “create and fund a massive governmentwide paid separation benefit.” The commenter cited public reporting estimating the cost of 2025 deferred resignation programs at approximately $11.1 billion and urged OPM to work with Congress on a legislated transition or severance program. The commenter urged OPM to withdraw the proposal in its entirety, begin using administrative leave as intended by Congress, and seek legislation for any broader paid transition or severance program.
Comment 0016 similarly argued that VERA and VSIP already provide bounded, accountable voluntary-reduction tools with statutory caps, making open-ended administrative leave unnecessary, and that codifying open-ended administrative leave as a “transition-to-separation tool” invites agencies to route around the disciplined mechanisms Congress enacted, and to do so with public funds and no meaningful oversight. Comment 0026 recommended that OPM work with Congress to raise the statutory cap on voluntary separation incentive payments to make it a more useful tool. An individual commenter argued that the proposed rule weakens the due process protections that have sustained a competent, professional, merit-based civil service, and that it will harm Federal recruitment and retention and requested withdrawal of the proposed rule. Due process concerns are addressed further in section III.F.
OPM disagrees that a separate statutory authorization is required to use administrative leave in conjunction with a DRP. Administrative leave provided in connection with a DRP is administrative leave under section 6329a, provided pursuant to a written agreement in which the employee voluntarily commits to separate on a specified future date. Such leave is not “placed” on an unwilling employee; it is a benefit the employee elects to accept as part of a voluntary transition to separation. The concerns that animated the Administrative Leave Act—open-ended, involuntary removal of employees from the workplace during unresolved personnel matters—are not implicated where an employee has voluntarily agreed to separate and to the terms of the transition period.
The existence of VSIP and VERA does not preclude the use of administrative leave as a complementary workforce-shaping tool. Those authorities address different benefits—lump-sum incentive payments and modified retirement eligibility, respectively—and nothing in those statutes states or implies that they are the exclusive means by which agencies may facilitate voluntary separations. Indeed, the new § 630.1403(c)(9) expressly contemplates that administrative leave may be used in conjunction with VSIP and VERA. Section 630.1403(c)(9) is limited to cases where employees sign voluntary written agreements to separate on a specified future date and receive administrative leave as a part of that voluntary agreement. Agencies have long had discretion to determine how employees in a transition-to-separation posture will be utilized, and the final rule confirms that discretion while subjecting it to Governmentwide limits established by OPM and applicable agency limits.
OPM acknowledges that VERA and VSIP are separate authorities with their own limits; the inclusion of those authorities in the same example is descriptive of the range of voluntary transition tools and does not subject administrative leave to, or exempt it from, the statutory conditions governing VERA or VSIP, which continue to apply on their own terms.
OPM does not agree that this final rule expands administrative leave into a workforce reduction tool that circumvents RIF procedures. The final rule does not waive, suspend, or displace any requirement of
5 CFR part 351
. Retention registers, retention standing, veterans' preference, and all
(
printed page 65926)
other RIF requirements continue to apply in full to any involuntary RIF separation. The only change made to part 351 is to § 351.806, which addresses an employee's duty status during the RIF notice period. Paragraph (a) retains the general expectation that an employee will remain in a duty status during the notice period. It replaces the “when possible” language with “under ordinary circumstances,” which is consistent with the language used in
5 CFR 752.404(b)(3)
that addresses duty status during an advanced notice period in connection with a proposed removal or suspension. The new paragraph (b) permits—but does not require—administrative leave for all or part of that period when the agency determines such leave is appropriate. This regulatory clarification is consistent with OPM policy guidance
[
3
]
which already provided that an authorized agency official may provide administrative leave between an employee's receipt of a notice of involuntary separation and the effective date of that separation.
New § 630.1403(c)(10) and revised § 351.806 address only whether an employee may be placed in a paid, non-duty status during a RIF notice period. Those provisions do not alter the substantive or procedural requirements governing RIF, which continue to apply in full whenever an agency conducts a RIF. Nothing in this rule authorizes an agency to bypass RIF competition, retention registers, or appeal rights.
As to cost, OPM addresses costs in section III.B and regulatory-impact matters in section III.E. OPM notes here that the DRPs conducted in 2025 were undertaken pursuant to existing regulatory authority and OPM guidance; this rule codifies the availability of administrative leave for DRP programs prospectively, subject to the limits described above. OPM agrees that Congress remains free to enact additional workforce-transition authorities but disagrees that such legislation is a prerequisite to the uses identified in this rule. The sponsors of the Administrative Leave Act were concerned about costs associated with open-ended investigations of employees and did not consider a use of administrative leave that would produce long-term cost savings by facilitating workforce reductions.
OPM declines to withdraw the rule or to make changes based on this line of comments. The final rule is a lawful exercise of OPM's authority under
5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1)
, strengthens the regulatory framework by converting policy guidance into binding prohibitions and clarifying acceptable uses, preserves the duty-status presumption during RIF notice periods, and does not alter the statutory 10-workday limit or the investigative- and notice-leave framework of section 6329b.
B. Cost of Administrative Leave and DRP
Several comments, including 0004, 0016, 0022, and 0025, objected to the cost of using administrative leave in conjunction with a DRP. Comment 0004 stated the 2025 deferred resignation programs showed waste, including paying employees who performed no work and later rehiring. The commenter believes a full accounting of the DRPs should be conducted before similar programs are codified in regulation. Comment 0016 noted that the 2025 DRP placed tens of thousands of employees in paid non-duty status for months while delivering no work to the public, a direct payroll expenditure for zero output, compounded by the loss of institutional knowledge, the collapse of continuity in mission-critical functions, and the documented degradation of agency capacity that followed. Comment 0022 commented that the proposed rule attempts to justify the administration's costly workforce reduction efforts, including widespread use of administrative leave, by promising “large long-term savings” without providing concrete support or considering downstream effects of letting employees participate in DRP.
Comment 0022 also stated that OPM failed to provide concrete support that justifies costly workforce reduction efforts, even as it acknowledges the costs of the workforce reduction initiatives that began in early 2025. The organization cited two recent studies that highlight significant expenses tied to these workforce reduction programs: (1) a June 2026 study estimated that deferred resignation programs alone have cost at least $11 billion; and (2) another analysis from April 2026 found that the Government paid approximately $4.5 billion in salary and benefits to employees who were not working under DRP agreements.
OPM respectfully disagrees with the commenters on the costs associated with the original DRP. OPM acknowledged in the proposed rule that there is a temporary cost to providing administrative leave and stated its judgment that use of administrative leave in connection with deferred resignation programs and other workforce restructuring initiatives can generate long-term savings by reducing Federal staffing levels. OPM did not project costs or savings from the proposed regulations themselves because the regulations codify Governmentwide policies already in place, and OPM does not expect codification to produce significant changes in the usage of administrative leave.
Further, OPM policy guidance has stated that use of administrative leave in connection with DRP is in the interest of the agency and of the Government as a whole because it facilitates workforce restructuring and realignment efforts leading to a leaner, less expensive, less wasteful, more efficient, and more mission-focused Federal workforce. OPM also notes that this policy is not open-ended: beginning in calendar year 2026, use of administrative leave by an employee in connection with a workforce realignment initiative is limited to 12 weeks in any individual instance unless a higher threshold has been jointly approved by OPM and the Office of Management and Budget. In addition, § 630.1403(a)(6) requires an authorized agency official to consider the effect on productivity and mission needs and the strength of the justification for using appropriated funds.
OPM calculates that DRP separations in 2025 represented a workforce reduction of over 6 percent, which contributed to the overall reduction of the Federal workforce of over 12 percent from December 2024 to March 2026. Those workforce reductions create significant long-term savings even after accounting for the one-time costs of DRP administrative leave, which represent less than 3 percent of total basic payroll for Federal employees. Because the payroll savings from a smaller workforce recur in every subsequent fiscal year while the administrative leave outlays are one-time transition costs, the long-term savings substantially exceed the short-term costs even under the commenters' own estimates.
OPM makes no changes in the regulations in response to this line of comments.
C. 10-Workday Limit
Comment 0025 asserted that the proposed rule exceeds OPM's authority under the Administrative Leave Act of 2016,
5 U.S.C. 6329a-6329c
, by establishing a regulatory exception to the statutory 10-workday calendar year limit. The commenter argued that the section 6329a(b) 10-workday calendar-
(
printed page 65927)
year limit reflects Congress's intent to curb extended agency-directed paid non-duty status, that OPM's authority under section 6329a(c)(1) to prescribe acceptable uses does not include authority to override that limit, and that authorizing months of administrative leave for workforce realignment, RIF notice periods, and settlements would render the statutory cap “optional and meaningless.” The commenter urged OPM to withdraw the proposal and seek legislation for any broader paid transition or severance program. Similarly, comment 0029 asserted that the proposed rule conflicts with the 10-workday limit Congress enacted in section 6329a(b)(1) by “re-authorizing exactly the indefinite, uncontestable leave status Congress acted to eliminate.”
However, comment 0029 supported retaining the language found in proposed § 630.1403(b)(3) concerning the use of administrative leave for investigative purposes. A labor organization (0030) similarly argued that the text and structure of the Act—including the separately defined and expressly limited investigative leave authority in
5 U.S.C. 6329b
—show that Congress withheld the power to provide unlimited amounts of administrative leave, and cited the sense-of-Congress findings accompanying the Act (
5 U.S.C. 6329a note
) that agency use of administrative leave had exceeded reasonable amounts and that administrative leave should be used sparingly.
OPM disagrees that the rule exceeds its statutory authority. Congress expressly directed OPM to “prescribe regulations to carry out” section 6329a, including regulations governing the “acceptable agency uses of administrative leave” and the recording of such leave (
5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1)
). The final rule is an exercise of precisely that delegated authority: it identifies acceptable and prohibited uses of administrative leave and codifies existing Governmentwide policies to promote consistency and accountability across agencies.
The final rule does not waive, extend, or otherwise modify the 10-workday limit in section 6329a(b)(1). As OPM explained in the December 2024 final rule (
89 FR 102256
), the statutory limit applies where an agency “place[s]” an employee on administrative leave for investigative purposes. The 10-workday limit directly connects to a provision in the investigative leave law (section 6329b(b)(3)(A)), which bars placing an employee on investigative leave until the 10-workday limit is reached.
The final rule preserves and indeed strengthens the statutory framework. New § 630.1403(b)(3) provides clarity by expressly prohibiting use of administrative leave for investigative purposes once the employee has reached the 10-workday limit. If necessary, an agency may then use investigative leave under section 6329b, with all of that section's procedural safeguards, approvals, time limits, and reporting requirements. Thus, the final rule gives fuller effect to the statutory scheme Congress designed for the specific problem that motivated the Administrative Leave Act—prolonged, agency-directed removal of employees from the workplace during personnel investigations.
The commenter's reading—under which the 10-workday limit would govern all extended uses of administrative leave—is inconsistent with the position the commenter itself acknowledges: that general administrative leave for purposes such as voting, blood donation, and emergency closures remains outside the cap. The statute does not enumerate acceptable purposes; it delegates that task to OPM. Nothing in the text of section 6329a confines OPM's authority under subsection (c)(1) to brief or de minimis uses, and the enumerated examples in § 630.1403(c) operate within, not around, the statutory limits: uses that fall within the investigative context remain subject to the 10-workday limit, which when reached triggers coverage under section 6329b, while the workforce-realignment uses in paragraphs (c)(9) through (c)(11) address categorically different circumstances, discussed further below. The December 17, 2024, final rule cited by the commenter included this sentence: “An incidence of administrative leave lasting more than 1 workday may be approved when determined to be appropriate by an agency” (
5 CFR 630.1403(a)(3)
). This final rule simply adds specific examples of appropriate uses of administrative leave for periods of more than 1 workday.
The rule does not authorize unlimited administrative leave: the workforce-realignment uses in § 630.1403(c)(9) and (c)(11) are expressly subject to Governmentwide limits established by OPM—currently 12 weeks in any individual instance absent joint OPM and Office of Management and Budget approval of a higher threshold—and to any agency limits, and every use of administrative leave remains subject to the principles and decision factors in § 630.1403(a).
Finally, the “Sense of Congress” accompanying the Act—that agencies should use administrative leave “sparingly” and manage its costs prudently—is a non-binding statement of policy that informs, but does not displace, the operative statutory text. The final rule is consistent with that policy: it retains the general principles in § 630.1403(a) that administrative leave is discretionary, should be limited to the amount reasonably necessary, and ordinarily should not exceed one workday for a single incidence, while identifying the limited circumstances in which longer periods are appropriate. It also adds new binding prohibitions (§ 630.1403(b)(3)-(5)) that constrain agency use of administrative leave. As noted above, the sponsors of the Administrative Leave Act were concerned about costs associated with open-ended investigations of employees and did not consider a use of administrative leave that would produce long-term cost savings by facilitating workforce reductions.
OPM makes no changes in response to these comments.
D. Mission Capacity
Three individual commenters (comments 0007, 0008, 0009) raised concerns about the consequences of workforce reductions on the delivery of Federal services. Comment 0007 described the impact of workforce reductions on various public health services, communications during emergencies, and technical assistance to states, and argued that the proposed rule facilitates those reductions without accounting for their effect on the public. Comment 0008 noted OPM's analysis should evaluate the cost of reduced program capacity, including reduced preparedness and loss of scientific expertise, rather than treating the cost of administrative leave in isolation. Comment 0009 was concerned about the loss of institutional and technical expertise, especially in specialized topics and areas of work and requested that OPM clarify that administrative leave is not to be used as a tool for permanent downsizing and should not be used as a routine workforce reduction strategy and that agencies should first demonstrate that mission requirements can still be met.
OPM appreciates the comments and does not dispute that changes in agency staffing can affect the delivery of public services. Those effects are addressed in the existing regulatory framework at the point of decision rather than through the list of examples of acceptable uses.
This final rule does not require an agency to provide administrative leave in any workforce realignment scenario and does not state that administrative
(
printed page 65928)
leave should be used as a routine workforce reduction strategy. An authorized agency official retains the sole and exclusive discretion to decline to provide it based on agency judgments regarding mission needs (§ 630.1403(a)(2) and (a)(4)). Decisions about the size and composition of an agency's workforce, and about which program functions must remain staffed, are made by the agency under separate authorities and are outside the scope of this rulemaking.
As to the request that agencies first demonstrate that mission requirements can still be met, OPM declines to change the regulatory text. Section 630.1403(a)(6) already requires the authorized agency official to consider the effect on productivity and the agency's ability to meet mission needs. The loss of specialized expertise the commenters describe is a workforce planning consideration for the agency exercising its staffing authorities rather than a matter to be governed by the administrative leave regulations.
E. Economic Impact Analysis
Comment 0025 argued that OPM's cost-benefit analysis is incomplete because it does not disclose amounts already spent on extended administrative leave, quantify affected employees, compare projected savings against service losses and replacement costs, or justify the determination that the rule will not have a $100 million annual economic effect.
Several commenters argued that the no-cost certification is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) because it conflates the
act of codifying
with the
substance being codified.
Comment 0004 stated that OPM fails to account for the major economic effects of workforce reductions in its costing of the proposed rule. The commenter suggested that OPM should measure more than the payroll impact of Federal employees and requested that OPM conduct a complete and honest economic impact analysis—that accounts for local economic multiplier effects, the impact on housing markets, and the cost of lost public services—and make that analysis available for a minimum of 60 days of public comment before any rule is finalized.
Comment 0010 argued that extended administrative leave under a DRP operates as a benefit that bridges employees to retirement eligibility or to other employment and that the asserted cost savings are not credible. The same commenter stated the purported reduction in costs is nonsense unless it is accompanied by a legislative reduction in tasking to the affected agency, because the work will just fall to the remaining employees and will either be done with less rigor and attention to detail or will be contracted out to a company that is profit-motivated instead of mission-motivated.
Comment 0016 stated that months of payroll expenditures for tens of thousands of DRP participants performing no work, the loss of institutional knowledge, the collapse of continuity in mission-critical functions, and the documented degradation of agency capacity cannot be a de minimis cost. Comment 0029 stated that real-world impacts of authorizing administrative leave for employees facing a RIF include “not only billions of dollars in direct financial losses but also serious constraints on agencies' ability to carry out their statutory missions.” Comment 0004 objected that OPM “must conduct a complete economic impact analysis that accounts for the multiplier effect of federal employee spending in local economies, the impact on housing markets, the downstream consequences for private sector businesses that depend on stable federal employment in their communities, and the economic value of public services that go undelivered when federal employees are placed on administrative leave rather than deployed productively.” Comment 0030, a labor organization, further asserted that OPM's claimed cost savings are contrary to publicly available data, citing a June 2026 Public Citizen analysis estimating that the 2025 deferred resignation programs cost approximately $11 billion, and Government Accountability Office (GAO) reports documenting that agencies subsequently rehired employees who had participated in those programs.
OPM disagrees that a more extensive cost analysis is required. The relevant question under
E.O. 12866
and
E.O. 13563
is the incremental effect of this rule relative to the baseline. The baseline includes the Governmentwide policies already in effect—including the Agency Policy Template—that parallel the rule's provisions. The distinction commenters draw between the act of codifying and the substance being codified is precisely what the baseline concept captures: because the substance is already in effect, the incremental effect of codifying it is the appropriate measure of this rule's costs and benefits. Because the rule primarily codifies those existing policies, OPM does not project that the rule itself will significantly change the usage of administrative leave or result in incremental costs or savings approaching the $100 million significance threshold. Expenditures associated with the 2025 deferred resignation programs were incurred under prior policies and are not costs of this rule; a retrospective accounting of those programs is beyond the scope of this rulemaking.
OPM further notes that decisions to conduct particular workforce realignment initiatives—and their associated costs and savings—are made by individual agencies under separate authorities and processes; this rule does not mandate any such initiative. To the extent the rule has effects, OPM expects them to be beneficial: greater consistency across agencies, a firmer legal foundation for existing policies, and fewer disputes. The rehiring and cost data the commenters cite concern the execution of the 2025 programs under then-existing authorities and policies; those data may inform how agencies design and administer future initiatives, but they do not alter the incremental analysis of a rule that codifies the governing framework and directs no particular program.
The economic analysis accurately reflects the impact of this rule, which applies only to Federal agencies and Federal employees and codifies policies already in effect Governmentwide through the OPM Fact Sheet: Administrative Leave and the Agency Policy Template. The certification under the Regulatory Flexibility Act addresses the absence of a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The rule does not authorize, fund, or direct any particular workforce reduction; decisions on staffing levels are made by agencies under separate authorities and remain subject to appropriations law.

However, the indirect effects the commenters identify—the multiplier effect of Federal employee spending in local economies, impacts on housing markets, downstream consequences for private-sector businesses, and the economic value of public services—are consequences of agency staffing decisions made under separate authorities, not incremental effects of this rule, and
E.O. 12866
does not require quantification of speculative indirect effects of actions that this rule neither mandates nor funds.
OPM notes that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs designated this action significant under
(
printed page 65929)
E.O. 12866
section 3(f) and that OPM examined the impact of the rule as required by E.O.s 12866 and 13563. An agency must consider the important aspects of the problem before it (see
Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association of the United States, Inc.
v.
State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.,
463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)), but that obligation does not require quantification of the indirect effects of separate agency staffing decisions that this rule does not direct, and an agency's predictive judgments about the effects of its rules need only be reasonable and reasonably explained (see
FCC
v.
Prometheus Radio Project,
592 U.S. 414 (2021)).
Section D.1.b of the Agency Policy Template already contemplates that workforce restructuring initiatives such as deferred resignation or VERA may lead to a separation for retirement. Section 630.1403(c)(9) is drafted consistently with that policy: it reaches employees who sign a written agreement to voluntarily separate on a specified future date. OPM does not agree that administrative leave may be provided for the purpose of enabling an employee to obtain other employment. An employee in an administrative leave status remains a Federal employee subject to applicable standards of conduct and to agency requirements governing outside employment.
OPM acknowledged in the proposed rule that there is a temporary cost to providing administrative leave and stated its judgment that these programs can generate long-term savings by reducing Federal staffing levels. Whether an agency's remaining workload should be reduced, redistributed, or performed under contract is a matter for the agency and, where applicable, for Congress, and is outside the scope of this rulemaking. OPM makes no changes in response to these comments.
F. Due Process
Two individual commenters (comments 0019 and 0021) urged OPM to withdraw this proposal and preserve the due process protections that have helped maintain a competent, professional, merit-based civil service for decades. Comment 0019 expressed concern that the rule significantly weakens longstanding due process protections for Federal employees. Comment 0021 expressed concern that expanded and largely unreviewable agency discretion in the proposed rule is inconsistent with the merit system principles in
5 U.S.C. 2301
and with the independence, professionalism, and nonpartisan character of the career civil service. The commenter further stated that regulations should be written to withstand misuse by any future administration by anchoring workforce management authority to merit system principles in
5 U.S.C. 2301
.
OPM does not agree that the final rule is inconsistent with the merit system principles in
5 U.S.C. 2301
. Agency discretion under these regulations is not unbounded. As the proposed rule states, acceptable uses are those uses, within the bounds of law and regulation, that an agency determines to be appropriate in its sole and exclusive discretion; the merit system principles, appropriations law, and other governing law continue to apply.
The regulatory framework contains the structural safeguards the commenter seeks. A use of administrative leave must satisfy one or more of the four guiding principles in § 630.1403(a)(1); it must be permitted under written agency policy or, if not specifically authorized in policy, be approved on a case-by-case basis by an authorized agency official at least one level higher than the official making the initial determination (§ 630.1403(a)(5); Agency Policy Template (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025), section B.3.b); and the authorized agency official must consider the decision factors in § 630.1403(a)(6), which include consistent treatment of similarly situated employees. Each authorized agency official is accountable for the policies he or she establishes and should be prepared to show how due consideration was given to the principles and requirements in law, regulations, and policy (Agency Policy Template, section B.3.a). Use of administrative leave must be recorded as a stand-alone category of leave and reported to OPM's Enterprise Human Resources Integration database (
5 U.S.C. 6329a(b)(2)
;
5 CFR 630.1406(c)
; Agency Policy Template, section G), and managers are responsible for administering the program with integrity and for identifying, investigating, and correcting leave errors and abuse (Agency Policy Template, section H.1).
These provisions create no new authority to separate, demote, or discipline an employee. Involuntary separations remain governed by
5 CFR part 351
and, where applicable,
5 U.S.C. chapters 43
and
75
. OPM declines to withdraw the rule and views these comments as largely outside the scope of the rule.
G. Allegations That the Rulemaking Is Arbitrary and Capricious
A labor organization (comment 0030) objected that OPM's process of codifying policy decisions that OPM has already made renders this rulemaking arbitrary and capricious. The labor organization also asserted that OPM failed to make reasoned conclusions based on objective evidence about the rule's ramifications, and that the supporting analysis is internally inconsistent because it states both that the use of administrative leave in connection with deferred resignation programs and other workforce restructuring initiatives can generate large long-term savings and that OPM does not project that costs or savings will result from the regulations. Similarly, comment 0025 argued that the rule is arbitrary and capricious because OPM did not acknowledge and adequately explain a departure from the December 2024 final rule, citing
FCC
v.
Fox Television Stations, Inc.,
556 U.S. 502 (2009).
OPM disagrees with the premise that this rule reverses the 2024 final rule. The final rule leaves the 2024 rule's core interpretive framework intact: the 10-workday limit continues to apply to agency-directed placement for investigative purposes; general administrative leave for civic, operational, and employee-support purposes continues outside that cap; and the general principles of § 630.1403(a)—including the principle that administrative leave ordinarily should not exceed one workday for a single incidence—are retained. What the rule adds are clarifying examples of acceptable uses, three new binding prohibitions, and conforming terminology. The examples largely codify OPM policies issued after the 2024 rule, including the Agency Policy Template (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025), and were fully explained in the proposed rule's preamble.
To the extent the rule refines the 2024 framework—for example, by expressly addressing extended leave in transition-to-separation contexts that the 2024 rule did not specifically discuss—OPM has acknowledged the additions and explained the basis for them, including agencies' experience administering the 2024 regulations and the need for greater consistency and a firmer legal foundation for existing policies. That explanation satisfies the standard articulated in
Fox Television,
556 U.S. at 515, which requires a reasoned explanation for a change, not a heightened one, except in circumstances not present here.
As explained in the Statement of Need, after more than a year of experience applying the December 2024 final regulations, OPM identified the need to clarify certain matters, and
(
printed page 65930)
while OPM has issued policy guidance that largely addresses those matters, regulations are needed to achieve greater consistency across agencies and a firmer legal foundation for the policies.
Notice-and-comment rulemaking is the appropriate means of converting Governmentwide policy into binding regulation, and OPM has proposed for public comment both new prohibitions that would bind agencies and new examples of acceptable uses. OPM further notes that CPM 2025-12 described the Agency Policy Template as a living document that would be improved and refined to address issues arising during implementation.
Further, the premise that OPM had already adopted the policies being codified does not render the rulemaking arbitrary and capricious. An agency does not prejudge a rulemaking by proposing to codify its existing policies; the APA requires that the agency maintain an open mind and consider the comments received, not that it begin with an empty one (see
Association of National Advertisers, Inc.
v.
FTC,
627 F.2d 1151 (D.C. Cir. 1979) (rulemaker may be disqualified only on a clear and convincing showing of an unalterably closed mind)).
This final rule demonstrates that consideration: in response to the comments, OPM is adding a new acceptable-use example for physical fitness activities, adding a regulatory definition of “sole and exclusive discretion,” and making other changes described in this preamble. As to the asserted lack of factual support and internal inconsistency, OPM responds in section III.E of this preamble. In brief, the projection that codification will not significantly change the usage of administrative leave rests on the fact that agencies have operated under parallel Governmentwide policies since July 2025, and there is no inconsistency between OPM's judgment that workforce restructuring initiatives can generate long-term savings and its projection that this rule—which neither mandates nor funds any such initiative—will not itself produce significant incremental costs or savings.
OPM makes no changes in response to these comments.
H. “Sole and Exclusive” Discretion
Comment 0025 argued that describing agency discretion (in §§ 630.1403(a) and 715.202(b)) as “sole and exclusive” is unnecessary and misleading because agency discretion remains bounded by statute, regulation, appropriations law, collective-bargaining obligations, merit system principles, and judicial review. The commenter also stated the “sole and exclusive discretion” language “sits uneasily with OPM's own governmentwide oversight role.”
One labor organization, comment 0030, asserted that the “sole and exclusive discretion” language is unlawful and arbitrary in that it removes administrative leave from collective bargaining by reference to OPM's own judgment without a statutory basis (invoking Federal Labor Relations Authority precedent and the right of an exclusive representative to negotiate over conditions of employment under
5 U.S.C. 7102
and
7114
). Another labor organization (comment 0022) commented that this amendment would create significant legal consequences because, under the Federal labor statute, “agencies are not required to bargain over matters over which they have sole and exclusive discretion.” AFGE National Veterans Affairs Council # 53, 71 F.L.R.A. 410, 412 & n.22 (2019). Similar comments were made by an anonymous commenter (comment 0031).
Comment 0030 asserted that OPM lacks statutory authority to insert “sole and exclusive discretion” into
5 CFR 630.1403(a)
and
5 CFR 715.202(b)
. Under the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), an involuntary resignation or a resignation induced by coercion, duress, or agency misrepresentation constitutes an adverse action (constructive removal) within the mandatory appellate jurisdiction of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB). The commenter states that OPM cannot divest the MSPB of jurisdiction over involuntary-resignation and constructive-removal claims, or foreclose Federal Circuit review, because an involuntary or coerced resignation is an appealable adverse action (citing
Scharf
v.
Department of the Air Force,
710 F.2d 1572 (Fed. Cir. 1983);
Luecht
v.
Department of the Navy,
87 M.S.P.R. 297 (2000); and
Lindahl
v.
Office of Personnel Management,
470 U.S. 768 (1985)). The comment asks that OPM remove “sole and exclusive discretion” and explicitly state that resignation withdrawal denials remain subject to MSPB review under
5 U.S.C. chapter 75
.
As the preamble to the proposed rule stated, acceptable uses of administrative leave are those an agency determines appropriate “within the bounds of law and regulation.” The “sole and exclusive” formulation clarifies allocation of decision-making responsibility—that the decision whether to provide administrative leave in a given circumstance rests with the agency, that no use of administrative leave is a mandatory entitlement, and that OPM's enumeration of acceptable uses does not obligate any agency to provide leave in those circumstances. This is consistent with Congress's assignment of leave-management responsibility to agency heads. The phrase does not diminish the binding prohibitions in § 630.1403(b), the statutory limits in sections 6329a and 6329b, applicable appropriations law, or the recording and reporting requirements that continue to apply, and it does not alter any applicable standard of review.
OPM's intent regarding the use of “sole and exclusive discretion” in the administrative leave regulations (in § 630.1403(a)(2), (a)(4), and (c)) is to make explicit that the
acceptable-use determination
—whether a given circumstance qualifies for administrative leave at all—rests with the agency and cannot be converted into a mandatory entitlement, including through negotiated agreement. The statutory basis for using the term “sole and exclusive discretion” is that the law in
5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1)
authorizes the OPM Director to prescribe regulations that address the acceptable agency uses of administrative leave. OPM believes the change better reflects the decision of Congress to give this discretionary leave authority to agency heads, who make final decisions on mission needs and the use of limited budget resources, and the sense of Congress that agency heads would be responsible for managing and overseeing the effective and prudent use of the leave.
OPM believes the intent of Congress was for agencies to always retain discretion in providing or not providing administrative leave in any circumstance (subject to law and OPM regulations) and has regulated accordingly. The use of the “sole and exclusive discretion” language is consistent with the existing text of § 630.1403(a)(4), which already requires that an agency retain the discretion to provide or not provide administrative leave in any circumstance based on agency judgments regarding mission needs and already prevents an agency from establishing any application of administrative leave as a mandatory entitlement.
In response to the comments invoking Federal Labor Relations Authority precedent, OPM confirms that the “sole and exclusive discretion” language is intended to preserve the agency's discretion over acceptable-use determinations, which may not be limited or conditioned by a negotiated agreement or converted into a mandatory entitlement; collective
(
printed page 65931)
bargaining obligations under
5 U.S.C. chapter 71
otherwise continue to apply according to their terms. Under
5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1)
, the duty to bargain in good faith extends to matters that are the subject of a rule or regulation only if the rule or regulation is not a Governmentwide rule or regulation; the regulations in this subpart are Governmentwide regulations issued under
5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1)
. OPM likewise confirms that nothing in this rule divests the MSPB of jurisdiction over a claim that a resignation was involuntary or the product of coercion, duress, or agency misrepresentation—which remains an appealable constructive removal—or forecloses judicial review of a final Board decision. See section III.R of this preamble.
In the preamble for the proposed regulations issued on June 29, 2026, OPM stated that an agency's use of its sole and exclusive discretion in providing administrative leave must be done “within the bounds of law and regulation” (
91 FR 39033
). Given the comments about the “sole and exclusive discretion” language related to administrative leave, we are adding a definition of the term in § 630.1402 to make clear that it is discretion that rests with an agency alone; that is exercised within the bounds of
5 U.S.C. 6329a
and other applicable law, applicable Presidential directives, and the regulations in this subpart; and that may not be limited or conditioned by any agreement or established as a mandatory entitlement. Other than that change, OPM is making no changes in response to this line of comments. The term “sole and exclusive discretion” in § 715.202(b) should be interpreted in a similar manner.
I. Physical Fitness Activities
OPM's proposed regulations requested “comments on the policy of allowing limited use of administrative leave for physical fitness activities and on whether this policy should be included in the regulatory examples of acceptable uses.” OPM received numerous comments on this proposal. See, for example, comments 0012, 0013, 0018, 0020, 0024, 0028, and 0030.
Generally, the comments were favorable for including physical fitness as an acceptable use. Comment 0011 stated that as “someone who has recommitted to better health, I would appreciate having the administrative leave available” to make time for physical fitness, which is currently difficult to do outside of duty hours with a three-hour daily commute and home commitments. Comment 0012 recounted substantial personal improvements in weight and blood pressure after adopting a daily walking and gym regimen during Federal service, along with increased energy, no medical issues, and over 2,000 hours of unused sick leave. The commenter recommended authorizing administrative leave for physical fitness, reasoning that duty time to exercise would spur participation, improve employee health, and reduce sick leave usage.
Comment 0013 stated: “Research has shown that a healthier workforce lowers healthcare & benefit costs, enhances productivity & performance, reduces stress, improves employee engagement, & improves overall mental health.” The commenter proposed authorizing a total of 3 hours of administrative leave per week (1 hour per day, three days per week, to include time for changing, travel, and showering), depending on workload and agency requirements.
Comment 0015 contended that administrative leave for physical exercise would yield near-immediate improvements in engagement and productivity and, given the connection between physical and mental well-being, would also improve job satisfaction and retention. Comment 0018 stated that permitting a limited amount of duty time for physical fitness is increasingly common across Federal agencies, typically up to one hour per day, three days per week, and recommended that OPM adopt a comparable allowance to align with prevailing practice and support employee health, morale, and readiness.
Comment 0020 described duty-time physical fitness as a strategic “people first” initiative, citing improved workforce readiness and resiliency, enhanced productivity and focus, higher morale and reduced burnout, decreased sick leave usage and absenteeism, and—because the benefit would be available annually rather than once in a career—the formation of lasting healthy habits. Noting significant return on investment and widespread private-sector adoption, the commenter urged OPM to retain physical fitness as an authorized use of administrative leave.
Comment 0023 supported the provision authorizing limited administrative leave for physical fitness, endorsing the retention of agency discretion based on mission needs, and stated that the provision would reduce burnout and improve work-life balance, well-being, motivation, and concentration. The commenter also noted that the rule's predictability should reduce disputes.
Comment 0024 recommended permitting and encouraging administrative leave for fitness activities similar to the Civilian Fitness Program, with program goals aligned to Army fitness standards, reasoning that because Federal employees are mobilized to support the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), immigration efforts, and other demand-based taskings, a physically capable workforce improves contingency readiness. Comment 0028, citing Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data on physical inactivity, obesity, diabetes, and heart disease, and CDC's
Physical Activity in the Workplace: A Guide for Employers,
stated that administrative leave for physical activity would support employers and their business needs because engaging in physical activities can result in reduced sick days, increased productivity, lower health care costs, and decreased risk of developing costly chronic diseases. Pointing to existing agency programs offering up to one hour three times per week, the commenter recommended permitting onsite or offsite activity.
A labor organization (comment 0022) stated that it “supports this policy and recommends including it in the regulatory examples of acceptable uses.” The commenter explained that it “has negotiated a Physical Fitness Program into its contract with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).” The commenter “accordingly supports similar programs across the government and supports the idea of OPM including physical fitness activities as an example of acceptable use in the administrative leave regulations.” Another labor organization (comment 0030), while opposing the proposed rule overall, stated that in the event OPM does not withdraw the rule, it supports allowing administrative leave to be used for physical fitness activities.

The commenter further stated: “Employees must then extend their workday by the equivalent amount of time of the break.” The agency stated the use of administrative leave for physical fitness activities is unnecessary at their agency, as the unpaid health and wellness break period policy has been successful in balancing employee personal needs with limited agency resources toward accomplishing its critical mission.
Following consideration of the comments, OPM is adding a new
(

§ 630.1403(c)(8) in this final rule listing approved physical fitness activities as an acceptable use of administrative leave and is redesignating the examples proposed as paragraphs (c)(8) through (c)(10) as paragraphs (c)(9) through (c)(11).
