J. Employee Geographic Relocation
Three individual commenters (comments 0002, 0003, 0005) proposed that OPM add an example authorizing administrative leave for an employee who must relocate his or her residence to accept a new appointment or assignment. Comment 0002 argued that omitting such a use is inconsistent with providing administrative leave for a civilian employee accompanying a military spouse under
5 CFR 630.1403(c)(7)
. Comment 0003 argued that a recruitment, relocation, or retention incentive is not the exclusive means of addressing relocation burdens and that administrative leave is needed to avoid a gap in pay status when an employee moves between appointments. Comment 0005 noted administrative leave for employees relocating a significant distance from their current duty station would allow employees to better manage the transition without depleting their earned personal leave. All three of these commenters acknowledged that agencies already have the discretion to offer administrative leave for this purpose. Two of the commenters (comments 0002 and 0003) proposed regulatory text authorizing administrative leave for an employee's own relocation to a new appointment or assignment.
OPM does not support adding an example that allows general use of administrative leave for activities related to an employee's move to a different permanent duty station. Adding such an example would indicate a Governmentwide policy that such use is acceptable. OPM prefers to let agencies adopt their own policies in this area. The example in § 630.1403(c)(7)—allowing use of administrative leave for an employee whose spouse, a member of the uniformed services or a Federal civilian employee, must relocate as a result of military orders or agency direction, as applicable—does reflect an established Governmentwide policy in section D.1.c of the Agency Policy Template (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025). That policy implements a specific Presidential directive—
E.O. 14100
of June 9, 2023—and OPM's related memorandum of November 9, 2023, to agency heads. There is no comparable Governmentwide directive addressing an employee's own change of residence to accept a new appointment or assignment, and OPM does not view the absence of such an example as an inconsistency in the proposed list.
We note that, if an employee has been approved to receive a house hunting allowance under
41 CFR part 302-5
(which an agency may choose to apply to employees under certain specified conditions), time spent on house hunting activities during regular work hours is treated as official duty time. Also, time spent on activities to accomplish tasks that are directly required in connection with an approved move to a new permanent duty station determined to be in the Government's interest (resulting in payment of relocation expenses)—such as obtaining passports and vaccinations, adhering to government housing authority requirements (if applicable), or being present for packing and receiving of household goods—is considered official duty time. Finally, the list in § 630.1403(c) is noncomprehensive. An agency may adopt its own written policy to allow limited use of administrative leave for move-related activities that are not duty time, if such use is determined to be in the Government's interest and the use satisfies the guiding principles in § 630.1403(a)(1), the authorized agency official considers the decision factors in § 630.1403(a)(6), and the use is approved consistent with § 630.1403(a)(5) and section D.2.h of the Agency Policy Template.
OPM declines to add the suggested example.
K. Reliance Interests
Comment 0025 argued that OPM failed to consider reliance interests, citing
Department of Homeland Security
v.
Regents of the University of California,
591 U.S. 1 (2020), including agencies' investments in implementing the 2024 rule and operational reliance on employees remaining in duty status through reorganizations and RIF notice periods.
OPM has considered the reliance interests the commenter identifies and concludes they do not counsel against finalizing the rule. First, because the rule largely codifies policies already in effect under the Agency Policy Template since July 2025, agencies, payroll providers, and employees have been operating under substantially these policies for approximately a year; codification reduces, rather than disrupts, transition burdens by confirming the framework agencies have already implemented. The changes required—principally conforming terminology, incorporating the new binding prohibitions, and providing specific examples of acceptable uses—are modest.
Second, as to operational reliance, the rule is permissive, not mandatory. It does not require any agency to place any employee on administrative leave during a workforce realignment or RIF notice period. Agencies retain full discretion to keep employees in duty status—and under revised § 351.806, duty status remains the rule under ordinary circumstances—precisely so that agencies can weigh mission needs, knowledge transfer, records preservation, and service continuity in each case. The judgment about whether an employee's continued presence serves the Government's interests during a particular realignment is one the agency, not OPM, is best positioned to make.

M. Duty Status Presumption During RIF Notice Periods (§ 351.806)
Comment 0025 urged OPM to preserve the existing duty-status presumption during RIF notice periods, arguing that RIF notices are not disciplinary, that employees perform valuable transition work during notice periods, that existing authorities already address unusual cases, and that OPM has not identified a gap warranting a RIF-specific administrative-leave authorization.
The final rule preserves the duty-status presumption with a minor change in terminology. Revised § 351.806(a) provides that “[u]nder ordinary circumstances, an employee will remain in a duty status during the notice period.” The change from “when possible” to “under ordinary circumstances” conforms the RIF regulation to the parallel standard in
5 CFR 752.404(b)(3)
governing notice periods for proposed removals and suspensions, and more accurately reflects that the determination involves an assessment of circumstances rather than literal possibility. Paragraph (b) then confirms—consistent with the Agency Policy Template—that an agency may place a RIF-affected employee on administrative leave for all or part of the notice period when the agency determines that such leave is appropriate and consistent with part 630, subpart N.
OPM agrees that RIF notice periods are not inherently disciplinary and that employees frequently perform valuable work during them; that is why duty status remains the default. But circumstances vary: an agency may determine, for example, that continued systems access during a large-scale reorganization presents security or records-integrity risks, that available work has genuinely ceased for the affected positions, or that other Government interests warrant non-duty status. The rule leaves that judgment to the agency familiar with the facts, rather than requiring agencies to rely on a patchwork of assignment, telework, and leave authorities that may not fit the circumstances of a RIF. Nothing in the revision permits use of administrative leave inconsistent with subpart N of part 630.
N. Nomenclature Change (“Grant” To “Provide”) (Part 630, Subpart N)
Comment 0025 objected to replacing “grant/granted/granting” with “provide/provided/providing” throughout subpart N, arguing that the change extends agency-directed administrative leave beyond the limits of the Act and the 2024 rule by encompassing leave imposed without employee consent.
OPM disagrees that the nomenclature change effects any substantive expansion of authority. As explained in the proposed rule, “grant” inaccurately implies that administrative leave is furnished only at an employee's request, which has never been the case—for example, employees have long been placed on administrative leave for investigative purposes without their consent, a practice Congress itself recognized and regulated in sections 6329a and 6329b. “Provide” is a neutral term that accurately describes the provision of administrative leave with or without the employee's consent. The statutory 10-workday limit continues to apply to employees “placed” on administrative leave for investigative purposes, as provided in § 630.1404(a). For other uses of administrative leave, which may be voluntarily accepted or imposed without the employee's consent, we are using the term “provide.” The terminology change harmonizes the regulatory text with existing practice and with the structure of the statute; it does not authorize any use of administrative leave that would otherwise be impermissible.
O. Prohibition on Administrative Leave for Poll Workers (§ 630.1403(b)(5))
Several comments, including 0016, 0022, 0030, and 0031, objected to the prohibition of administrative leave for service as a poll worker or poll observer found in proposed § 630.1403(b)(5). The commenters argued that the prohibition is unrelated to workforce realignment, discourages civic participation amid documented poll-worker shortages, saves little, and reverses OPM's prior guidance that agencies allow up to 4 hours of administrative leave for nonpartisan poll service. A labor organization (comment 0022) characterized limited administrative leave for nonpartisan poll service as an important, pro-democracy policy choice. Another labor organization (comment 0030) argued that OPM offered no reasoned explanation or evidence for the prohibition and characterized it as an attempt to stifle Federal employees' exercise of their constitutional rights.
OPM notes that the changes in the administrative leave regulations are not limited to changes related to workforce realignment. OPM acknowledges that this provision changes OPM's prior policies that agencies could allow limited administrative leave for nonpartisan poll service. However, those prior policies were a departure from longstanding Governmentwide policies that existed before 2020, which focused on administrative leave for voting, not for poll workers. Based on its authority to regulate acceptable uses of administrative leave, OPM has determined that administrative leave should be limited to the purpose of ensuring employees a reasonable opportunity to vote (see § 630.1403(c)(2)). OPM policy (section E.1.d of the Agency Policy Template) already provided that administrative leave may not be used to cover service by poll workers or poll observers in connection with elections, whether that service is partisan or nonpartisan and whether paid or unpaid. Limiting administrative leave to voting itself also avoids placing agencies in the position
(
printed page 65934)
of assessing whether particular election-related service is partisan or nonpartisan.
The prohibition does not restrict any employee's ability to serve as a poll worker or poll observer; it addresses only whether that service will be subsidized with paid leave from Federal duty, and a decision not to subsidize an activity does not infringe the right to engage in it (see
Regan
v.
Taxation With Representation of Washington,
461 U.S. 540, 549 (1983)). Employees who wish to serve as poll workers or poll observers may use other available workforce flexibilities, including annual leave, compensatory time off earned via overtime work, compensatory time off for travel, credit hours under a flexible work schedule, an adjustment of working hours under a flexible work schedule, or leave without pay. OPM makes no change in response to these comments.
P. Administrative Leave Prior to a Holiday (§ 630.1403(c)(5))
Regarding § 630.1403(c)(5), comment 0024 stated that early dismissal before a Federal holiday should not be subject to a hard 2-hour cap and that longer dismissals should be available for particular occasions, including days of national observance.
OPM notes that § 630.1403(c)(5) does not establish a hard cap since it states that the administrative leave should “generally” be no more than 2 hours. This regulation should be read with sections D.2.d and E.2.a of the Agency Policy Template (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025), which provide that such leave may not exceed 2 hours unless specifically approved by the agency head. The flexibility the commenter seeks for longer periods of dismissal for particular occasions is therefore already available through agency head approval. Presidentially directed closures and days of national observance provided by the President using his or her constitutional authority as head of the Executive branch are not administrative leave under
5 U.S.C. 6329a
and are not governed by subpart N or by an agency's administrative leave policy (Agency Policy Template, section A.2.b and Appendix 1). Such occasions are therefore outside this rulemaking. OPM notes separately that proposed § 630.1403(b)(1) continues to prohibit use of administrative leave to mark the memory of a deceased former Federal official (see also
5 U.S.C. 6105
).
Q. Settlement Agreement (§ 630.1403(c)(11))
Comment 0025 argued that authorizing extended administrative leave to facilitate the voluntary resignation of employees with documented poor performance or misconduct under a settlement agreement recreates the pre-Act practices Congress sought to control, and that the provision lacks meaningful time limits, approval procedures, or reporting requirements.
Comment 0026 recommended that the settlement agreement example at proposed § 630.1403(c)(10) (redesignated as § 630.1403(c)(11) in this final rule) be removed or relocated to the investigative leave framework so the leave is tracked with specificity and that OPM not conflate administrative leave with the performance and conduct action procedures in
5 U.S.C. chapters 43
and
75
.
OPM disagrees. Section 630.1403(c)(11) is a narrow provision subject to multiple conditions: there must be documented allegations of poor performance or misconduct by the employee (see discussion later in this section); the leave must be provided under a settlement agreement; the agency must determine that the settlement is in the Government's best interests; and the agency must first consider all other reasonable alternatives. The leave is also subject to Governmentwide limits established by OPM and any agency-specific limits.
These conditions distinguish the provision from the pre-Act practice GAO documented, in which employees remained in indefinite paid non-duty status during unresolved investigations and adverse actions with no resolution in sight. By contrast, leave under paragraph (c)(11) is tied to a negotiated resolution—a definite separation date—and serves to conclude, not prolong, the personnel matter. Settlement of disputed personnel actions can avoid protracted litigation costs and expedite the removal of employees whose performance or conduct has been identified as unsatisfactory—outcomes consistent with efficient and prudent management of the workforce. Where an agency instead pursues an adverse action, the notice-leave framework of section 6329b continues to apply according to its terms; nothing in this rule alters it.
Accordingly, OPM declines to remove § 630.1403(c)(11) or to relocate this use to investigative leave. Investigative leave under
5 U.S.C. 6329b
is available only in connection with an ongoing investigation and only after the 10-workday administrative leave period has been exhausted, and notice leave is available only after an agency has proposed an adverse action. As the commenter recognizes, a settlement may be reached after an investigation has concluded, and it may also be reached where no investigation was opened; in those circumstances neither section 6329b category is available. If an employee is being excused from duty for investigative purposes after reaching the 10-workday limit, § 630.1403(b)(3) forecloses the pre-2016 practice, since it requires that section 6329b be applied. OPM notes that, if administrative leave is used in connection with a settlement agreement, that usage will be documented in the settlement agreement and will be tracked as administrative leave in agency timekeeping and payroll systems. OPM has revised the language in § 630.1403(c)(11) to make clear that, while no final determination of poor performance or misconduct need be found, an agency may apply this provision only where the allegations of poor performance or misconduct are documented.
R. Resignation Withdrawal (§  715.202(b))
Many commenters opposed treating an employee's acceptance of deferred-resignation benefits as a valid reason to deny a resignation withdrawal. Two individual commenters (comments 0014 and 0016) opposed any proposal that would categorically prohibit employees from withdrawing a resignation before its effective date because they believed an employee who may have decided under duress/short deadlines may feel trapped. Comment 0016 urged OPM to withdraw provisions proposed in §  715.202(b) arguing that an employee's acceptance of deferred-resignation benefits should not by itself justify denying withdrawal of the resignation. The commenter stated that prior practice permitted withdrawal before the effective date absent a concrete agency reason such as a committed replacement hire or administrative disruption and that OPM had offered no principled basis for foreclosing reconsideration before the resignation takes effect. The commenter further argued that recharacterizing the receipt of leave benefits—benefits the employee did not design and the commenter asserted were often accepted under duress and compressed deadlines—as itself a valid reason to deny withdrawal “inverts the protective purpose of the rule,” and that resignation should remain a decision an employee can reconsider until it takes effect.
Comment 0014 believes OPM should adopt a policy that balances the interest of both employees and agencies and that an agency be permitted to decline a withdrawal request before its effective
(
printed page 65935)
date only where granting it would cause the agency substantial hardship or prejudice. A labor organization (comment 0022) objected to this provision stating it is unfair to employees who frequently make these decisions under needlessly short deadlines, without complete or accurate information. The labor organization suggested that, if OPM insists on making resignation decisions irrevocable, it should at a minimum give employees more time to make these difficult and important choices. In addition, comments 0026 and 0031 argued the change is unnecessary because § 715.202 already says “may” and that whether to accept a withdrawal or seek repayment should be left to individual agencies and to collective bargaining, and that OPM failed to consider less-restrictive alternatives and offered two: (1) retaining the traditional operational-disruption standard (committed replacement hire or position abolition, per
Luecht
), and (2) permitting withdrawal conditioned on retroactively reclassifying the administrative leave to annual leave, compensatory time, or leave without pay (LWOP) (recoupment). Comment 0026 stated that changing the resignation regulations is unnecessary because § 715.202(b) is already permissive, with a recommendation that a time component be added within which an employee may withdraw a deferred resignation.
This final rule does not categorically prohibit the withdrawal of a resignation. Revised § 715.202(b) retains the requirement that an agency may decline a request to withdraw a resignation before its effective date only when the agency has a valid reason and explains that reason to the employee, and it retains the rule that avoidance of adverse action proceedings is not a valid reason.
OPM notes that the revision to § 715.202(b) makes two changes. It states that the decision to accept or decline a withdrawal request is made in the agency's sole and exclusive discretion, and it adds one further example to the nonexclusive list of valid reasons—the employee's acceptance of benefits provided under a deferred resignation agreement. The list continues to read “includes, but is not limited to,” and continues to identify administrative disruption and the hiring or commitment to hire a replacement, which are the agency-reliance circumstances the commenter describes. Nothing in the final rule requires an agency to decline a withdrawal request in any case, and an agency remains free to accept one where it determines that retaining the employee serves its interests.
OPM identified the need for this example because, when an employee has agreed to resign on a future date and has received paid administrative leave in connection with that agreement, there is no authority to require or permit repayment of the administrative leave benefits after they have been provided. Identifying acceptance of such benefits as a valid reason gives agencies a clear and specific regulatory basis for a determination they may already make under the existing regulation. OPM declines to adopt the additional balancing standard the commenter proposes, which would constrain discretion the existing regulation affords agencies.
In response to comments 0026 and 0031, OPM acknowledges that § 715.202(b) already uses permissive language, and the final rule retains it: an agency may, in its sole and exclusive discretion, accept or decline an employee's request to withdraw a resignation, and may decline only when it has a valid reason and explains that reason to the employee. OPM has also considered the less-restrictive alternatives commenters offered and declines to adopt them. Retaining only the traditional operational-disruption standard is unnecessary because the regulation continues to identify administrative disruption and the hiring or commitment to hire a replacement as valid reasons; the revision adds one further nonexclusive example rather than displacing those reasons. OPM likewise declines to condition withdrawal on retroactive reclassification of administrative leave to annual leave, compensatory time, or leave without pay because, as explained above, there is no authority to require or permit repayment or reclassification of administrative leave benefits after they have been provided. OPM does not agree that a separate statutory authority for deferred resignation is needed to support the provision: the resignation is effected under § 715.202(a), and the paid leave provided before its effective date is administrative leave under
5 U.S.C. 6329a
. As to the recommendation to add a time component within which an employee may withdraw a deferred resignation, OPM declines to add a fixed period to § 715.202. That section applies at any time before the resignation becomes effective, and the timing terms of a particular deferred resignation offer, including the length of any decision window, are a matter of program design rather than of this regulation. As to concerns that employees accept deferred resignation offers under compressed deadlines or duress, nothing in this rule prevents an agency from granting a withdrawal request, and an employee who contends that a resignation was involuntary or the product of duress, coercion, or agency misrepresentation retains the right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board; this rule does not affect that review. To the extent comments 0030 and 0031 suggest that these matters be left to case-by-case collective bargaining, § 715.202 is a longstanding Governmentwide regulation, and under
5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1)
the duty to bargain does not extend to matters that are the subject of a Governmentwide rule or regulation. OPM makes no changes in response to these comments.
S. Miscellaneous Comments
Comment 0027 asked how agency limits on workforce realignment leave interact with the Governmentwide limit and whether the regulatory text should state that a longer agency limit requires OPM approval; whether the regulations will address employees in Schedule Policy/Career positions and agency grievance procedures; and whether extended administrative leave is cost-effective relative to reduction-in-force procedures, with a recommendation that deferred resignation leave be limited to 10 days unless the employee is retirement eligible.
Agency limits must operate within the Governmentwide limit; an agency may adopt a more restrictive limit but may not exceed the Governmentwide limit on its own authority. The current Governmentwide limit, stated in section D.1.b of the Agency Policy Template (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025), is that beginning in calendar year 2026, use of administrative leave by an employee in connection with a workforce realignment initiative is limited to 12 weeks in any individual instance unless a higher threshold has been jointly approved by OPM and the Office of Management and Budget in a specified set of circumstances. A higher threshold of 6 months was later approved for workforce-restructuring-related DRP agreements that took effect in FY 2026. OPM notes that the phrase “subject to Governmentwide limits established by OPM or agency limits” in § 630.1403(c)(9) and (c)(11) specifically incorporates any Governmentwide limit. To clarify that agency limits cannot supersede Governmentwide limits, we are revising the phrase in those two paragraphs by substituting “and” for “or”.
Employees in Schedule Policy/Career positions who have an established work schedule are covered on the same basis
(
printed page 65936)
as other covered employees. As the comment notes, agencies retain the sole and exclusive discretion to determine whether to provide administrative leave to any employee or category of employees based on their consideration of agency mission requirements, and an agency may address specific categories or scenarios in its own written policy under § 630.1403(a)(5).
Agency grievance procedures are governed by
5 CFR part 771
and any applicable negotiated grievance procedure and are outside the scope of these leave regulations.
OPM acknowledged in the proposed rule that there is a temporary cost to providing administrative leave and stated its judgment that these programs can generate long-term savings by reducing Federal staffing levels and can reduce the need to apply administratively burdensome and disruptive reduction-in-force procedures. OPM declines to limit administrative leave for deferred resignation participants to 10 days. Agencies need the flexibility to provide longer periods of administrative leave (within the bounds of Governmentwide limits) if they determine a longer period is necessary to incentivize more employees to agree to voluntarily separate and to achieve workforce reduction goals.
On continuity of institutional knowledge, § 630.1403(a)(6) requires an authorized agency official to consider the effect on productivity and the agency's ability to meet mission needs before providing administrative leave, and an agency retains discretion to structure an agency-specific initiative, including the amount of leave provided and any transition or knowledge-transfer expectations, accordingly.
Comment 0017 objected to the provision in subpart H of part 351 under which, in an emergency, an agency that lacks work or funds may place a RIF-affected employee on annual leave during the notice period without the employee's consent, and argued that the employee should be able to choose between annual leave and leave without pay in those circumstances.
This comment is outside the scope of this rulemaking. OPM did not propose any substantive change to that longstanding provision, which appears in this final rule at § 351.806(c) only because § 351.806 is being restructured and republished in full. OPM notes that, under § 351.806(c), an employee may not be placed on leave without pay without the employee's consent, and the emergency annual leave provision applies only when, in an emergency, the agency lacks work or funds for all or part of the notice period.
OPM makes no changes in response to these comments.
IV. Section-By-Section Analysis
In this section IV, we provide descriptions of the regulatory changes by section and paragraph. More detailed explanations and justifications for the regulatory changes may be found in the Supplementary Information for the June 29, 2026, notice of proposed rulemaking (
91 FR 39032
) and in the responses to comments in this preamble.
Section 351.806 (RIF and Administrative Leave)
OPM is revising § 351.806 to clarify that use of administrative leave during a RIF notice period is permissible, if an agency determines that there is justification for putting the RIF-affected employee in non-duty status. OPM is also revising § 351.806 to state that the general rule of keeping an employee in duty status during a RIF notice period applies in “ordinary circumstances” instead of “when possible,” consistent with the language in § 752.404(b)(3) (dealing with keeping an employee in duty status during the notice period for a proposed removal or suspension).
Subpart N of Part 630 (Administrative Leave—Nomenclature Changes)
OPM is replacing the word “grant” (and associated variations of “granted” and “granting”) with the word “provide” (or applicable variations “provided” and “providing”) throughout subpart N. These changes occur in §§ 630.1402, 630.1403, and 630.1405. The word “provide” has a broader meaning that would encompass uses of administrative leave with or without the employee's consent.
Section 630.1401 (Administrative Leave—Applicability)
OPM is revising § 630.1401(b) to add another category of employees to which subpart N does not apply—namely, Presidential appointees or other employees who are excluded from coverage under the title 5 leave laws under
5 U.S.C. 6301(2)(x)-(xiii)
.
Section 630.1402 (Administrative Leave—Definitions)
OPM is removing a no-longer-relevant definition of “head of the agency” from § 630.1402. Changes made in the December 17, 2024, final regulations made the definition unnecessary, and it should have been deleted at that time.
OPM is adding a definition of “sole and exclusive discretion” to make clear that agency discretion is exercised within the bounds of applicable law, Presidential directives, and the regulations in subpart N, and may not be limited or conditioned by any agreement or established as a mandatory entitlement.
Section 630.1403 (Administrative Leave—Principles, Prohibitions, and Acceptable Uses)
In paragraphs (a)(2) and (4) of § 630.1403, OPM is adding the words “sole and exclusive” before the word “discretion” to better reflect the decision of Congress to give this new discretionary leave authority to agency heads who make final decisions on mission needs and use of limited budget resources and the sense of Congress that agency heads would be responsible for managing and overseeing the effective and prudent use of the leave. This regulatory change reflects OPM's judgment that acceptable uses are those uses, within the bounds of law and regulation, that an agency determines to be appropriate in its sole and exclusive discretion.
In paragraph (a)(3), OPM is adding a sentence that points to examples of when it is appropriate for an agency to approve an incidence of administrative leave lasting more than 1 workday, which are found in a new paragraph (c).
In paragraph (b), OPM is revising the regulatory prohibitions on use of administrative leave. In paragraph (b)(2), OPM is clarifying that the prohibition on using administrative leave to recognize employee performance or contributions does not prevent an agency from providing administrative leave to the general workforce of the agency (or an organization within the agency) as a morale-boosting special goodwill gesture, even if that action is broadly linked to the accomplishments of the workforce. OPM is also adding three new regulatory prohibitions in paragraphs (b)(3) through (b)(5), which are already addressed in OPM's Agency Policy Template.
Paragraph (b)(3) provides that administrative leave may not be used for the purpose of placing an employee in a non-duty status during an investigation of the employee's conduct or performance once the employee has reached the 10-workday calendar year limit in
5 U.S.C. 6329a(b)(1)
and § 630.1404 in connection with a given investigation. Once the 10-workday limit is reached, the agency must use investigative leave under
5 U.S.C. 6329b
if it wishes to continue to conduct an investigation and continue to keep the employee in a paid non-duty status.
(
printed page 65937)
The language “in connection with a given investigation” is intended to cover situations in which an employee was placed on administrative leave due to an investigation, reached the 10-workday limit in that calendar year, and is then placed on section 6329b investigative leave as part of a continuing investigation. Once an employee has reached the 10-workday limit in connection with a given investigation, that limit is no longer applicable in governing the use of section 6329b investigative leave with respect to the same investigation. Thus, if the investigation continues into the next calendar year, the agency can continue to place the employee on section 6329b investigative leave even though the employee has not reached the 10-workday limit on section 6329a administrative leave in the new calendar year. (Section 6329b(b)(3)(A) bars use of section 6329b investigative leave until expiration of the 10-workday period, but this bar applies only in making a decision to start an initial period of investigative leave in connection with a given investigation.)
Paragraph (b)(4) provides that administrative leave may not be used for a purpose for which sick leave could be used under OPM regulations (
5 CFR 630.401(a)
)—unless such use in a particular scenario is specifically approved by Governmentwide policy issued by OPM or the President. The exception to the general bar requires OPM or Presidential approval, which should be provided only in exceptional circumstances.
Paragraph (b)(5) provides that administrative leave may not be used to cover service by poll workers or poll observers in connection with elections. OPM's current policies allow administrative leave to give employees a reasonable opportunity to vote on an election day (see § 630.1403(c)(2)); however, OPM does not believe it is appropriate to use administrative leave for other election-related matters beyond facilitating an opportunity for an employee to vote.
OPM is adding a new paragraph (c) that provides a noncomprehensive list of examples of acceptable uses of administrative leave. This list signals that an agency can provide administrative leave in the covered scenarios without having to be concerned that it may be contrary to Governmentwide policies. At the same time, agencies are not required to provide administrative leave in the listed scenarios. Agencies retain the sole and exclusive discretion to determine whether to provide administrative leave to any employee or category of employees based on their consideration of agency mission requirements—within the bounds of law and regulation. The listed examples are generally consistent with current OPM policies in its Agency Policy Template. Of particular note, the list includes examples of using administrative leave in connection with deferred resignation programs and other workforce restructuring initiatives. Paragraph (c)(8), added in this final rule in response to comments, addresses the limited use of administrative leave for physical fitness activities; the examples proposed as paragraphs (c)(8) through (c)(10) are redesignated as paragraphs (c)(9) through (c)(11). See the discussion of this topic earlier in the preamble.

Section 715.202 (Resignations)
OPM is revising § 715.202(b), which deals with employees' requests to withdraw a resignation before its effective date. OPM is making clear that the decision to accept or decline a resignation withdrawal request is made at the agency's sole and exclusive discretion. Also, OPM is adding another example of a valid reason for declining an employee's request—namely, that the employee accepted benefits under a deferred resignation agreement. For example, if an employee received paid administrative leave in connection with a deferred resignation agreement, an agency may determine that it would be inappropriate to allow an employee to withdraw the resignation and keep the paid leave benefits.
Severability
OPM intends the provisions of this final rule to be severable. If any provision, or its application to any person or circumstance, is held invalid or unenforceable, OPM intends that the remaining provisions and their applications remain operative to the fullest extent permitted by law. OPM would have adopted those remaining provisions independent of the provision or application held invalid.
The rule addresses distinct matters, including coverage and agency discretion under the administrative leave regulations, specific prohibited and acceptable uses of administrative leave, employee status during a reduction-in-force notice period, and withdrawal of resignations. Each change serves the purposes explained separately in this preamble. For example, the prohibitions and examples of acceptable uses in § 630.1403 address different circumstances; removing one would not prevent agencies from applying the others under the remaining governing requirements. Likewise, the withdrawal of resignation provisions in § 715.202 can operate independently of the examples authorizing administrative leave because they govern whether an agency may decline a withdrawal request when it has a valid reason. Although § 351.806(b) references part 630, subpart N, that reference does not depend on every provision of subpart N remaining effective. Agencies could continue to apply § 351.806(b) subject to the surviving administrative leave requirements. Accordingly, the remaining provisions would continue to provide useful guidance and function sensibly without any provision held invalid, subject to applicable law and court rulings.
V. Regulatory Analysis
A. Statement of Need
After having over 1 year of experience in applying the final regulations on administrative leave issued in December 2024, OPM has identified the need to clarify certain matters in the regulations. While OPM has issued policy guidance (see footnote 2) that largely addresses these matters, regulations are needed to achieve greater consistency across agencies and a firmer legal foundation for the policies. OPM is adding certain prohibited uses of administrative leave so that the prohibitions are binding on agencies. OPM is adding examples of acceptable uses of administrative leave so that agencies can be assured those uses have a regulatory foundation. For example, OPM is including the extended use of administrative leave in connection with a deferred resignation program as an acceptable use of administrative leave. Also, through
(
printed page 65938)
these regulations, OPM is better fulfilling its statutory charge to prescribe regulations that address agency uses of administrative leave (
5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1)
). OPM also identified the need to clarify that agencies have sole and exclusive discretion in making decisions to provide or not provide administrative leave, subject to governing law and regulations.
OPM is amending the RIF regulation in
5 CFR 351.806
to clarify when administrative leave may be provided during a RIF notice period.
OPM is also amending the resignation regulation in
5 CFR 715.202
to identify the acceptance of benefits, such as administrative leave, as a valid reason for an agency to deny an employee's request to withdraw a resignation commitment made as part of a deferred resignation agreement. This gives agencies a clearer regulatory basis for denying a resignation withdrawal request by a participant in a deferred resignation program.
B. Regulatory Alternatives
OPM considered the alternative of not adding additional regulatory prohibitions or examples of acceptable uses of administrative leave and instead relying on OPM policies. For the reasons given in the Statement of Need section, OPM concluded that various policies should be codified in regulation. With respect to the revision of the resignation regulation, OPM considered the possibility of not making the change but determined agencies would be better served by a regulation that gives them a clear and specific legal basis for denying a resignation withdrawal request by an employee participating in a deferred resignation program.
C. Impact
Since OPM is codifying in regulation existing policies on administrative leave, OPM does not expect significant changes in the usage of administrative leave. Agencies generally follow OPM policies even if they are not legally binding in the way regulations are. Codifying policies in regulations provides a firmer legal foundation for those policies, promotes consistency across agencies, and avoids disputes between employees and agencies. Since this final regulation affects only Federal agencies and employees, it will have no substantial impact on local economies or labor markets.
D. Costs
As explained in the Impact section, OPM does not expect the regulations to result in significant changes in the usage of administrative leave. Governmentwide policies that parallel the final regulations are already in place. OPM is simply giving its policies an enhanced legal standing by incorporating them in regulation. Accordingly, OPM does not project that costs or savings will result from the regulations. OPM believes the administrative burdens associated with implementing these final regulations will be de minimis, since agencies are already operating under parallel OPM policies. There could be minor administrative cost savings to the extent that codifying policies in regulations reduces disputes. Several commenters challenged this assessment, arguing that OPM must account for the costs of the 2025 deferred resignation programs and for broader economic effects of workforce reductions. As explained in section III.E of this preamble, the relevant measure under
E.O. 12866
and
E.O. 13563
is the incremental effect of this rule against a baseline that includes the Governmentwide policies already in effect. Expenditures associated with the 2025 programs were incurred under existing authorities and policies and are part of that baseline, and decisions to undertake particular workforce realignment initiatives are made by agencies under separate authorities that this rule neither mandates nor funds.
Similarly, OPM does not expect the change to the resignation regulation to have a significant effect on the number of resignation withdrawals. The existing regulation already allows an agency to deny an employee's request to withdraw a resignation for a valid reason. The regulation simply identifies an employee's acceptance of benefits (such as administrative leave) as part of a deferred resignation agreement as a specific example of a valid reason. The final regulation could result in fewer or less lengthy disputes, but the number of affected cases would be very small.
E. Benefits
This rule has important benefits. The regulations provide more transparency and accountability, provide a firmer legal foundation for allowing or prohibiting certain uses of administrative leave, promote consistency across agencies, clarify the authority of agencies, and reduce potential disputes. With respect to the revision of the RIF regulation, it clarifies when it is appropriate to provide administrative leave during a RIF notice period. With respect to the revision of the resignation regulation, it will provide a regulatory basis for denying a resignation withdrawal request and set clear expectations for employees who enter into a deferred resignation agreement.
