OPM appreciates the two comments (0004 and 0054) highlighting these provisions, but recommendations concerning QSI policy, within-grade increase administration, or performance-rating distribution are outside the scope of this rulemaking, which is limited to the TIG eligibility restriction in
5 CFR part 300, subpart F
, and conforming amendments.
OPM addresses one point raised by two comments (0054 and 0068) that bears on how this rule will operate in practice. Those comments ask how supervisors are to use performance to determine readiness for promotion if OPM implements a standard distribution of ratings. Three points relevant to this rule should be noted. First, nothing in this rule makes a rating of record either necessary or sufficient for promotion. Section 335.103(b)(3) requires that due weight be given to performance appraisals and incentive awards, but qualification for a higher-graded position is established by the candidate's demonstrated experience, education, and job-related competencies measured against the applicable qualification standard—not by the rating alone.
Second, agencies may use evidence beyond the rating of record when assessing readiness, including the evaluation methods described in Part III.C. Nothing in this rule or in any separate OPM action requires an agency to treat a rating of record as the sole or controlling measure of an employee's readiness for higher-graded work.
Third, OPM expects that imposing a standardized distribution of the highest performance ratings will ensure that agency performance appraisal systems will more reliably distinguish and identify high performers and help eliminate widespread ratings inflation across the Federal Government. That expectation rests on the reasoning OPM set out in the recently finalized appraisal rule.
See
Performance Appraisal for General Schedule, Prevailing Rate, and Certain Other Employees,
91 FR 41521
(July 7, 2026) (RIN 3206-AP06) (effective August 6, 2026). That rule removed the categorical prohibition, formerly codified at
5 CFR 430.208(c)
, on any method that would “limit or require the use of particular summary levels (
i.e.,
establish a forced distribution of summary levels),” and replaces it with authority for OPM to “establish, and refine as needed, a standardized distribution of some or all rating levels which agencies must apply when rating employees.”
5 CFR 430.208(c)
. The companion provision confirms that the method for deriving and assigning a summary level “may involve comparing, categorizing, and ranking employees or groups on the basis of their performance,” and that “[s]uch procedures may also be used, where otherwise authorized by law and regulation, to inform award determinations and promotion decisions.”
5 CFR 430.208(d)
.
OPM explained in that rulemaking why a standardized distribution is expected to yield more rigorous and more accurate ratings. Ratings under the prior framework were not meaningfully differentiated: the Government Accountability Office found that 99 percent of permanent, non-SES (Senior Executive Service) employees received ratings at or above “Fully Successful,” and agency-submitted data for fiscal years 2022 through 2024 show that only approximately 0.3 percent of non-SES employees under five-level programs received a Level 2 rating and approximately 0.1 percent received an “Unacceptable” rating. 91 FR at 41521-22, 41528, 41530. Only 42 to 51 percent of Federal employees report that their supervisors distinguish and recognize performance in a meaningful way. Id. at 41522. OPM concluded that this pattern reflects “leniency bias whereby supervisors arbitrarily issue inflated performance ratings to avoid confrontation,”
id.
at 41524, and that “the current degree of rating inflation has so egregiously undermined the credibility and accountability of performance appraisal systems that implementing a standardized distribution is the best alternative,”
id.
at 41525-26. OPM further explained that because “any human judgment is by nature comparative,” an appraisal method that makes the comparison explicit “will more accurately and objectively measure individual performance than one that prohibits any comparative judgments between employees and requires that any measurement of employee performance be framed in absolute terms.” Id. at 41523. The distribution operates only after each employee has been appraised against established, job-related performance standards; it does not displace those standards; it is to be applied at the agency or department level rather than at the work unit level; and OPM has stated that it intends any standardized distribution to limit only the highest rating levels rather than to prescribe limits at or below Level 3. Id. at 41523-24, 41528, 41533; see
5 CFR 430.208(a)(1)
(a rating of record “must be based only on the evaluation of actual job performance for the designated appraisal period”).
The consequence for promotion readiness, which is what the two comments (0054 and 0068) ask about, is direct. By “establishing a limit on the number of non-SES employees who can receive a rating above the fully successful level,” the appraisal rule is expected to produce “a clear distinction of the highest performers across an agency and the Federal Government.” 91 FR at 41536. That rule also confines the term “Outstanding” to a Level 5 rating.
5 CFR 430.208(e)(2)(iv)
,
(e)(3)
. A rating of record will accordingly carry information about relative performance that it did not carry when nearly all employees were rated at or above “Fully Successful,” and a supervisor recommending an employee for higher-graded work will be able to point to a rating that reflects a considered judgment about how that employee's performance compares to the performance of others.
The requirement in
5 CFR 335.103(b)(3)
that due weight be given to performance appraisals and incentive awards can do meaningful work only where ratings in fact distinguish among levels of performance. The two rules are therefore complementary rather than in tension: this rule removes a calendar-based barrier that delayed consideration of employees who are ready for higher-graded work, while the appraisal rule improves the quality of the performance information that agencies use, together with the qualification requirements and the evaluation methods described in Part III.C, to identify which employees those are. Neither rule, however, makes any particular rating of record a prerequisite to promotion or entitles an employee who receives a high rating to be promoted; promotion remains contingent on the existence of higher-
(
printed page 65899)
graded work, proper classification, and selection under the agency's merit promotion plan.
I. Comments Regarding Cost Estimates and Regulatory Analysis
Comment 0076 argued that OPM's proposed cost estimate—approximately 250 hours and $39,075 per agency in the first year, or approximately $3,126,000 governmentwide, to update merit promotion plans—understates the cost to large, decentralized departments with multiple components and bargaining units, citing its own decentralized merit promotion programs administered across multiple subordinate components with separate bargaining units as an example. Comment 0014 separately argued that OPM's cost analysis does not adequately address possible long-term compensation costs from faster promotions, grade compression, accelerated career-ladder movement, classification disputes, or grievances, and recommended fuller fiscal analysis before finalization.
OPM acknowledges that implementation costs will vary across agencies, and that large, multi-component departments with numerous subordinate organizations and bargaining units may experience higher first-year implementation costs than OPM's governmentwide average estimate reflects. OPM's cost estimate, consistent with the approach used in the proposed rule, is intended to represent an average per-agency cost across the Federal Government for the purpose of governmentwide regulatory analysis; it is not intended to represent the specific cost that any individual department will incur. OPM does not believe this variation warrants revising the governmentwide estimate methodology in this final rule. With respect to Comment 0014's concern regarding long-term compensation costs, OPM notes that promotion under this rule remains discretionary and contingent on the existence of higher-level work, proper classification, and available agency funding; this rule does not require agencies to promote any employee or to accelerate compensation growth, and OPM does not expect the rule, by itself, to produce a predictable or quantifiable increase in aggregate Federal payroll costs. Agencies remain responsible for managing promotion actions within their existing budgetary authority.
Comment 0069 raised a distinct objection to OPM's regulatory analysis: that OPM's assumption that removing a bright-line eligibility requirement will reduce administrative constraints is likely to prove wrong in practice. Because TIG establishes an objective threshold below which a promotion request need not be entertained, the comment argued, its removal leaves no comparable limiting principle; human capital offices would face substantially more promotion requests to evaluate, more supporting documentation to review, and more requests for reconsideration, grievances, equal employment opportunity complaints, and prohibited personnel practice complaints when requests are denied. The comment further argued that agencies faced with that volume may adopt internal waiting periods that replicate TIG's function while producing inconsistent practice across Government and recommended that OPM evaluate the anticipated increase in promotion requests, human resources workload, review requirements, training needs, and litigation risk before finalizing. Comment 0076 raised a related concern about increased supervisor documentation burden, and Comment 0036 raised a related concern about human resources capacity.
OPM has considered these arguments but does not agree that they warrant withdrawing or delaying the rule for three reasons.
First,
the premise that TIG limits the volume of promotion requests is only partly correct. TIG does not restrict what an employee may request or what a supervisor may recommend; it restricts what an agency may lawfully do. An agency that receives a request from an employee who has not completed 52 weeks may decline it quickly today, and after this rule takes effect an agency may decline it just as quickly on any other applicable ground—that no higher-graded position exists, that the position is not funded, that the employee does not meet the qualification standard, or that the agency's merit promotion plan requires competition for the vacancy. What changes is that the reason given will be a job-related reason rather than a calendar computation.
Second,
this rule removes recurring administrative work as well as creating one-time implementation work. Under the prior regulations, agencies were required to determine and document TIG eligibility for covered internal promotion actions; to compute creditable service under § 300.605, including converting non-General Schedule service to an equivalent General Schedule grade by comparing the candidate's rate of basic pay to representative rates; and, where an exception was needed, to obtain agency-head approval under § 300.603(b)(7), OPM authorization under § 300.603(b)(8), or OPM approval of a training agreement under § 300.603(b)(6). Those determinations, and the recordkeeping and internal appeals associated with them, are eliminated. OPM's cost estimate in Part V.D captures the first-year cost of revising merit promotion plans; it does not attempt to monetize this offsetting reduction in recurring administrative work, which OPM expects to be positive but cannot reliably quantify. The estimate is therefore conservative in that respect.
Third,
OPM does not regard the possibility that some agencies will adopt their own job-related service requirements as an unintended consequence to be avoided. As explained in Part III.G, that outcome is permitted, and in some occupations it may be sound personnel administration. The difference between an agency-established requirement and the governmentwide restriction OPM is removing is consequential: the agency requirement must be justified as job-related for the positions to which it applies, must be published in the agency's merit promotion plan and available in writing to candidates under
5 CFR 335.103(b)(1)
, and may be revised by the agency when it no longer serves the agency's needs. Variation across agencies that reflects genuine differences in occupations and missions is a feature of a merit promotion system administered by agencies subject to governmentwide standards, not a defect in it.
OPM further observes that the substantial portions of the Federal workforce that already operate without a time-in-grade restriction have not produced the pattern of workload or litigation the comment anticipates, and no comment identified data showing otherwise. OPM will consider promotion-related workload and complaint activity in the course of its ordinary oversight of agency personnel management programs.

V. Regulatory Analysis
A. Statement of Need
The current TIG requirement originated in the Whitten Amendment, section 1302 of the Supplemental Appropriation Act, 1951, Public Law 81-843, 64 Stat. 1044, 1066 (Sept. 27, 1950), enacted during the Korean conflict to prevent a permanent, uncontrolled buildup of higher-graded civil service positions. That statute expired on September 14, 1978. The
(
printed page 65901)
Civil Service Commission, OPM's predecessor, elected to preserve the TIG restriction in regulation notwithstanding the statute's expiration, and the restriction has been carried forward in successive recodifications, most recently at
56 FR 23002
(May 20, 1991). Nearly five decades later, OPM has concluded, consistent with Executive Order (E.O.) 14170 and OPM's Merit Hiring Plan, that governmentwide qualification standards, agency merit promotion procedures under
5 CFR part 335
, classification requirements, and the merit system principles and prohibited personnel practices codified in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 provide a more direct and effective means of ensuring merit-based promotion than a uniform, calendar-based waiting period.
The comment record, summarized in Part II, confirms that TIG frequently operates to exclude employees who are otherwise qualified—based on demonstrated performance (Comments 0011, 0015, 0027, 0053, 0060), prior military or private-sector experience (Comments 0003, 0006, 0016, 0026, 0041, 0043, 0052, 0058), or specialized experience gained in a different occupational series (Comment 0056)—from consideration for promotion for reasons unrelated to their readiness to perform higher-graded work.
As Comment 0069 correctly observed, merit principles in Federal employment did not originate with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978. Congress rejected the spoils system in the Pendleton Act of 1883, and the Civil Service Commission administered merit-based examination, promotion, and classification requirements well before 1950. OPM's point is narrower. The specific framework on which this rule relies—the governmentwide qualification standards published in the OPM Operating Manual, Qualification Standards for General Schedule Positions; the merit promotion requirements in
5 CFR part 335
; the merit system principles and prohibited personnel practices codified at
5 U.S.C. 2301
and
2302
; and the institutions that administer them, including the Office of Special Counsel, the Merit Systems Protection Board, and the Federal-sector equal employment opportunity complaint process—postdates enactment of the Whitten Amendment. It is the availability of that framework, rather than the absence of any merit principle in 1950, that supports OPM's conclusion that a uniform calendar-based waiting period is no longer necessary or appropriate.
B. Impact
OPM expects this rule to result in a more efficient, skills-based promotion process for General Schedule competitive service employees. Employees whose demonstrated qualifications, performance, and experience meet the requirements for a higher-graded position will be eligible for consideration without an additional, non-merit waiting period. Agencies will retain full authority to establish job-related promotion criteria, career-ladder progression standards, and documentation practices suited to their occupations and missions, as discussed in Part III.C and III.G. This rule is also expected to reduce administrative burden by eliminating the recurring determinations that TIG required: computation of creditable service under former § 300.605, including the conversion of non-General Schedule service to an equivalent General Schedule grade by comparison of representative rates; agency-head approval of exceptions to avoid hardship to an agency or inequity to an employee under former § 300.603(b)(7); OPM authorization of additional exceptions under former § 300.603(b)(8); and OPM approval of training agreements providing for consecutive accelerated promotions under former § 300.603(b)(6).
C. Regulatory Alternatives
OPM considered and rejected the following alternatives, each addressed in greater detail in Part III:
No-action alternative.
OPM considered retaining the current TIG requirement without change. OPM rejected this alternative for the reasons explained throughout Part III and Part V.A.
Grade-banded or graduated TIG schedules (Comments 0008, 0042).
OPM considered replacing the uniform 52-week requirement with a schedule of waiting periods that varies by grade level, or with a framework allowing a single accelerated promotion followed by a reduced but still-applicable waiting period. OPM rejected these alternatives for the reasons discussed in Part III.B.
Competency-based and high-performer waiver frameworks (Comments 0024, 0072).
OPM considered retaining the 52-week requirement as a governmentwide baseline while creating a formal waiver process requiring the highest performance rating, an OPM-certified assessment tool, and independent review board approval for early promotion, and considered more generally adding a high-performer flexibility to an otherwise retained TIG requirement. OPM rejected these alternatives for the reasons discussed in Part III.B.
Two- or three-year eligibility for multi-grade advancement (Comment 0050).
OPM considered a proposal to make employees eligible to compete for positions up to two grades above their current grade after two or three years of service in grade. OPM rejected this alternative for the reasons discussed in Part III.B.
Occupation-limited elimination (Comment 0002).
OPM considered limiting elimination to technical, medical, and scientific occupations while retaining TIG elsewhere. OPM rejected this alternative for the reasons discussed in Part III.B.
Mandatory governmentwide documentation, certification, review-board, and reporting requirements (Comments 0030, 0063, 0064, 0067, 0068, 0069, 0073, 0074, 0076).
OPM considered requiring, as a condition of eliminating TIG, that agencies adopt standardized written promotion criteria, obtain higher-level or independent review of every promotion occurring before 52 weeks would otherwise have elapsed, certify compliance with merit system principles for each such promotion, and publicly report aggregate data on the use of this flexibility. OPM rejected mandating these requirements in the regulatory text for the reasons discussed in Part III.C and III.D, including that requirements governing how agencies conduct promotion actions belong in
5 CFR part 335
and were not proposed for amendment in this rulemaking.
Retaining TIG for VEOA-based competition only (Comment 0076).
OPM considered retaining the TIG restriction solely as applied to current status employees competing for merit promotion positions for which preference-eligible veterans are also eligible to compete under
5 U.S.C. 3304(f)
. OPM rejected this alternative because it would reintroduce, for a subset of vacancies, the same calendar-based eligibility restriction OPM has determined is not merit-based, and because, as explained in Part III.E, status employees and VEOA-eligible veterans competing for the same vacancy remain subject to the same qualification standards and the same competitive procedures, so removing an internal eligibility restriction does not disadvantage the external candidate.
Delayed, phased, or conditional effective date (Comments 0008, 0013, 0030, 0072, 0076).
OPM considered a longer or phased implementation period, a fixed governmentwide
(
printed page 65902)
transition window of 90 to 180 days or more prescribed in the regulatory text, a mandatory 24-month phased implementation, and an effective date conditioned on OPM certification regarding the adjudicatory capacity of other Federal agencies. OPM adopted an effective date 90 days after publication and rejected the remaining variants for the reasons discussed in Parts III.A, III.B, and III.F.
D. Costs
Consistent with the proposed rule, OPM estimates that agencies will need an average of 250 hours in the first year following publication of this final rule to review the rule and revise merit promotion plans, policies, and training materials, at an assumed fully loaded labor cost of $156.30 per hour (based on the 2026 GS-14, step 5, Washington-DC locality rate, with total labor costs assumed at 200 percent of the base wage rate). This results in an estimated first-year implementation cost of approximately $39,075 per agency and approximately $3,126,000 governmentwide. OPM acknowledges, in response to Comment 0076, that large multi-component departments with numerous bargaining units may experience implementation costs above this governmentwide average but does not believe this warrants revising the estimate used for governmentwide regulatory analysis purposes. In response to Comment 0014, OPM notes that promotion actions taken under this rule remain subject to existing agency budgetary authority and funding availability, and this rule does not require agencies to promote any employee or to accelerate compensation growth.
OPM's estimate reflects one-time implementation cost and does not monetize the recurring administrative work this rule eliminates. As described in Part III.I and Part V.B, agencies will no longer determine and document TIG eligibility for covered internal promotion actions, compute creditable service under former § 300.605, or process exception approvals under former § 300.603(b)(6) through (b)(8). OPM expects the net effect on recurring administrative burden to be a reduction but does not have data permitting a reliable quantification and therefore does not claim a monetized cost saving. The estimate is conservative in that respect.
In response to Comment 0069, OPM acknowledges that it has not quantified any change in promotion-request volume, human resources workload, grievance activity, or litigation risk associated with this rule. OPM does not possess data that would support a reliable estimate of those quantities, and the portions of the Federal workforce already operating without a time-in-grade restriction do not exhibit the pattern the comment anticipates. OPM will consider promotion-related workload and complaint activity in the course of its ordinary oversight of agency personnel management programs.
E. Benefits
This rule benefits agencies by allowing them to consider and promote qualified employees more quickly when higher-graded work, funding, and a properly classified position are available, improving agencies' ability to retain employees who might otherwise leave Federal service for faster-advancing opportunities elsewhere, consistent with the experience described in four comments (0009, 0040, 0045, and 0076). It benefits employees by ensuring that demonstrated performance, relevant experience, and qualifications—rather than the passage of a fixed calendar period—determine eligibility for consideration. It benefits the public by supporting a more efficient and merit-based Federal workforce.
VI. Regulatory Compliance
1. Regulatory Review
OPM has examined the impact of this rule as required by E.O.s 12866 and 13563, which direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if a regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public, health, and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity). A regulatory impact analysis must be prepared for rules that have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local, or tribal governments or communities. This rulemaking does not reach that threshold. It has nonetheless been designated a “significant regulatory action” under section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
, as supplemented by
E.O. 13563
, and has been reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). This rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
2. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Director of the Office of Personnel Management certifies that this regulation will not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities because it applies only to Federal agencies and employees.
3. Federalism
This rule will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the National Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Therefore, no Federalism Assessment is required.
4. Civil Justice Reform
This rule meets the applicable standards set forth in sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2) of
E.O. 12988
.
5. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule that would impose spending costs on State, local, or tribal governments in the aggregate, or on the private sector, in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. That threshold is currently approximately $206 million. This rulemaking will not result in the expenditure by State, local, or tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, in excess of the threshold. Thus, no written assessment of unfunded mandates is required.
6. Congressional Review Act
OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has determined this rule does not meet the criteria for a “major rule” as defined in
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
. In addition, this is a rule relating to agency management or personnel and does not come within the meaning of the term “rule” as used in
5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C)
. Therefore, the reporting requirement of
5 U.S.C. 801
does not apply.
7. Paperwork Reduction Act
Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no person is required to respond to, nor shall any person be subject to a penalty for failure to comply with, a collection of information subject to the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
), unless that collection of information displays a currently valid OMB Control Number. This final rule does not create a new collection of
(
printed page 65903)
information and does not revise an existing one. The existing OMB-approved collection identified in the proposed rule, USAJOBS 3.0 (OMB Control Number 3206-0219), is unaffected, and OPM does not anticipate that implementation of this rule will increase the burden associated with that control number. This rule removes the OPM approval process for training agreements providing for consecutive accelerated promotions under former
5 CFR 300.603(b)(6)
.

SUMMARY:
As part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork burdens, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC or the Commission) invites the general public and other Federal Agencies to take this opportunity to comment on the following information collection. Pursuant to the Small Business Paperwork Relief Act of 2002, the FCC seeks specific comment on how it can further reduce the information collection burden for small business concerns with fewer than 25 employees.

Needs and Uses:
In January 2026, the Federal Communications Commission adopted the
Foreign Adversary Control Report & Order
which established new attestation and disclosure requirements for Commission regulated entities to report whether and the extent to which they are owned, controlled, or subject to the jurisdiction of a foreign adversary. The Order categorized each Commission assigned license, authorization, and other approval into different schedules with different levels of attestation and disclosure requirements based on their
(
printed page 66136)
importance to national security. Respondents who indicate they are subject to control by a foreign adversary must report additional information on the nature of that control. The Order additionally establishes ongoing reporting triggers and a streamlined enforcement and revocation process for non-compliance when necessary. Finally, the Order directed the Commission to establish a new system and procedures for collecting the information from regulated entities.
The information collected in the Foreign Adversary Risk Report will fill critical information gaps in the existing understanding of the threat that adversaries pose to U.S. networks. As such, the information from the collection will improve the Commission's situational awareness of the threat that foreign adversaries currently pose. The Commission will use this information in support of various rulemakings and proceedings as they relate to national security and in developing appropriate actions to mitigate and eliminate threats from adversarial control or influence. Additionally, certain information from the attestation and the additional disclosures will be made available to the public for inspection, subject to privacy and confidentiality considerations, to improve transparency into U.S. communications network and enable outside parties to raise concerns where appropriate.

SUMMARY:
The Postal Service is revising Publication 52,
Hazardous, Restricted, and Perishable Mail
(Pub 52), to improve package integrity and container identification for live animal shipments during processing and handling.
DATES:
Effective: October 19, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Drew Mitchum, (202) 268-7351, or Jennifer Cox, (202) 268-2108.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Postal Service hereby amends Publication 52,
Hazardous, Restricted, and Perishable Mail
(Pub 52 or Publication 52), with the provisions set forth herein. While not codified in
title 39 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR), Publication 52 is a regulation of the Postal Service, and changes to it may be published in the
Federal Register
.
39 CFR 211.2(a)(2)
. Moreover, Publication 52 is incorporated by reference into
Mailing Standards of the United States Postal Service,
Domestic Mail Manual (DMM) section 601.8.1, which is incorporated by reference, in turn, into the Code of Federal Regulations.
39 CFR 111.1
and
111.3
. Publication 52 is publicly available, in a read-only format, via the Postal Explorer® website at
https://pe.usps.com
.
In addition, links to Postal Explorer are provided on the landing page of
USPS.com,
the Postal Service's primary customer-facing website, and on
Postal Pro,
an online informational source available to postal customers.
Summary of New Measures
On August 6, 2026, the Postal Service published a notice of proposed rulemaking (
91 FR 50741
) requiring mailers to individually address and number live animal shipments composed of multiple containers bound together for shipment, recommended mailers write the recipient's name and address directly on the packaging of adult bird shipments and prohibited the reuse of fiberboard containers for all live animal shipments.
Response to Comments
In response to the proposed rule, the Postal Service received 32 formal responses to the proposed changes to Pub 52. The comments received are as follows:
Comment:
One commenter suggested that USPS establish stronger protection against temperature extremes, minimize transportation and delays, require clear emergency procedures to protect animal welfare, require appropriate employee training, review which animals are appropriate for shipment at all and consider prohibiting live animal shipments when safe transportation can't be assured.
Response:
The Postal Service appreciates this feedback. Currently, embargo notices are issued for live animal shipments when there are travel interruptions due to weather related events or holiday transportation schedules are minimized. To the extent possible, the Postal Service limits live animal exposure to temperature extremes while in transit and ensures all animals are safely shielded from the elements while awaiting transport. Alternatively, the mailer must also ensure that the live animal shipments are protected against extreme temperatures by properly packaging them and considering both originating and destinating weather conditions when shipping, especially during summer and winter seasons. The postal service has been actively creating and providing additional education related to emergency procedures and proper handling practices for live animals.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that the name and address requirement be extended to all lives shipments not just adult birds, urged USPS to modify its delivery time period to 48 hours for day-old poultry, require a delivery by date on the container for day-old poultry; and employ specialized tracking and data collection on lives perished to better understand the root causes of documented issues, urges climate-controlled transportation modes, requests that USPS issue moratoriums on the acceptance of lives as it deems necessary.
Response:
The addressing requirement may be considered for all live animal shipments in a future regulatory update. The Postal Service believes the 48-hour delivery time is not necessary as the conditions of acceptance are that the day-old poultry must not be more than 24 hours old, can be delivered within 72 hours of hatching and the hatching date and hour are required to be indicated on the shipment. The Postal Service utilizes tracking data to identify live animal shipments and monitors data related to incidents to determine root causes for documented issues when shipments are accurately identified by the mailer through application of the pertinent USPS extra service codes within their electronic shipping files. Climate-controlled transportation for all modes is not currently feasible, but to the extent possible, the Postal Service limits live animal exposure to temperature extremes while in transit and ensures they are shielded from the elements while awaiting transport. Alternatively, the mailer must also ensure that the live animal shipments are protected against extreme temperatures by properly packaging them and considering both originating and destinating weather conditions when shipping, especially during summer and winter seasons. As mentioned in the previous comment response, the Postal Service does employ embargoes for live animal shipments when issues arise.
Comment:
Several commenters suggested that USPS require advanced reservations and confirm transportation capacity.
Response:
The Postal Service is in contact with major animal shippers and is provided advance notice of large shipments of live animals.
Comment:
One commenter suggested that USPS includes specific test standards for all lives outer packaging and suggests an alternative to the address and phone number requirement of a barcode instead and to require each container in a multi-container shipment to have its own address label.
Response:
The Postal Service appreciates the feedback and will
(
printed page 66003)
possibly consider this in a future rulemaking process.
Comment:
One commenter suggested that live animals should only be shipped by overnight delivery.
Response:
Depending upon the type of live animal being shipped and the shipping distance, Priority Mail and USPS Ground Advantage may also be used to ensure the shipment arrives safely.
Comment:
One commenter suggested that USPS prohibit the mailing of all adult roosters due to gamecock breeders and cockfighters illegal use of the Postal Service to mail animals for fighting ventures.
Response:
The Postal Service permits domestic mailings of disease-free adult birds when in compliance with all applicable governmental laws and regulations, including the Lacey Act, the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the Animal Welfare Act, regulations of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and any state, municipal, or local ordinances. Any violation of these regulations is handled by local authorities and the Postal Inspection Service.
Comment:
One commenter indicates USPS has no procedures or precautions within USPS publications to exclude shipments of live animals used for animal-fighting ventures. The commenter suggests USPS refuse shipments of roosters or imposes more stringent requirements by reviewing and recording interstate health documentation for each rooster, mandate mailers provide written certification of each rooster's non-fighting purpose, limit the number of roosters that can be shipped per day and restrict the breeds of roosters that are permitted.
Response:
The Postal Service will research these suggestions and determine whether more stringent requirements will be considered in a future rulemaking process.
The Postal Service adopts the following changes to Publication 52,
Hazardous, Restricted, and Perishable Mail,
incorporated by reference into Mailing Standards of the United States Postal Service, Domestic Mail Manual (DMM), section 601.8.1, which is further incorporated by reference in the Code of Federal Regulations.
39 CFR 111.1
,
111.3
. Publication 52 is also a regulation of the Postal Service, changes to which may be published in the
Federal Register
.
39 CFR 211.2(a)
. Accordingly, for the reasons stated in the preamble, the Postal Service amends Publication 52 as follows:
