AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management and the Office of Management and Budget.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) are issuing a final rule to strengthen the performance appraisal of senior-level (SL) and scientific or professional (ST) employees, collectively referred to as “senior professionals.” This final rule establishes a new subpart dedicated exclusively to senior professional performance appraisal that aligns more closely with Senior Executive Service (SES) performance appraisal regulations. The rule also eliminates senior professional appraisal programs, removes the prohibition of a standardized distribution of performance rating levels, and enhances oversight of the appraisal process.
DATES:
Effective November 18, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Aaron Gottesman, Senior Advisor to the Director, 202-606-8046 or by email at
SESpolicy@opm.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing this final rule to revise the performance appraisal framework applicable to senior-level (SL) and scientific or professional (ST) employees, collectively referred to as “senior professionals.” These positions are established under
5 U.S.C. 5376
and are classified above GS-15 and just below the Senior Executive Service (SES). Senior professionals serve in positions that require a high level of expertise and are expected to exercise significant responsibility and independent judgment in support of agency missions. As such, they play a critical role in advancing agency priorities and delivering mission outcomes comparable in impact to those of SES members.
Although Congress has aligned the pay structure for senior professionals with that of the SES, including through the Federal Employees Pay Comparability Act of 1990
[
1
]
and the Senior Professional Performance Act of 2008,
Public Law 110-372
(October 8, 2008), the performance management requirements applicable to senior professionals have remained governed by the general appraisal provisions in
5 CFR part 430, subpart B
. These regulations have not been updated since the mid-1990s and were designed to meet the needs of a broad population of federal employees such as prevailing rate employees, seasonal employees, and employees across all grades and steps of the General Schedule. Over time, these regulations have become increasingly incompatible with OPM's efforts to develop a dedicated modern senior professional performance appraisal system. Hence, OPM has determined that this misalignment between pay, responsibilities, and performance appraisal requirements warrants regulatory revision.
In the proposed rule published on February 24, 2026 (
91 FR 8763
), OPM explained that the current performance appraisal framework does not sufficiently support meaningful differentiation in performance among senior professionals. As noted in the proposed rule, despite prior efforts by OPM to curb ratings inflation through guidance,
[
2
]
Governmentwide data showed that, in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, approximately 90 percent of senior professionals received ratings at Levels 4 and 5, while less than a half of one percent of senior professionals received ratings below Level 3 (“Fully Successful”).
[
3
]
Additionally, the 2024 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) results showed that only 47% of federal employees agreed with the statement, “In my work unit, differences in performance are recognized in a meaningful way.”
[
4
]
This was the lowest
(
printed page 65905)
positive response rate for any question and has consistently been the lowest over the past three years.
[
5
]
OPM noted that these data raise concerns regarding rating inflation and the effectiveness of existing appraisal systems in holding senior professionals accountable for performance. In this final rule, OPM eliminates the prior prohibition on forced, or standardized, distribution for senior professionals and provides that OPM may establish a standardized distribution of some or all rating levels for agencies to apply with respect to their senior professional cohorts, except that senior professionals appointed under Schedules C and G may be excluded from such requirements.
[
6
]
Consistent with OPM's authority under
5 U.S.C. chapter 43
and the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, this final rule is intended to strengthen performance management for senior professionals by better aligning appraisal practices with the scope and impact of their duties. The new subpart generally mirrors the provisions and structure of the SES appraisal regulations at
5 CFR part 430, subpart C
, but certain elements of the non-SES appraisal regulations at
5 CFR part 430, subpart B
, are retained in the new subpart due to the different statutory authorities and requirements that apply to the SES and senior professionals. The reforms in this final rule are designed to promote greater rigor, transparency, oversight, and accountability in the evaluation of senior professional performance.
Digest of Public Comments
In response to the proposed rule, OPM received 12 comments during the 30-day public comment period from various individuals, organizations, and a professional association representing employment law attorneys. Of the 12 comments received, nine were posted to
Regulations.gov
, including one comment that was substantively identical to another submission. Three of the comments received were outside the scope of this rulemaking and therefore not posted. At the conclusion of the public comment period, OPM reviewed and analyzed the comments.
The comments are summarized and discussed in the subsequent sections, beginning with general comments followed by comments specific to each section. A discussion of the suggested revisions that were considered and either adopted, adopted in part, or declined, and the rationale therefor is included.
General Comments
The comments received reflect a range of views, with some expressing support, others acknowledging the need for performance management reforms but disagreeing with OPM's approach, and others strongly objecting to the rule. For example, Commenter 0007 stated “I support the proposed rule to implement standardized distributions for senior professional performance appraisals. The reasoning is that for too long, `leniency bias' has led to rating inflation.” Another individual characterized the rule as “a step in the wrong direction to ensure high level performers necessary for these positions are willing to become civil servants.” (Commenter 0011). Most commenters focused their objections on only a few specific provisions of the rule and framed their concerns in terms of the potential impact on the Federal workforce, implementation challenges, and perceived legal issues, which OPM addresses below in the relevant sections of the preamble.
Commenter 0011 argued that OPM failed to provide sufficient time to address the proposed rule and that an additional 60 to 180 days should be provided, citing the complexity of the rule and the fact that OPM has recently issued several other proposed rules. Respectfully, OPM provided sufficient time for the public to review the proposed rule and submit comments. Courts have held that a 30-day comment period is generally sufficient to comply with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
[
7
]
Commenters 0010 and 0011 also urged OPM to withdraw the rule based on the broader context in which it was proposed, arguing that other recent personnel actions have destabilized the Federal workforce and that performance data generated in that environment cannot justify reform. Those objections are directed at actions and policies outside the scope of this rulemaking, and OPM does not address them here. OPM notes, however, that the ratings data on which this rule relies are from fiscal years 2023 and 2024, and the FEVS results it cites span 2022 through 2024, largely predating the events the commenters describe. OPM has evaluated this rule on its own record and pursuant to its own statutory authorities, as discussed throughout this preamble.
Part 430—Performance Management
This final rule revises
5 CFR part 430
by establishing a new subpart E dedicated to managing senior professional performance. In the following sections, we address the public comments related to the specific sections of the regulation to which each comment applied.
Section 430.501 General
This section identifies the statutory and regulatory basis for the senior professional performance appraisal subpart. This section also describes the conditions under which agencies and employees not covered by the provisions of this subpart can receive performance evaluations and ratings that are considered ratings of record for reduction in force purposes.
Commenter 0011 asserted that OPM lacks statutory authority for this rulemaking. As described in more detail in the Background and the proposed rule,
[
8
]
OPM not only has authority to regulate performance management but is required to do so.
Chapter 43 of title 5, U.S. Code
, remains the applicable authority for performance appraisal systems and establishes OPM's responsibility to prescribe regulations governing performance management for senior professionals. The commenter's constitutional objections are likewise unavailing. This rule implements an express delegation of rulemaking authority from Congress at
5 U.S.C. 4305
,
1103
, and
1104
; it does not purport to enact, amend, or repeal any statute. Nor does
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
603 U.S. 369 (2024), assist the commenter: that decision concerns judicial deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes and does not diminish an agency's exercise of authority Congress has expressly conferred. Nothing in this
(
printed page 65906)
rule purports to limit judicial review otherwise available by law.
Although
5 U.S.C. 4305
provides OPM the authority to prescribe regulations governing performance appraisal under
subchapter I of chapter 43 of title 5, U.S. Code
, Commenters 0005 and 0008 recommended that OPM instead use the demonstration project authority under
5 U.S.C. 4703
to test the proposed reforms in this final rule before implementing them Governmentwide. These commenters argue that the proposed changes, including the use of a standardized distribution of performance ratings and other structural modifications, are untested in the Federal context and may carry significant risks for workforce morale, retention, and organizational effectiveness. Commenters suggested that pilot programs, randomized trials, or phased implementation approaches would provide an evidence-based foundation for broader adoption and allow OPM to assess potential unintended consequences.
OPM appreciates the commenters' recommendations regarding the use of demonstration project authority and agrees that demonstration projects can be a valuable tool for testing innovative personnel management approaches in appropriate circumstances. However, OPM has determined that the use of a demonstration project under
5 U.S.C. 4703
is not necessary and would create unacceptable delays to the urgently needed reforms adopted in this final rule.
Demonstration projects, by definition, “must require the waiver of a provision of law, rule, or regulation which is eligible for waiver under the demonstration authority contained in
5 U.S.C. 4703
.”
[
9
]
OPM requires no waiver of any provision of law or rule to exercise its statutory authority under
5 U.S.C. 4305
to prescribe non-SES performance appraisal regulations. Many of the provisions in this final rule are grounded in longstanding principles of effective performance management, including the need for meaningful differentiation in performance ratings, clear accountability, and alignment between performance outcomes and organizational goals.
Additionally, senior professionals have already been operating under a new senior professional performance appraisal system and plan
[
10
]
since October 1, 2025, which in many ways is similar to the new SES performance appraisal system and plan.
[
11
]
OPM also notes that the rule, Assuring Responsive and Accountable Federal Executive Management, published on September 15, 2025 (
90 FR 44291
), authorized OPM to establish a standardized distribution of rating levels for the SES and this final rule seeks to establish parity with that SES rule. The effects of standardized distribution systems have been extensively studied across multiple organizational contexts,
[
12
]
and OPM relied on this robust existing body of evidence in both the SES rulemaking and this current rulemaking. Conducting further study through a demonstration project is, therefore, unlikely to produce novel results that have not been documented elsewhere in the literature. Moreover, OPM will diligently monitor the implementation of all the reforms in this rule and through ongoing oversight, data analysis, and engagement with agencies, continue to refine its senior professional performance appraisal guidance to ensure the final rule achieves its intended objectives.
For these reasons, OPM has determined that proceeding with Governmentwide implementation of the final rule, rather than using demonstration project authority, is appropriate and consistent with the objectives of improving the rigor and effectiveness of senior professional performance appraisal and increased parity with the SES performance appraisal framework. Accordingly, OPM is adopting the language in this section as proposed.
Section 430.502 Coverage
This section addresses coverage under the new subpart. It applies only to senior professionals paid under
5 U.S.C. 5376
, which includes all SL positions that are classified above GS-15 pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 5108
and all ST positions established under
5 U.S.C. 3104
. It also authorizes OPM to exclude certain excepted service positions where applicable.
OPM received no comments on this section and is adopting the language as proposed.
Section 430.503 Definitions
This section provides definitions necessary for administration. Key defined terms include “agency,” “appraisal period,” “critical element,” “initial summary rating,” “oversight official,” “performance standard,” “PRB (Performance Review Board),” “progress review,” and “rating official.” Certain defined terms in the new subpart are retained from both the SES appraisal framework and non-SES appraisal regulations, tailored for senior professionals to reflect their unique performance management context. Notably, the definition of “agency” reflects that, under
5 U.S.C. 5108
, OPM determines the maximum number of SL positions that may be established in an Executive agency and, under
5 U.S.C. 3104
, OPM determines the maximum number of ST positions in any agency, except for the Library of Congress, which also may establish eight ST positions under
5 U.S.C. 3104
.
OPM received no comments on this section and is adopting the language as proposed.
Section 430.504 Senior Professional Performance Appraisal Systems
This section requires agencies to establish performance appraisal systems specifically for senior professionals. OPM proposed to revise these systems to require that they be developed and administered in accordance with the system standards in § 430.505, which more closely align with those applicable to SES appraisal systems. To further align senior professional appraisal with SES appraisal, OPM also proposed to eliminate the requirement that agencies develop separate performance appraisal programs and instead require that senior professional appraisal systems encompass all policies, parameters, procedures, and requirements necessary for OPM approval and be consistent with the criteria for performance appraisal system certification.
Commenter 0006 challenges OPM's underlying authority to change the evaluation system for senior professionals, asserting that OPM's final rulemaking errs in interpreting the Senior Professional Performance Act of 2008 “as constituting Congressional authority to change the performance evaluation system for SL/ST employees.” The commenter contends that because Congress did not make substantive changes to senior professional performance appraisal at the time of the 2008 Act, that OPM is
(
printed page 65907)
precluded from making the regulatory reforms included in this final rule.
OPM respectfully disagrees because the commenter misunderstands OPM's authority. While OPM referenced the Senior Professional Performance Act of 2008 in the proposed rule as an example of legislation that has increased pay parity with the SES, the fact that the legislation did not also make statutory changes to how senior professionals' performance is appraised cannot be interpreted as Congress barring OPM from exercising its statutorily-conferred authority at
5 U.S.C. 4305
to prescribe non-SES performance management regulations. Coverage of senior professionals under
subchapter I of chapter 43 of title 5, U.S. Code
has not changed. Therefore, OPM is authorized to prescribe regulations affecting the performance management of senior professionals, consistent with statute.
Commenter 0010 argues that OPM has not sufficiently explained why the SES appraisal system is the right comparator to guide the development of the senior professional appraisal system rules, as opposed to constructing a more tailored model that reflects the actual duties of senior professionals. Along a similar line, Commenter 0005 asserts that because senior professionals perform such highly specialized and diverse work across a wide range of competencies, it makes more sense for their performance appraisal systems to align with non-SES appraisal systems as opposed to SES systems—which are focused on executive management competencies.
OPM recognizes and appreciates the broad range of competencies possessed by senior professionals. Using the SES appraisal framework as a model for developing the senior professional appraisal rules in no way equates to senior professionals being evaluated on the same competencies as SES members. The final rule maintains important distinctions that reflect the non-supervisory and highly specialized nature of senior professional roles. Agencies retain the flexibility to tailor senior professional performance plans through inclusion of position-specific performance objectives. Additionally, since senior professionals do not supervise employees other than personal assistants, they do not have “employee perspectives” included as a performance factor for their appraisals, nor do their performance plans include a critical element focused on holding others accountable. Although senior professionals do not carry supervisory or executive management responsibilities like SES, they are comparable in terms of their organizational impact, influence on agency mission, and level of accountability. Senior professionals frequently serve as the Federal Government's leading experts in critical fields, provide authoritative technical or scientific advice, and contribute directly to high-level policy, programmatic, or mission outcomes. Thus, given the importance of these positions, OPM continues to believe that a more rigorous and structured appraisal framework—similar to that used for the SES—is appropriate to ensure meaningful differentiation, accountability, and consistency for these positions. Accordingly, OPM is adopting the language in this section as proposed.
Section 430.505 System Standards for Senior Professional Performance Appraisal Systems
This section sets forth the system standards that agencies' senior professional performance appraisal systems must incorporate. Standards include the use of critical elements, alignment of performance requirements with agency mission and strategic planning activities, defined performance standards for each summary rating level, annual performance appraisals, a mathematical method for deriving ratings, establishment of five summary performance levels, and that performance appraisals be used as a basis to adjust pay, reward, retain, develop, and remove senior professionals. OPM also proposed to eliminate the prohibition on a forced, or standardized distribution of rating levels and authorize OPM to establish and refine, as needed, a standardized distribution of some or all rating levels for senior professionals.
Justification of Policy Change
Commenter 0010 asserted that OPM has not provided sufficient justification for departing from its longstanding policy prohibiting pre-established distributions of performance ratings, as reflected in OPM's 1979 regulation.
[
13
]
The commenter argued that the prior rule barred forced, or standardized distributions because they could interfere with appraisal of actual performance against standards, and that OPM has not adequately explained its change in position.
OPM respectfully disagrees that it has not articulated a sufficient reason for departing from its prior policy. The APA requires, as relevant here, that OPM provide a reasoned explanation and show awareness that there is, in fact, a change in policy.
[
14
]
The Court also held that an agency's reasoning need not prove to be a better solution than the status quo but rather that there are good reasons the agency believes support the change in policy.
[
15
]
In the proposed rule, OPM expressly acknowledged its prior prohibition on pre-established rating distributions and explained that, based on current data, experience, and research, a different approach is warranted to address the persistent lack of meaningful differentiation that exists within senior professional performance ratings. OPM further notes that the 1979 regulatory prohibition was directed at rigid, pre-established “bell curve” distributions for fear that requiring a specific distribution of all rating levels would impede appraisal of actual performance against standards. As is common in rulemakings from that time, there is virtually no accompanying preamble explaining the rationale for the provision.
This final rule does not espouse adoption of the rigid “forced distribution” approach that animated the prohibition in the 1979 regulation. OPM has explained that it has no intention of imposing any limits on ratings at the Level 3 (“Fully Successful”) level or below and instead, will limit only the highest rating levels. As discussed in the Background, Governmentwide data show that performance ratings for senior professionals are heavily concentrated at the highest levels, with the vast majority of employees receiving top ratings and very few receiving lower ratings.
[
16
]
As further explained throughout the proposed rule, this lack of meaningful differentiation limits the effectiveness of performance appraisal systems as tools for accountability, recognition, and workforce management. OPM emphasizes that such rating inflation raises concerns regarding whether existing systems are fully achieving the objectives reflected in
5 U.S.C. 4302
permitting the accurate evaluation of job performance, as systems that do not distinguish among levels of performance fail to meaningfully assess differences in contribution and impact. OPM believes the lack of differentiation in ratings under the current system is so severe that, because previous efforts to normalize ratings through guidance
[
17
]
have failed, adoption of a standardized
(
printed page 65908)
distribution is a necessary remedy. As such, OPM concludes that it has provided a reasoned explanation for its change in policy, grounded in current data, research, and statutory considerations, and that the final rule represents a permissible exercise of its authority under
5 U.S.C. chapter 43
.
Commenter 0010 also asserted that OPM failed to consider narrower alternatives, such as clearer performance standards, stronger supervisory training, or more tailored agency-specific rating systems. OPM considered less sweeping approaches, including continued reliance on guidance, and explains in the Regulatory Alternatives section of this preamble why they are inadequate. Guidance-based efforts to instill rigor have been in place since at least 2019 and have not curbed ratings compression, and clearer standards and training do not address the structural incentives toward leniency documented by GAO. Nor does the final rule displace agency tailoring: agencies continue to design their own performance plans, standards, and position-specific requirements under the new subpart.
Consistency With
5 U.S.C. 4302
Commenters 0003 and 0010 argue that the proposed rule is inconsistent with
5 U.S.C. 4302(c)(1)
, which requires that performance appraisal systems permit the accurate evaluation of job performance on the basis of objective criteria related to the job in question. These commenters argued that a distribution framework substitutes relative comparisons for job-based standards and may result in ratings that do not reflect actual performance where multiple employees perform at a similarly high level. Commenter 0010 further articulated the argument stating, “If several employees satisfy the criteria for a high rating, but the system permits only a fixed percentage or number of such ratings, some employees necessarily will receive lower ratings for reasons unrelated to whether they met the requirements of their jobs.”
OPM does not agree that the final rule is inconsistent with
5 U.S.C. 4302
. The statute requires that appraisal systems “to the maximum extent feasible, permit the accurate evaluation of job performance on the basis of objective criteria . . . related to the job in question for each employee or position under the system”
[
18
]
; it does not prescribe or prohibit a specific rating methodology or preclude the use of a standardized distribution to differentiate among levels of performance. Under this final rule, agencies remain responsible for establishing performance plans with clear, job-related expectations and for evaluating employees against those expectations. The standardized distribution framework provides a structured mechanism to support consistent application of performance distinctions; it does not authorize ratings based on non-performance factors or require agencies to disregard evidence of individual performance.
OPM intends, in exercising its authority to establish a standardized distribution, to instruct that any established rating limits be applied at the appropriate aggregate level as opposed to supervisors applying the rating limits within their own group or team. Thus, the requirement to differentiate between relative levels of performance through the use of a standardized distribution operates only after employees are assessed against established performance standards and does not replace or supplant those standards. The concern put forth by commenters claiming that distributional requirements create tension with statute where multiple employees perform at similarly high levels is misplaced. The final rule does not require the mechanical application of quotas without regard to objective, job-related performance evidence. Rather, it requires agencies to exercise informed judgment within a structured framework designed to support meaningful differentiation.
The final rule also provides sufficient flexibility to accommodate circumstances in which performance is uniformly high, as determined through centralized review and the application of professional judgment, including recommendations from the Performance Review Board (PRB). Where an agency determines that adherence to the limits imposed by the standardized distribution is not appropriate because the performance of its senior professional population was genuinely outstanding, OPM's new senior professional performance appraisal system
[
19
]
provides that the President may waive the standardized distribution requirement by certifying that the performance of the agency's senior professionals was outstanding during the relevant time period.
Merit System Principles
Several commenters, including Commenters 0003 and 0010 object to the rule on the basis that it undermines merit system principles at
5 U.S.C. 2301(b)
. Commenter 0003 specifically claims that a standardized distribution undermines principles calling for “efficient use of the Federal workforce” (
5 U.S.C. 2301(b)(5)
) and that “Employees should be retained on the basis of the adequacy of their performance.” (
5 U.S.C. 2301(b)(6)
). The commenter suggests that because a forced distribution centralizes control over ratings, it creates leverage for an agency to use ratings punitively against experts whose results or conclusions displease political appointees. The commenter argues that this creates an invitation for prohibited personnel practices such as discrimination based on political affiliation (
5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(1)(E)
) and coercion of political activity (
5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(3)
). Similarly, a commenter argued that “OPM's proposed rule creates an unconstitutional loophole and attempts to remove power from established laws, tying employee “performance” to political perspectives.” (Commenter 0011).
OPM does not agree that the final rule undermines the merit system principles or creates an increased risk of prohibited personnel practices. The merit system principles require that employees be managed in a manner that promotes efficiency, effectiveness, and fair treatment based on performance. The final rule specifically includes “compliance with merit system principles” as a factor taken into account when appraising senior professionals.
5 CFR 430.508(d)(5)
. The final rule further advances merit system principles by strengthening the rigor and credibility of performance appraisals and ensuring that ratings meaningfully differentiate between levels of contribution and impact.
Any argument that this final rule negatively affects an employee's ability to be retained on the basis of the adequacy of their performance is unfounded. As previously mentioned, OPM intends that the standardized distribution will apply only to the assignment of the highest performance rating levels (Levels 4 and 5) and will not impose limitations on any of the levels at or below Level 3 (“Fully Successful”), such as a “quota” requiring the issuance of a certain amount of Level 1 (“Unacceptable”) ratings. Because Level 3 represents fully adequate performance and remains unrestricted, the application of a standardized distribution will not require a senior professional to receive lower than a Level 3 rating, invalidating concerns over associated performance-based demotion or removal. As such, OPM concludes that a standardized
(
printed page 65909)
distribution does not interfere with an employee's ability to be retained on the basis of the adequacy of their performance and, therefore, does not conflict with
5 U.S.C. 2301(b)(6)
.
OPM also disagrees with the commenter's assertion that the rule invites prohibited personnel practices and will have a chilling effect on the independent professional judgment of experts. Under the final rule, performance ratings remain based on individual merit and individual performance—not on irrelevant factors like race, political affiliation, or religion. Supervisors who assign ratings based on personal favoritism or engage in political coercion would continue to violate merit system principles regardless of the rating structure in place. OPM emphasizes that all existing statutory protections remain fully applicable. Allegations of retaliation, discrimination, or coercion remain subject to review by appropriate oversight bodies, including the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), and equal employment opportunity (EEO) processes. Hence, distinguishing employees based on relative performance does not conflict with the merit system principles or undermine fair and equitable treatment.
Relatedly, Commenter 0010 argued that requiring supervisors to distinguish among similarly performing employees will shift appraisals toward subjective judgments about style, visibility, or personality, increasing the risk of favoritism and implicit bias, and cited Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) best-practices guidance recommending neutral and objective criteria. OPM disagrees that the final rule invites such subjectivity. Ratings remain anchored to written, job-related critical elements and performance standards established in advance, and OPM intends for any rating limits to be applied at an aggregate level rather than within a supervisor's own team. Moreover, the multilayered review structure adopted in this rule—higher-level review, centralized PRB review, and the involvement of approving and oversight officials—provides more checks against idiosyncratic or biased judgments than the current framework, under which a rating may rest largely on a single supervisor's unreviewed assessment. These features are consistent with the EEOC guidance the commenter cites, and all EEO protections and remedies remain fully available to senior professionals.
OPM has also taken additional steps in the final rule to ensure that senior professional appraisals under standardized distribution are free from undue political influence. Consistent with the standardized distribution approach adopted for the SES, which excluded noncareer appointees from the standardized distribution requirements, OPM is excluding Schedule C and Schedule G excepted service appointees from these requirements. This exclusion eliminates even the perception that rating distributions could be used in a manner that favors issuing high ratings to political appointees over career employees.
For these reasons, OPM concludes that the final rule is consistent with the merit system principles and continues to support accurate, objective, and job-related evaluation of employee performance.
Differentiation Among High Performers
Commenters 0003, 0005, and 0010 asserted that the use of a standardized distribution is inappropriate for senior professional employees because these positions are, by design, filled by highly qualified experts who are expected to perform at consistently high levels. These commenters argued that the concentration of ratings at the highest levels may not be indicative of rating inflation but rather a reflection of the inherently high caliber performance demonstrated by the senior professional workforce.
OPM recognizes that senior professional employees are selected based on their advanced expertise, qualifications, and ability to perform work of significant difficulty and responsibility. OPM agrees that senior professionals are expected to perform at a high level and that agencies rely on these employees to provide critical technical, scientific, and professional contributions. However, OPM does not agree that the presence of a highly qualified workforce obviates the need for meaningful differentiation in performance ratings.
As discussed in the proposed rule, available data indicate that performance ratings for senior professionals are heavily concentrated at the highest levels across agencies. While this may, in part, reflect the high caliber of the workforce, it also reflects the failure of agencies to distinguish among varying levels of performance, contribution, and impact. Even within a highly skilled population, differences in performance outcomes, innovation, leadership within technical domains, and contributions to mission results can and do exist. A performance appraisal system must be capable of recognizing these distinctions to support accountability and the effective use of performance-based personnel decisions. As mentioned above, OPM's new senior professional performance appraisal system provides an exception to the standardized distribution requirements by Presidential waiver, so as to avoid a situation where truly high performing senior professionals are precluded from receiving appropriately high ratings.
Consideration of Empirical Evidence
Several commenters, including 0003, 0008, and 0010, asserted that the research literature generally does not support the use of standardized distribution in performance management systems and may, in some cases, demonstrate negative effects. Others suggested that such approaches lead to inaccurate ratings, can reduce collaboration, discourage knowledge sharing, and increase perceptions of unfairness. Commenter 0008 argued that OPM needs to consider the limits of the evidence it is relying on and the mixed experience employers have had with strategies like forced ranking.
In the proposed rule, OPM noted that the literature on standardized distribution reflects a broad range of findings with respect to its efficacy and potential impacts on collaboration, morale, and perceptions of fairness. However, OPM does not agree that the existence of contrary or mixed research findings precludes adopting the changes in the final rule. The APA does not require agencies to resolve all disagreements in the academic literature or to demonstrate that a policy is supported by uniform empirical consensus. OPM has considered the evidence cited in the proposed rule and in comments and has determined that the amendments made in the final rule are necessary to address longstanding concerns regarding the lack of meaningful differentiation in performance ratings across the Federal workforce.
Additionally, other research has demonstrated positive outcomes with respect to the accuracy of comparative judgments. Performance appraisal inherently involves human judgment and any human judgment is by nature comparative.
[
20
]
Thus, the quality of an evaluation is improved by ensuring that it is comparative in nature (that is, involving relative judgments of a target in comparison to other individuals and groups), instead of absolute (that is, involving judgments on scales that do
(
printed page 65910)
not reference others).
[
21
]
One study, for example, concluded that “[t]he relatively few studies that have investigated the validity of comparative performance appraisal methods have tended to support their validity.”
[
22
]
It found significant evidence from “at least three important and quite different domains that comparative evaluative judgments of the self or others may be more advantageous than absolute evaluative judgments.”
[
23
]
These findings suggest that a performance appraisal framework that permits comparative judgments among employees, by utilizing a standardized distribution of ratings, will more accurately and objectively measure individual performance than one that prohibits any comparative judgments between employees and requires that any measurement of employee performance be framed in absolute terms. Moreover, OPM's reforms in this final rule not only address longstanding challenges in Federal performance management with respect to ratings inflation but also provide an approach designed to increase appraisal accuracy.
Use in Private Industry
Other commenters, including Commenters 0008 and 0010, asserted that standardized distribution approaches have been broadly abandoned in the private sector and argued that this trend demonstrates that such systems are ineffective or inappropriate for use in the Federal Government. They cite examples of large individual companies that have moved away from forced ranking systems and suggested that these developments undermine the rationale for adopting a standardized distribution framework.
OPM acknowledges that some private sector organizations have moved away from rigid forced ranking systems. However, the context of the Federal Government differs greatly from the private sector in terms of the relative value that utilizing a standardized distribution framework can provide. For instance, private sector companies have an inherent profit motive to drive distinctions among levels of performance. In contrast, the Federal Government has no such profit motive and instead provides broad procedural and legal protections for employees that discourage supervisors from holding them accountable.
The reluctance of Federal supervisors to identify poor performers has been an issue for decades. In 1990, GAO issued a Governmentwide report on the management of poor performers and found that more than 60% of the personnel officials, managers, and supervisors interviewed believed that not all supervisors were identifying poor performers. According to those officials, supervisors were often reluctant to identify poor performers because the process was too time-consuming, they wanted to avoid confrontation, or they believed they lacked management support. GAO further reported that many supervisors found it especially difficult to address employees performing at the minimally successful level and that the Government had often tolerated less-than-fully-successful performance for extended periods because supervisors had limited options for addressing such employees.
[
24
]
As a result, over time supervisors have defaulted to issuing lenient ratings, thereby avoiding the procedural hurdles and negative personal interactions associated with issuing low ratings. This tendency of supervisors to avoid issuing low ratings and instead issue high ratings inflates the overall ratings distribution and diminishes the value and meaning of a high rating. As previously mentioned, the 2024 FEVS results showed that only 47% of federal employees agreed with the statement, “In my work unit, differences in performance are recognized in a meaningful way.”
[
25
]
This was the lowest positive response rate for any question and has consistently been the lowest over the past three years.
Impact on Individual Employee Motivation
Commenter 0005 argues that standardized distribution will be demotivating to senior professionals because it will lead to lower ratings and reduced incentives.
On the contrary, because performance ratings for senior professionals are so heavily concentrated at the highest rating levels and agencies have limited awards budgets, the size of performance-based awards has decreased, along with the connection between ratings and rewards. In this environment, modestly sized awards are broadly distributed. However, under the framework established by the final rule, with fewer employees receiving the highest ratings, those ratings will carry greater meaning and warrant more significant recognition and reward. OPM's Governmentwide awards guidance
[
26
]
directly supports this approach by calling for agencies to allocate the majority of awards spending for the highest performers. By increasing the magnitude and visibility of rewards for top performance, the standardized distribution approach enables a stronger performance-reward connection and helps to establish a culture of excellence.
Impact on Teamwork
Several commenters contend that standardized distribution may specifically have a negative impact on teamwork. For instance, Commenter 0010 cited an MSPB study
[
27
]
as well as a study by Loberg et al. (2021)
[
28
]
to argue that standardized distribution may reduce collaboration, discourage knowledge sharing, and negatively affect team performance. The commenter suggests that such findings demonstrate that standardized distribution is not appropriate for the Federal workforce, where work is often collaborative in nature.
OPM acknowledges the studies cited and agrees that performance management systems must be carefully designed to support both individual accountability and effective collaboration. However, OPM does not agree that such findings warrant rejecting the use of a standardized distribution framework for senior professional performance appraisal. The Loberg et al. (2021) study itself found that the effectiveness of standardized distribution systems depends on the work context and, where the need for teamwork is not essential and there exist individual performance measures on which to base performance, that standardized distribution increases performance.
[
29
]
OPM acknowledges that the study observed these positive effects only where individuals worked alone and found reduced collaboration and knowledge sharing in team settings; that
(
printed page 65911)
limitation, however, reinforces rather than undermines the approach adopted here. OPM also notes that senior professionals frequently perform highly specialized, expert-level work that is individually driven and assessed based on the quality and impact of their contributions. In such contexts, a structured approach to differentiating performance will enhance accountability and recognition. To the extent collaboration and teamwork are essential to mission outcomes, agencies retain the ability to incorporate those elements into senior professional performance plans and evaluate employees accordingly. Teamwork and collaboration may also be promoted through team-based awards.
Interaction With Other Rulemakings
Commenter 0010 claims that OPM has not adequately addressed how this rule will interact with other pending rules that give performance ratings greater weight. For instance, OPM has separately finalized a reduction in force rule that prioritizes ratings over tenure or length of service for determining retention standing.
[
30
]
The commenter argues that this makes ratings more consequential Governmentwide, given that this final rule will force greater distinctions in performance appraisal.
OPM notes that commenters had an opportunity to submit comments during the public comment period for each of its rulemakings including the proposed rule on reductions in force, and OPM continues to receive higher comment response rates than it has historically received. OPM has since issued a final rule in the reduction in force rulemaking, in which it responded to relevant concerns, and it will respond to comments in its other rulemakings if or when it issues a final rule in each.
OPM observes, however, that performance ratings have long affected retention standing in a reduction in force. Such usage is consistent with
5 U.S.C. 3502(a)
, which requires that OPM issue regulations that “give due effect” to,
inter alia,
“performance ratings” in determining retention standing among competing employees in a reduction in force.
See Am. Fed'n of Gov't Emps., AFL-CIO
v.
Off. of Pers. Mgmt.,
821 F.2d 761, 765 (D.C. Cir. 1987). Further,
5 U.S.C. 4302(a)(3)
contemplates using appraisal results as a basis for training, rewarding, reassigning, promoting, reducing in grade, retaining, and removing employees. Thus, the interaction between this rulemaking and OPM's reduction in force rulemaking does not represent an unexplained gap in OPM's reasoning, but a longstanding feature of the Title 5 statutory scheme.
Further, this rule is complementary to OPM's reduction in force rule, as it seeks to ensure that performance appraisal systems accurately evaluate employee performance while better distinguishing levels of performance. A rule that makes performance matter more in RIF retention and a rule that seeks to improve the accuracy and differentiation of performance ratings address complementary parts of the same merit-based personnel system. Indeed, the current compression of ratings at the highest levels would deprive any performance-based retention criterion of meaningful content; improving the accuracy and differentiation of ratings makes any lawful downstream use of those ratings more, not less, merit-based.
While OPM recognizes that implementing standardized distribution could involve some risks, the current failure of senior professional appraisal systems to meaningfully distinguish performance presents an even greater risk. Therefore, OPM continues to believe that any potential negative effects in areas such as teamwork or collaboration can be adequately addressed through modifications to performance plans and tailored team-based awards. The increased accuracy and rigor that will be achieved by a standardized distribution directly addresses longstanding issues of leniency bias and rating inflation across the Federal Government, thereby strengthening accountability and the effectiveness of senior professional performance management. Accordingly, OPM adopts the language in this section as proposed.
Section 430.506 Planning and Communicating Performance
This section explains the requirements for planning and communicating performance expectations. OPM proposed that rating officials must consult with senior professionals to develop written performance plans that include critical elements (no non-critical elements or additional performance elements), performance standards, and performance requirements. Performance plans must be communicated to senior professionals on or before the beginning of the appraisal period, or upon appointment to a new senior professional position. OPM also proposed that agencies may require a review of senior professional performance plans by the PRB or another body of the agency's choosing to ensure consistency of agency-specific performance requirements.
OPM did not receive comments specifically addressing this section. However, several commenters raised general concerns regarding the establishment of objective, job-related performance expectations and the challenges of applying standardized approaches to highly specialized senior professional roles. These comments are addressed in the relevant sections of this preamble. Accordingly, OPM is adopting the language in this section as proposed.
Section 430.507 Monitoring Performance
This section establishes expectations for ongoing performance monitoring and feedback throughout the appraisal period. Notably, this section requires that progress reviews be held at least quarterly, during which the rating official must inform senior professionals of how they are performing. Rating officials must also provide advice and assistance to senior professionals on how to improve their performance and may also discuss available development opportunities for the senior professional. The intent of this section is to promote frequent performance-related communication between the rating official and senior professional.
Commenter 0005 objected to the requirement that senior professionals receive progress reviews at least quarterly, claiming that it adds an unnecessary administrative burden. This commenter also noted that if OPM's intention is to align the senior professional appraisal system more closely with the SES performance appraisal system, that the SES regulations only require senior executives to receive at least one progress review per year.
While it is true that the SES regulations require conducting progress reviews at least once during the appraisal period,
[
31
]
on February 25, 2025, OPM issued a new Senior Executive Service performance appraisal system and performance plan,
[
32
]
requiring that “[a]t least quarterly, supervisors and executives must meet to discuss, and document, progress toward meeting the critical elements in the senior executive's performance plan.” Thus, requiring that senior professional progress reviews be conducted at least quarterly aligns with the progress review frequency OPM
(
printed page 65912)
expects agencies to be providing for SES members.
OPM believes that frequent feedback is critical to effective performance management and that the benefits of such increased communication outweigh the costs, especially in the context of other changes that are being made in this final rule. Accordingly, OPM is adopting the language in this section as proposed.
Section 430.508 Appraising Performance
This section describes how agencies must appraise senior professionals' performance. It generally parallels the SES appraisal rules, requiring timely communication of expectations, establishment of appraisal timelines, and assessment of both individual and organizational performance. Appraisals must take into account factors such as results achieved, the overall quality of performance, appraisal guidelines based upon assessments of the agency's performance provided by the oversight official, customer perspectives, and compliance with merit system principles. The section clarifies that certain SES-specific factors, such as employee perspectives, are excluded given senior professionals' non-supervisory roles.
OPM received no comments on this section and is adopting the language as proposed. We note that the NPRM contained a typographical error in which the word “and” was omitted from the end of proposed § 430.508(d)(4). In this final rule, we correct that error.
Section 430.509 Rating Performance
This section specifies procedures for deriving and finalizing senior professional ratings. It mirrors certain aspects of the SES rating procedures, such as requiring rating officials to prepare initial summary ratings in writing, share them with senior professionals, and provide an opportunity for written response and higher-level review before finalizing ratings of record. OPM also proposed that agencies with ten or more senior professionals use their agency-level Performance Review Board (PRB) to conduct centralized review of the initial summary ratings and corresponding recommended pay actions. OPM additionally proposed that senior professional performance appraisals and ratings are not appealable, beyond what is otherwise provided under applicable law and regulation.
Commenter 0003 claims the final rule eliminates procedural protections by removing appeal rights and replacing mandatory review of Level 1 (“Unacceptable”) ratings with discretionary processes, thereby increasing the risk of arbitrary action.
On the contrary, while § 430.509(e) establishes that senior professional performance appraisals and ratings are not appealable beyond what is otherwise provided under applicable law or regulation, this provision does not limit or eliminate employees' ability to pursue recourse through established statutory or regulatory avenues, such as EEO processes or appeals to the MSPB, where applicable. The final rule simply eliminates the informal grievance process and the mandatory review of Level 1 ratings that previously applied to senior professionals under
5 CFR part 430, subpart B
. In place of those mechanisms, the rule establishes a more structured and robust review framework aligned with SES review processes. OPM emphasizes that SES members are similarly prohibited by statute
[
33
]
from appealing performance appraisals or ratings, yet the SES rating process is widely recognized as providing strong procedural safeguards through multilayered review. Mirroring these SES provisions, the final rule provides that senior professionals are afforded the opportunity to receive a higher-level review of their initial summary rating regardless of the rating level. In addition, the employee's written response and the findings of the higher-level review are provided to the PRB, which conducts an independent review and makes recommendations to the approving official.
Commenter 0011 further argued that the rule violates the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment, citing
Cleveland Board of Education
v.
Loudermill,
470 U.S. 532 (1985), by eliminating review by a neutral adjudicator and foreclosing judicial review. OPM disagrees. A performance rating, standing alone, does not deprive an employee of a constitutionally protected property or liberty interest;
Loudermill
concerned the procedures required before removal from employment. Any suspension, reduction in grade or pay, or removal based on performance remains subject to the applicable statutory procedures, including advance notice, an opportunity to respond, and, where provided by law, appeal to the MSPB and judicial review under
5 U.S.C. 7703
. Nothing in this rule alters those protections or forecloses any review otherwise available by law.
The final rule adopts a strong oversight framework for senior professional ratings that has proven to be effective for the SES, ensuring that ratings are subject to multiple levels of review and oversight before being finalized. For these reasons, OPM concludes that the final rule maintains appropriate procedural protections, reduces the risk of arbitrary action, and strengthens the consistency and integrity of the senior professional rating process. Accordingly, OPM is adopting the language in this section as proposed.
Section 430.510 Details and Job Changes
This section addresses how performance appraisal systems are to handle senior professionals who experience job changes, such as details, temporary assignments, transfers, or reassignments during the appraisal period. It closely mirrors SES provisions, requiring performance goals and requirements to be established for such assignments and ensuring that written appraisals are completed and transferred appropriately to the receiving organization or agency.
OPM received no comments on this section and is adopting the language as proposed.
Section 430.511 Performance Review Boards (PRBs)
This section refines existing requirements for agency-level centralized review of senior professional performance ratings and pay actions. As discussed in the proposed rule, current senior professional pay regulations at
5 CFR part 534, subpart E
, require agencies with 10 or more senior professionals to conduct a centralized review of proposed ratings and pay actions by a panel designated by the agency head. This final rule requires that agencies subject to the SES must use their established agency-level PRB to conduct the centralized review, including providing written recommendations to the approving official on senior professional ratings of record, performance awards, and pay adjustments. However, agencies not subject to the SES must establish a body equivalent to the PRB.
Commenter 0010 argues that the use of PRBs could introduce politicization into the appraisal process, citing a separate directive by the Administration to reconstitute ERBs with a majority of senior noncareer officials. The commenter states, “If that same approach is extended to PRBs reviewing SL/ST employees, the result would be a more politicized performance-review process at precisely the point where the proposal centralizes more authority in
(
printed page 65913)
PRBs and makes ratings less contestable.”
OPM understands the commenter to be referring to the Presidential Memorandum titled, “Restoring Accountability for Career Senior Executives,”
[
34
]
which did direct agency heads to terminate their existing ERBs and reconstitute them with a majority of senior noncareer officials. However, the commenter erroneously conflates the ERB and PRB directives. The PRB directive makes no mention of noncareer officials. Rather, it calls for agency heads to reconstitute PRB membership “with individuals committed to full enforcement of SES performance evaluations that promote and assure an SES of the highest caliber.” 90 FR at 8482. This directive is specifically intended to strengthen accountability and ensure rigorous, consistent application of performance standards—not to politicize PRBs. OPM notes that both the SES appraisal regulations
[
35
]
and this final rule
[
36
]
require that the PRB, or equivalent body as appropriate, be comprised of a majority of career appointees when appraising the performance of a career appointee. The Presidential Memorandum does not alter that regulatory requirement: even a reconstituted PRB must consist of a majority of career appointees whenever it appraises the performance of a career senior professional—a structural safeguard that distinguishes PRBs from the ERB directive the commenter cites.
OPM also notes that prior approaches to PRB composition included practices which were determined to be inconsistent with merit-based principles, including the use of “DEI” considerations that were addressed in subsequent SES regulatory revisions.
[
37
]
Those changes clarified that PRB membership must be based on merit and free from impermissible considerations, reinforcing objectivity in the review process. Thus, reconstituting PRBs with members committed to full enforcement of performance evaluations enhances, rather than diminishes, merit-focused objectivity.
Further, the PRB, or the equivalent body conducting the centralized review, operates alongside higher-level review and other safeguards to ensure that ratings are not determined unilaterally but are subject to structured oversight. For these reasons, OPM concludes that PRBs, as implemented under this rule, strengthen the integrity, consistency, and accountability of the senior professional performance appraisal process. Accordingly, OPM is adopting the language in this section as proposed.
Section 430.512 Using Performance Results
This section requires agencies to use performance results as a basis for making human capital decisions, including pay adjustments, awards, retention decisions, and other personnel actions. OPM reiterates that actions to suspend, demote, or remove senior professionals from the civil service for unacceptable performance remain subject to the provision(s) of applicable law. OPM also proposed that performance appraisals be used as a factor in assessing a senior professional's continuing development needs and that agencies must provide appropriate incentives and recognition for high performance.
OPM received no comments on this section and is adopting the language as proposed.
Section 430.513 Training and Evaluation
To assure effective implementation of performance appraisal systems, this section requires agencies to provide appropriate information and training to individuals involved in the senior professional performance appraisal process, periodically evaluate the effectiveness of their appraisal systems, and implement improvements as needed. OPM proposed that these evaluations must provide for both assessment of effectiveness and compliance with relevant laws, OPM regulations, and OPM performance management policy.
OPM received no comments on this section and is adopting the language as proposed.
Section 430.514 OPM Review of Agency Systems
This section requires agencies to submit senior professional performance appraisal systems to OPM for review and approval. Appraisal systems are reviewed by OPM for compliance with statutory, regulatory, and OPM policy requirements. Consistent with
5 U.S.C. 4304(b)(3)
, this section also requires that if OPM determines a system does not meet the requirements of the law or regulation, OPM will identify the requirements that were not met and direct the agency to take corrective action, and the agency must comply. This review function supports consistent and compliant performance management practices across the Federal Government.
Commenter 0011 asserted that OPM lacks authority to review agency performance appraisal systems and direct corrective action, arguing that such oversight constitutes an impermissible intrusion into agency personnel management and conflicts with statutory roles assigned to other entities, such as the MSPB and the OSC.
OPM does not agree that the review and oversight provisions in
5 CFR 430.514
exceed its statutory authority or improperly intrude on agency personnel management. OPM's authority to oversee performance appraisal systems derives directly from
5 U.S.C. chapter 43
, which authorizes OPM to prescribe regulations governing performance appraisal systems and ensure that such systems comply with statutory requirements. Under
5 U.S.C. 4302
, agencies are required to develop performance appraisal systems in accordance with regulations prescribed by OPM. This statutory framework necessarily contemplates that OPM will not only establish requirements for agency systems but also ensure that those systems are implemented in a manner consistent with law and regulation. The authority to review agency systems for compliance and to require corrective action where deficiencies are identified is inherent in OPM's responsibility to administer and enforce these statutory requirements.
OPM also does not agree that its oversight role conflicts with the statutory functions of the MSPB or the OSC. Those entities serve distinct and complementary roles within the Federal personnel system. The MSPB adjudicates appeals and enforces merit system principles in individual cases, while the OSC investigates and prosecutes prohibited personnel practices. In contrast, OPM's role under chapter 43 is to establish Governmentwide performance management policy and ensure that agency systems comply with applicable requirements. The oversight provided in § 430.514 operates at the system level and does not replace or diminish the independent authorities of these entities. Nothing in this rule amends
5 U.S.C. 2302
or the Whistleblower Protection Act, and allegations of prohibited personnel practices remain fully within the jurisdiction of the OSC and the MSPB.
For these reasons, OPM concludes that the review and oversight provisions in § 430.514 are fully consistent with OPM's statutory authority and responsibilities under
5 U.S.C. chapter 43
and are necessary to ensure that
(
printed page 65914)
performance appraisal systems for senior professionals are implemented in a lawful, consistent, and effective manner across the Federal Government. Accordingly, OPM is adopting the language in this section as proposed.

Expected Impact of This Rulemaking
A. Statement of Need
OPM is issuing this rule pursuant to its authority to issue regulations governing performance appraisals under
subchapter I of chapter 43 of title 5, United States Code.
As discussed in the Background, the purpose of this rule is to establish separate regulations that will be better suited to the performance appraisal needs of senior professionals. While many provisions applicable to senior professionals such as pay, aggregate limit on compensation, leave accrual, and leave carryover limit have evolved over the years to match what the SES receive, senior professionals have remained subject to the same general performance appraisal regulations that apply to most non-SES federal employees, including rank-and-file GS and prevailing rate employees. The lack of appraisal rules specifically tailored to senior professionals' important roles and high level of compensation hinders agencies' ability to fully leverage the strategic potential of these positions.
OPM found that, despite its previous efforts to promote rigor in senior professional performance appraisal by encouraging agencies to develop more stringent performance requirements,
[
38
]
senior professional ratings distributions come nowhere close to resembling a normal bell curve. As mentioned in the Background, Governmentwide senior professional performance rating data for fiscal years 2023 and 2024
[
39
]
show that approximately 90 percent of senior professionals received a Level 5 (“Outstanding”) or Level 4 (“Exceeds Fully Successful”) rating and less than a half of one percent of senior professionals were rated below Level 3 (“Fully Successful”). The distribution of these ratings suggests there is inflation of senior professional ratings and poor performing employees are likely not being identified or held accountable through a rigorous appraisal process. As such, action must be taken to re-set and infuse rigor into the senior professional performance appraisal process.
OPM recognizes that agencies have operated under a regulatory framework that prohibited pre-established distributions of ratings for several decades. After evaluating Governmentwide ratings data, implementation experience, and academic literature, OPM has concluded that the previous approach has not adequately promoted meaningful distinctions in performance among senior professionals.
B. Impact
OPM is establishing a new subpart specifically dedicated to the performance appraisal of senior professionals and that more closely resembles the SES appraisal system—including changes that allow OPM to establish and enforce a standardized distribution of performance ratings—to enable agencies and senior professionals to be held to a higher standard of accountability and ensure only the truly deserving performers are rewarded for their performance.
Allowing for the establishment of limits on senior professional ratings will result in a more normalized distribution of performance ratings. OPM anticipates that a standardized distribution will incentivize improved performance of senior professionals as they no longer would expect to receive high ratings without demonstrating superior performance relative to the other senior professionals in their agency. Consequently, improved senior professional performance would ultimately improve the performance of the Federal Government in providing services to the American public.
(
printed page 65915)
Establishing senior professional performance appraisal regulations that more closely align with the Senior Executive Service appraisal regulations creates greater opportunities for oversight and review of senior professional ratings. In the final rule, agencies employing 10 or more senior professionals will utilize their agency-level PRB to conduct the centralized review required in subpart E of
5 CFR part 534
. Additionally, all senior professionals will now be able to request higher-level review of their initial summary rating, regardless of the rating level, bringing enhanced credibility, transparency, and accountability to the rating process.
C. Costs
This rule will affect the operations of more than 60 Federal agencies—ranging from cabinet-level departments to small independent agencies—that have SL or ST employees. To comply with the regulatory changes, individuals employed by affected agencies will need to spend time updating agency senior professional performance appraisal policies and procedures. For this cost analysis, the assumed average salary rate of federal employees performing this work will be the rate in 2025 for GS-14, step 5, in the Washington, DC, locality pay table ($161,486 annual locality rate and $77.38 hourly locality rate). We assume the total dollar value of labor, which includes wages, benefits, and overhead, is equal to 200 percent of the wage rate, resulting in an assumed labor cost of $154.76 per hour.
Additionally, affected agencies will need to review the rule and update their policies and procedures. We estimate that, in the first year following publication of the final rule, this will require an average of 80 hours of work by employees with an average hourly cost of $154.76 per hour. This will result in estimated one-time costs of about $12,400 per agency and about $744,000 Governmentwide.
Senior professionals revise their performance requirements each year as they develop their performance plans. OPM anticipates that adjusting their specific performance requirements to reflect the updated critical elements may take each senior professional slightly longer than usual in the first year. We estimate that this will require approximately 15 additional minutes in the first year of implementation compared to the time usually spent developing specific performance requirements for the annual performance plan. Based on the average salary of the SL and ST pay plans in September 2024 (most recent available data), we assume an overall average SL/ST salary rate of $204,735, or $98.43 per hour.
[
40
]
We assume the total dollar value of labor, which includes wages, benefits, and overhead, is equal to 200 percent of the wage rate, resulting in an assumed labor cost of $196.86 per hour. There are approximately 1,420 employees with an SL or ST pay plan in the executive branch. We estimate this will result in a one-year, transitional increase in costs of about $70,000 Governmentwide.
OPM anticipates that the overall implementation costs would be limited in duration and would total about $814,000. OPM did not receive any comments on its estimates of costs.
D. Benefits
Senior professionals are critical to the effective operation and strategic direction of the Federal Government. The changes in this rule enhance parity between senior professionals and the SES by establishing appraisal rules for senior professionals that are more closely aligned with SES appraisal rules. This relieves agencies from superfluous requirements found in subpart B of part 430 that are not well-suited to managing senior professional performance, such as the requirement to establish one or more performance appraisal programs.
By allowing OPM to establish a limit on the number of senior professionals who can receive the highest ratings, there will be a clear distinction of the highest performers across an agency and the Federal Government. Agencies will no longer be able to rate all of their senior professionals at the highest performance ratings, thus encouraging senior professionals to strive for increased levels of performance and ultimately provide better results for the Federal Government and the American public.
Senior professionals will benefit from increased feedback and oversight under the new subpart, as it requires more frequent progress reviews and provides the opportunity for a higher-level review of an initial summary rating at any level instead of a mandatory review of a Level 1 (“Unacceptable”) rating of record. Agencies employing 10 or more senior professionals will see enhanced oversight by utilizing agency-level PRBs to oversee recommended ratings of record, pay adjustments, and performance awards, thus providing overall increased Governmentwide consistency for senior professional performance appraisal.
E. Regulatory Alternatives
An alternative to this rulemaking is to not establish a new subpart in part 430 dedicated to senior professional performance appraisal and instead OPM could issue further guidance encouraging agencies to be increasingly rigorous in managing the performance of their senior professionals. However, without the provisions in this subpart, agencies would continue to be prevented from applying a standardized distribution of senior professional ratings by
5 CFR 430.208(c)
. As mentioned in the Statement of Need, previous attempts to curb rating inflation through guidance have not been successful; instead, it appears that the percentage of senior professionals receiving Level 4 or 5 performance ratings has reached a point where almost all senior professionals (
i.e.,
approximately 90%) are receiving a Level 4 or 5 rating. Without the ability to place limits on senior professional ratings, the pervasive inflation of senior professional ratings will likely continue, resulting in a lack of meaningful rating distinction and thus, lack of accountability.
Another alternative to this rulemaking is for OPM to pursue a different rulemaking that would amend subpart B of part 430 by excluding senior professionals from the forced distribution prohibition contained in that subpart. While this approach would achieve some of the intended purpose of the proposed rule, it would lack the meaningful reforms to senior professional performance appraisal that increase parity with the SES appraisal rules, such as providing for higher-level review of initial summary ratings and the PRB providing centralized review. Failing to establish a separate subpart in part 430 dedicated to senior professional performance appraisal would result in senior professionals continuing to be subject to the cumbersome provisions of subpart B of part 430, which require agencies to establish both appraisal systems and appraisal programs, which is burdensome and not aligned with OPM's vision of centralized, effective senior professional performance management.
Severability
OPM intends that, if any of the provisions of this rule as finalized were held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, that provision would be severable from its respective section(s) and would not affect the remainder thereof or the application of the
(
printed page 65916)
provision to other persons not similarly situated or to other dissimilar circumstances. For example, if the implementation of a standardized distribution of ratings were held to be unenforceable, the remaining provisions established by this final rule would be unaffected and could remain in effect.

A. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Director of OPM certifies that this rulemaking will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it will apply only to Federal agencies and employees.
B. Regulatory Review
OPM has examined the impact of this rule as required by
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
, which direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public, health, and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity). This rulemaking is not a “significant regulatory action” under section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
. This final rule is not an
E.O. 14192
regulatory action because it does not impose any more than de minimis regulatory costs.

This regulation will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the National Government and the States, or on distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Therefore, in accordance with
Executive Order 13132
, it is determined that this rule does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant preparation of a Federalism Assessment.

.
E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule that would impose spending costs on State, local, or tribal governments in the aggregate, or on the private sector, in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. That threshold is currently approximately $206 million. This rulemaking will not result in the expenditure by State, local, or tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, in excess of the threshold. Thus, no written assessment of unfunded mandates is required.
F. Congressional Review Act
