SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is proposing to establish a temporary safety zone for certain navigable waters in the Miami Marine Stadium Basin in connection with the FRL Inaugural Invitational eFoil Exhibition Race. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with eFoil race operations. This proposed rulemaking would prohibit persons and vessels from being in the safety zone unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector Miami. We invite your comments on this proposed rulemaking.
DATES:
Comments and related material must be received by the Coast Guard on or before November 18, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To submit comments and view available documents, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for USCG-2026-1162.

If you have questions about this proposed rule, contact MST2 Elliot Cortes, Sector Miami Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 786-295-9051, or email
SectorMiamiWaterways@uscg.mil
.

II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard was notified that an organization will be hosting the FRL Inaugural Invitational eFoil Exhibition Race on November 15, 2026, at the Miami Marine Stadium Basin, Miami, FL. Hazards from eFoil racing include high-speed blunt force impacts, propeller lacerations, and lithium battery failures. The Captain of the Port Sector Miami (COTP) has determined that potential hazards associated with eFoil racing are a safety concern for anyone within 100 yards of race operations. Therefore, the COTP is proposing this rule under the authority in
46 U.S.C. 70034
, which is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the safety zone.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This proposed rule would establish a safety zone on November 15, 2026, from 8:00 a.m. until 9:00 p.m. The safety zone would cover all navigable waters within 100 yards of the race area. No vessel or person would be permitted to enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative. The regulatory text we are proposing appears at the end of this document.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this proposed rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980,
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. Section 605 of the RFA allows an agency to certify a rule, in lieu of preparing an analysis, if the rulemaking is not expected to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The Coast Guard certifies under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
that this proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities for the following reasons.
Vessel traffic will be able to safely transit around this regulated area. This regulation will only impact a small area for a few hours. In addition, the Coast Guard will issue a Broadcast Notice to Mariners via VHF-FM marine channel 16, which will allow small entities to adjust their transit plans.
If you think that your business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction qualifies as a small entity and that this proposed rule would have a significant economic impact on it, please submit a comment (see
ADDRESSES
) explaining why you think it qualifies and how and to what degree this proposed rule would economically affect it.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), if this proposed rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247).
(
printed page 66034)
B. Collection of Information
This proposed rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this proposed rule under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this proposed rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
As required by The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
), the Coast Guard certifies that this proposed rule will not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this proposed rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
), and have determined that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment.
This proposed rule is a safety zone. It is categorically excluded from further review under paragraph L60(a) of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1.
V. Public Participation and Request for Comments
We view public participation as essential to effective rulemaking and will consider all comments and material received during the comment period. Your comment can help shape the outcome of this rulemaking. If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this rulemaking, indicate the specific section of this document to which each comment applies, and provide a reason for each suggestion or recommendation.
Submitting comments.
We encourage you to submit comments at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
To do so, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
,
type USCG-2026-1162 in the search box and click “Search.” Next, look for this document in the Search Results column, and click on it. Then click on the Comment option. If you cannot submit your material by using
https://www.regulations.gov
,
call or email the person in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this proposed rule for alternate instructions.
Viewing material in the docket.
To view available documents, find the docket as described in the previous paragraph, and then select “Supporting & Related Material” in the Document Type column. We will post public comments in our online docket. Additional information is on the
https://www.regulations.gov
Frequently Asked Questions web page.
Personal information.
We accept anonymous comments. Comments we post to
https://www.regulations.gov
will include any personal information you have provided. For more about privacy and submissions to the docket in response to this document, see DHS's eRulemaking System of Records notice (
85 FR 14226
, March 11, 2020).

§ 165.T07-1162
Safety Zone; FRL Inaugural Invitational eFoil Exhibition Race, Miami Marine Stadium Basin, Miami, FL
(a)
Location.
The following area is a safety zone: All waters of Miami Marine Stadium Basin, from surface to bottom, encompassed by a line connecting the following points beginning at 25.745062, −80.166891, 25.743008, −80.164699, thence to 25.741214, −80.166992, 25.743201, −80.169185 and back to the beginning point. These coordinates are based on the World Geodetic System (WGS 84).
(b)
Definitions.
As used in this section,
designated representative
means a Coast Guard Patrol Commander, including a Coast Guard coxswain, petty officer, or other officer operating a Coast Guard vessel and a Federal, State, and local officer designated by or assisting the Captain of the Port Sector Miami (COTP) in the enforcement of the safety zone.
(c)
Regulations.
(1) Under the general safety zone regulations in subpart C of this part, you may not enter the safety zone described in paragraph (a) of this section unless authorized by the COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
(2) To seek permission to enter, contact the COTP or the COTP's representative on VHF-FM channel 16 or by telephone at (833) 642-7271. Those in the safety zone must comply with all lawful orders or directions given to them by the COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
(d)
Enforcement period.
This section will be enforced from 8 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. on November 15, 2026.

II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard received a request under 33 CFR 100.15 from an organization regarding the Discover the Caribbean Regatta 2026, hosted by the Ponce Yacht and Fishing Club. The event is scheduled to take place on October 30, 2026, through November 1, 2026, and November 14, 2026, through November 15, 2026, from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. each day. The designated event includes specific waters within Ponce Harbor and is expected to involve approximately 100 participants and 10 spectator vessels.
The Captain of the Port San Juan (COTP) is issuing this Special Local Regulation (SLR) under the authority in
46 U.S.C. 70041
. The COTP has determined that potential hazards associated with the regatta poses potential safety concerns for individuals and vessels within the regulated area. Additional risks, such as sudden weather changes and shifting currents, further heighten the likelihood of collisions and other safety issues due to the increased maritime traffic. The purpose of this rulemaking is to protect event participants, non-participants, and transiting vessels before, during, and after the scheduled event.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. The Coast Guard must establish this SLR by October 30, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we have do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reasons, the Coast Guard finds that under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a temporary SLR on October 30, 2026, through November 1, 2026, and on November 14, 2026 through November 15, 2026, from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. daily. The special local regulation will cover navigable waters within the Ponce Harbor. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the regulated area without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The regulatory flexibility analysis provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980,
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, do not apply to rules that are not subject to notice and comment. Because the Coast Guard has, for good cause, waived the notice and comment requirement that would otherwise apply to this rulemaking, the Regulatory Flexibility Act's flexibility analysis provisions do not apply here.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247). The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
(

AGENCY:
Federal Communications Commission.
ACTION:
Notice of a modified system of records.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC, Commission, or Agency) proposes to rename and modify an existing system of records, FCC-2, Business Contacts, Disclosures, and Certifications (formerly: FCC-2, Business Contacts and Certifications), subject to the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended. This action is necessary to meet the requirements of the Privacy Act to publish in the
Federal Register
notice of the existence and character of records maintained by the Agency. The Commission uses this system to collect and maintain points of contact and to ensure compliance with FCC rules through certifications of disclosures and other information provided to the Commission. The FCC is modifying FCC-2 to include disclosures of prior misconduct from FCC program participants, consistent with the Office of Management and Budget Governmentwide Guidelines on Suspension and Debarment and FCC-specific rules. This modification changes the name of the system; updates the Purposes of the System, Categories of Records in the System, and Record Source Categories; and adds one routine use.
DATES:
This modified system of records will become effective on October 19, 2026. Written comments on the routine uses are due by November 18, 2026. The new or revised routine uses in this action will become effective on November 18, 2026 unless comments are received that require a contrary determination.

Send comments to Shana Yates, FCC, 45 L Street NE, Washington, DC 20554, care of the Office of General Counsel, Privacy Team; or to
privacy@fcc.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
FCC Office of General Counsel, Privacy Team, at
privacy@fcc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice serves to update and modify FCC-2 as a result of various necessary changes and updates. The substantive changes and modifications to the previously published version of the FCC-2 system of records include:
1. Renaming the system FCC-2, Business Contacts, Disclosures, and Certifications;
2. Updating the Purposes of the System, Categories of Records in the System, and Record Source Categories; and
3. Adding one new routine use (listed by the routine use number provided in this notice): (15) Suspension and Debarment Disclosure.

FCC-2, Business Contacts, Disclosures, and Certifications

Unclassified.

Federal Communications Commission (FCC), 45 L Street NE, Washington, DC 20554; Universal Service Administrative Company, 700 12th Street NW, Suite 900, Washington, DC 20005; or FISMA-compliant contractor.

47 U.S.C. 151
,
152
,
154
(i)-(j) & (o), 155, 251(e)(3), 254, 257, 301, 303, 332, 402, 1302; and

609(a)(3)
.
PURPOSES OF THE SYSTEM:
The FCC and organizations administering programs on behalf of the FCC use this system to collect and maintain points of contact, disclosures, and certifications from: (1) entities regulated by the FCC and in related industries, as well as contractors, vendors, and those performing collateral duties for the FCC; (2) individuals, including points of contact for and those who certify on behalf of entities, that participate in FCC programs; (3) other Federal, state, local, U.S. territorial, and Tribal government entities that administer, support, participate in, or receive information related to, FCC programs and activities; and (4) public interest organizations, nonprofit organizations, international organizations, and other non-business entities that participate in FCC proceedings or are included in FCC programs.
CATEGORIES OF INDIVIDUALS COVERED BY THE SYSTEM:
Individuals, including points of contact for and those who certify on behalf of, businesses, public interest organizations, nonprofit organizations, government organizations, international organizations, and other non-business entities that participate in FCC proceedings or programs, or are included in FCC programs; points of contact for Federal, state, local, U.S. territorial, or Tribal governmental entities.
CATEGORIES OF RECORDS IN THE SYSTEM:
Contact information, such as name, username, signature, phone numbers, emails, and addresses; work and educational history; suspension and debarment history and current status, as well as history of misconduct germane to suspension or debarment.
RECORD SOURCE CATEGORIES:
Information in this system is provided by individuals, including points of contact for and those who certify on behalf of: FCC contractors; vendors; those providing collateral duties to the FCC; regulated entities and entities in related industries; participants in FCC programs; Federal, state, local, U.S. territorial, and Tribal government entities; public interest organizations, nonprofit organizations, government organizations, international organizations, and other non-business entities that participate in FCC proceedings.
ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND THE PURPOSES OF SUCH USES:
In addition to those disclosures generally permitted under
5 U.S.C. 552a(b)
of the Privacy Act, all or a portion of the records or information contained in this system may be disclosed to authorized entities, as is determined to be relevant and necessary, outside the FCC as a routine use pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a(b)(3)
as follows.
1. Public Access—Contact information and certifications made by individuals contained in this system may be made available for public inspection to comply with FCC regulations that require public disclosure of this information, or in Commission releases, including notices of proposed rulemaking, public notices, orders, and other actions released by the Commission.
2. Authorized Third Parties—Contact information and certifications made by individuals contained in this system may be shared with authorized third parties, including individuals and businesses in regulated and related industries, FCC vendors, and their contractors, to administer, support, participate in, or receive information related to, FCC programs and activities; or to ensure compliance with the confidentiality and other rules regarding information sharing in the FCC's programs and activities.
3. Federal Agencies—Contact information and certifications made by individuals contained in this system may be shared with other Federal agencies in order to administer, support, participate in, or receive information related to: FCC programs and activities; and programs and activities the FCC supports.
4. State, Local, U.S. Territorial, and Tribal Government Entities—Contact information and certifications made by individuals contained in this system may be shared with authorized state, local, U.S. territorial and Tribal government entities to administer, support, participate in, or receive information related to: FCC programs and activities; and programs and activities the FCC supports.
5. Litigation—Records may be disclosed to the Department of Justice (DOJ) when: (a) the FCC or any component thereof; (b) any employee of the FCC in his or her official capacity; (c) any employee of the FCC in his or her individual capacity where the DOJ or the FCC has agreed to represent the employee; or (d) the United States Government is a party to litigation or has an interest in such litigation, and by careful review, the FCC determines that the records are both relevant and necessary to the litigation, and the use of such records by the DOJ is for a purpose that is compatible with the purpose for which the FCC collected the records.
6. Adjudication—Records may be disclosed in a proceeding before a court or adjudicative body, when: (a) the FCC or any component thereof; (b) any employee of the FCC in his or her official capacity; (c) any employee of the FCC in his or her individual capacity; or (d) the United States Government, is a party to litigation or has an interest in such litigation, and by careful review, the FCC determines that the records are both relevant and necessary to the litigation, and that the use of such records is for a purpose that is compatible with the purpose for which the agency collected the records.
7. Law Enforcement and Investigation—When the FCC investigates any violation or potential violation of a civil or criminal law, regulation, policy, executed consent decree, order, or any other type of compulsory obligation and determines that a record in this system, either alone or in conjunction with other information, indicates a violation or potential violation of law, regulation, policy, consent decree, order, or other compulsory obligation, the FCC may disclose pertinent information as it deems necessary to the target of an investigation, as well as with the appropriate Federal, State, local, Tribal, international, or multinational agencies, or a component of such an agency, responsible for investigating, prosecuting, enforcing, or implementing a statute, rule, regulation, order, or other compulsory obligation.
8. Congressional Inquiries—Information may be provided to a Congressional office in response to an inquiry from that Congressional office made at the written request of the individual to whom the information pertains.
9. Government-wide Program Management and Oversight—Records may be disclosed to the Department of Justice (DOJ) to obtain that department's advice regarding disclosure obligations under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA); or to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to obtain that office's advice regarding obligations under the Privacy Act.
(
printed page 66139)
10. Breach Notification—Records may be disclosed to appropriate agencies, entities, and persons when: (a) the Commission suspects or has confirmed that there has been a breach of PII maintained in the system of records; (b) the Commission has determined that as a result of the suspected or confirmed breach there is a risk of harm to individuals, the Commission (including its information system, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security; and (c) the disclosure made to such agencies, entities, and persons is reasonably necessary to assist in connection with the Commission's efforts to respond to the suspected or confirmed breach or to prevent, minimize, or remedy such harm.
11. Assistance to Federal Agencies and Entities Related to Breaches—Records may be disclosed to another Federal agency or Federal entity when the Commission determines that information from this system is reasonably necessary to assist the recipient agency or entity in: (a) responding to a suspected or confirmed breach or (b) preventing, minimizing, or remedying the risk of harm to individuals, the recipient agency or entity (including its information systems, program, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security, resulting from a suspected or confirmed breach.
12. Non-Federal Personnel—Records may be disclosed to non-Federal personnel, including contractors, other vendors (
e.g.,
identity verification services), grantees, and volunteers who have been engaged to assist the FCC in the performance of a service, grant, cooperative agreement, or other activity related to this system of records and who need to have access to the records in order to perform their activity.
13. Department of Treasury—Records may be disclosed to the U.S. Department of Treasury when disclosure of the information is relevant to review payment and award eligibility through the Do Not Pay Working System for the purposes of identifying, preventing, or recouping improper payments to an applicant for, or recipient of, Federal funds, including funds disbursed by a state (meaning a state of the United States, the District of Columbia, a territory or possession of the United States, or a federally recognized Indian tribe) in a state-administered, federally funded program.
14. Prevention of Fraud, Waste, and Abuse Disclosure—Records may be disclosed to Federal agencies, non-Federal entities, their employees, and agents (including contractors, their agents or employees; employees or contractors of the agents or designated agents); or contractors, their employees or agents with whom the FCC has a contract, service agreement, cooperative agreement, or computer matching agreements for the purpose of: (1) detection, prevention, and recovery of improper payments; (2) detection and prevention of fraud, waste, and abuse in Federal programs administered by a Federal agency or non-Federal entity; (3) detection of fraud, waste, and abuse by individuals in their operations and programs, but only to the extent that the information shared is necessary and relevant to verify pre-award and prepayment requirements prior to the release of Federal funds, prevent and recover improper payments for services rendered under programs of the FCC or of those Federal agencies and non-Federal entities to which the FCC provides information under this routine use.
15. Suspension and Debarment Disclosure—The FCC may disclose information from this system to other Federal agencies considering suspension or debarment action if the information is relevant to the suspension and debarment action.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
ORV Use by Residents of Anaktuvuk Pass
Anaktuvuk Pass is a small remote village, without road access, entirely within the administrative boundaries of Gates. Anaktuvuk Pass, named “the place of caribou droppings,” sits along an ancient migration route that has guided the caribou—and the people who follow them—for centuries. Most of the residents of Anaktuvuk Pass are inland Iñupiat, or Nunamiut people, and Anaktuvuk Pass is their last remaining settlement. These nomadic people roamed the Brooks Range for generations, living off the land, before dispersing in the early 1900s due to the collapse of the caribou population. By the 1940s, several Nunamiut families returned to their ancestral home, settling in the broad, treeless valley of Anaktuvuk Pass, decades before the 1980 establishment of Gates. Many residents continue to rely on subsistence activities like caribou hunting to support their way of life.
In 2024, Anaktuvuk Pass was home to 395 residents, with Iñupiat making up over 84% of the population. The community's economy is intertwined with the land, primarily relying on subsistence hunting of caribou. The pursuit of caribou, along with fishing and gathering, sustains the community.
Anaktuvuk Pass residents have long relied on motorized access, including snowmachines in winter and ORVs in summer, to pursue subsistence resources. The final nomadic Nunamiut relocated to the modern-day village during the 1950s. After permanent settlement, Nunamiut were unable to follow the caribou during their seasonal migrations, the people of Anaktuvuk Pass ventured out from the village within what is today, Gates, to subsistence hunt. Beginning in the 1960s, and increasing during the 1970s, ORVs were regularly used by the residents of Anaktuvuk Pass engaging in subsistence activities. In the years leading up to and immediately following the passage of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA), residents of Anaktuvuk Pass relied increasingly on ORVs for subsistence hunting as was documented in a 1985 study titled,
In the National Interest: A Geographically Based Study of Anaktuvuk Pass Iñupiat Subsistence Through Time.
The first documented observance of an ORV by residents of Anaktuvuk Pass is believed to have occurred in 1950 when the United States Geological Survey brought multiple large, tracked vehicles to the village to conduct summer exploration and mapping work. By the early 1970s, the number of ORVs owned and operated by residents of Anaktuvuk Pass began to increase. By 1980, the year ANILCA became law, it is estimated there were between fifteen and twenty-eight ORVs in Anaktuvuk Pass. ORVs in Anaktuvuk Pass were regularly deployed in the 1970s as the primary means of summer transportation that allowed subsistence hunters to reach and transport game farther from the village and considered the only effective means of subsistence hunting in the summer. ORV use had been particularly important for reaching locations fairly distant from the village where subsistence species are likely to be encountered during the summer months. Subsistence hunters interviewed about their summer hunts explained they used their ORVs to “bring meat back after animals had been killed out in the field” and traveled extensively throughout the region to find caribou. Additional information available to NPS demonstrates that ORVs were used around Anaktuvuk Pass for subsistence purposes in Gates before its establishment.
See, e.g.,
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Effects of All Terrain Vehicle Traffic on Tundra Terrain Near Anaktuvuk Pass, Alaska (1988); NPS, Effects of All-Terrain Vehicle Use in the Vicinity of Anaktuvuk Pass, Gates of the Arctic National Park, Alaska: I. Study of Established, Recovery, and New Trail Segments (1988); and NPS, The Anaktuvuk Pass All-Terrain Vehicle Study 1986-1988: A Narrative Report of Field Operation and Dispersed ATV Use (1989).
ANILCA Statutory Framework
Title VIII of ANILCA establishes a statutory framework intended to protect subsistence uses by rural Alaska residents. Congress expressly recognized the importance of subsistence resources to the physical, economic, traditional, and cultural well-being of rural Alaska communities and directed that such uses be protected on the public lands of Alaska. Section 201(4)(a) of ANILCA established Gates and provides, among other things, that subsistence uses by local residents shall be permitted in the park where such uses are traditional, in accordance with title VIII of ANILCA. In turn, Section 811(a) of ANILCA provides that the Secretary “shall ensure that rural residents engaged in subsistence uses have reasonable access to subsistence resources on the public lands.”
16 U.S.C. 3121(a)
. Section 811(b) of ANILCA provides that “[n]otwithstanding any other provision
(
printed page 66036)
of this Act or other law, the Secretary shall permit on the public lands appropriate use for subsistence purposes of snowmobiles, motorboats, and other means of surface transportation traditionally employed for such purposes by local residents, subject to reasonable regulation.”
16 U.S.C. 3121(b)
. ANILCA's text is clear and unambiguous, reflecting Congress's express intent “to provide the opportunity for rural residents engaged in a subsistence way of life to continue to do so.”
16 U.S.C. 3111(1)
.
Through enactment of this language, Congress directed that reasonable subsistence access be ensured and that traditionally employed means of surface transportation be permitted for subsistence purposes, subject only to reasonable regulation. Accordingly, Title VIII reflects a congressional policy favoring the continuation of subsistence uses and the practical ability of rural residents to reach and harvest subsistence resources. These congressional findings and policies inform the NPS's interpretation of Sections 811(a) and 811(b) and confirm that ANILCA's subsistence provisions are intended to preserve meaningful and practical access for subsistence purposes.
ANILCA distinguishes between requiring subsistence access and regulating subsistence access. Section 811(b) directs that the Secretary “shall permit” appropriate use of traditionally employed means of surface transportation for subsistence purposes while authorizing reasonable regulation of those uses. Accordingly, an agency may take only reasonable measures necessary to address demonstrated impacts of a means of surface transportation within the scope of Section 811(b), while at the same time ensuring that reasonable access is maintained consistent with the purposes of Title VIII.
NPS Prohibition of ORV Subsistence Access to Gates
On January 28, 1986, an official within the NPS Alaska Regional Office sent a memorandum to the superintendent of Gates concluding that all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) do not constitute means of surface transportation that have been “traditionally” employed for subsistence purposes in Gates. The terms ORV and ATV have been used interchangeably over time to refer to similar classes of vehicles. The 1986 Memorandum stated that “until it can be shown that ATVs are traditional in [Gates] as defined by Webster and Black [dictionaries], they are prohibited for subsistence uses in the park.” The 1986 Memorandum thus concluded that ATVs “are not permitted by ANILCA” and had “not been shown to be a traditionally employed means of surface transportation for subsistence uses.” This interpretation of “traditional” and the prohibition on ATV use for subsistence purposes was incorporated into the Gates General Management Plan (GMP), which stated that within Gates, “the use of ORVs, which are defined in the GMP to include ATVs, for subsistence is not allowed because the use has not been shown to be a traditional means of access.”
On December 17, 1992, NPS entered into a land exchange agreement (1992 Agreement) with the Nunamiut Corporation, the city of Anaktuvuk Pass, and the Arctic Slope Regional Corporation that was amended in 1993 and 1994. In 1996, Congress ratified the 1992 Agreement in section 302 of the Omnibus Parks and Public Lands Management Act of 1996 (Act). In the Act, Congress recognized that “[u]nlike most other Alaskan Native communities, the village of Anaktuvuk Pass is not located on a major river, lake, or coastline that can be used as a means of access. The residents of Anaktuvuk pass have relied increasingly on snow machines in winter and all-terrain vehicles in summer as their primary means of access to pursue caribou and other subsistence resources.”
Public Law 104-333
, 110 Stat. 4093 (1996).
The 1992 Agreement allowed some ATV access in Gates for subsistence uses. Specifically, certain non-wilderness areas of Federally-owned park land were opened to dispersed ATV use. The land exchange agreement was intended in part “to resolve the longstanding dispute over subsistence use of ATVs only on public lands in and around Anaktuvuk Pass.” H.R. Rep. No. 104-8 (1995). However, the land exchange agreement did not “conf[i]rm or deny that ATV access to public lands for subsistence use is a statutorily protected traditional access right under ANILCA,” and did “not purport to resolve this issue.”
Id.
Accordingly, the dispute over whether ORVs, including ATVs, may be used in Gates continued. Local residents of Anaktuvuk Pass contend the ATV access granted by the 1992 Agreement is insufficient for Anaktuvuk Pass residents who rely on subsistence uses, in part, because caribou herds now migrate further west and south of the village. As a result, local residents have reported that the subsistence hunters of Anaktuvuk Pass are unable to reach the caribou needed to feed their community because they are prohibited from using ORVs within the boundaries of Gates where the caribou now frequently congregate during hunting season.
On May 16, 2026, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum issued a Memorandum concluding that:
NPS's 1986 interpretation is inconsistent with ANILCA's broader statutory context regarding the continuance of subsistence uses. . . . The better reading of the term “traditionally employed” in Section 811(b) is one that allows for the continuation of surface transportation means that were in use for subsistence purposes at the time of Gates' creation. This interpretation is bolstered by ANILCA's legislative history as well as the agency interpretations associated with ANILCA implementing regulations enacted in 1981.
The Memorandum concludes that information contained in several studies from the mid- to late-1980s “demonstrates that ORVs were used for subsistence purposes in Gates before its establishment.” The Memorandum adopted technical corrections to the GMP that removed language that adopted the NPS's previous interpretation of “traditional” in the 1986 Memorandum. The language of the GMP was revised to state that in Gates, “the use of ORVs for subsistence is allowed because the use has been shown to be a traditional means of access.”
Proposed Rule
Purpose for the Rule
The NPS is proposing to amend the special regulations for Gates to codify in NPS regulations that, for purposes of implementing section 811(b) of ANILCA, off-road vehicles (ORV) used by local rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass constitute a means of surface transportation traditionally employed for subsistence purposes. This rule would codify technical corrections made to the 1986 GMP for Gates that reversed a previous conclusion that ORVs did not meet the dictionary definitions of “traditional” and were thus prohibited for subsistence purposes in Gates. This prohibition had confined local residents of Anaktuvuk pass to areas where subsistence uses were unreachable and only certain types of ORVs were allowed. As stated in a Memorandum issued by Secretary Burgum on May 16, 2026, that made the technical corrections to the GMP, the prohibition was based on a misreading of ANILCA, including lack of consideration of ANILCA's statutory purpose. The Memorandum directed NPS to “complete a regulatory process in consultation with key stakeholders within six months of this decision to
(
printed page 66037)
enact the minimal regulations that may be necessary to avoid adverse impacts.” This rule would implement that direction by establishing a process by which the Superintendent can establish reasonable mitigation measures on the use of ORVs for subsistence purposes by local rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass, but only when such use is causing or likely to cause an adverse impact.
The purpose of this proposed rule is to provide regulatory certainty and clarity regarding use of ORVs for subsistence purposes in Gates consistent with Federal law. This proposed rule implements ANILCA's affirmative protections for subsistence access within the specific factual circumstances present in Gates, where the residents of Anaktuvuk Pass rely extensively on subsistence resources for food security and cultural continuity. It reflects NPS's determination, based on the text of ANILCA, Congress's findings and statements of policy, the legislative history of Title VIII, and documented longstanding use of ORVs by residents of Anaktuvuk Pass, that ORVs constitute a means of surface transportation traditionally employed for subsistence purposes within the meaning of Section 811(b). This rule does not create a new subsistence access right. Rather, it provides a clear regulatory framework governing the exercise of an existing statutory right recognized and protected by ANILCA, as further explained below.
Consistency With ANILCA
The NPS's 1986 Memorandum was based on a misinterpretation of the phrase “traditionally employed” in ANILCA as explained in the Secretary's May 16, 2026, Memorandum. To reach the conclusion that ORV use was not “traditionally employed,” NPS looked to dictionary definitions of the word “traditional” rather than considering the meaning of “traditionally employed” in the context of ANILCA, the purpose behind the statute, the history of the peoples and lands, and the priority placed on subsistence uses. The dictionary definitions, generic definitions without the unique context of Alaska and ANILCA, employed concepts like “successive generations,” “[c]ultural continuity embodied in a massive complex of evolving social attitudes, beliefs,” and “[a]n inherited or established way of thinking, feeling or doing.” Based on this context-less definition, the NPS concluded in 1986 that ORV use was not “traditional” and prohibited its use, thereby cutting off the community of Anaktuvuk Pass from rights preserved by ANILCA that should have been recognized with the passage of that Act.
The NPS's 1986 interpretation was inconsistent with ANILCA's broader statutory context regarding the continuance of subsistence uses. Congress generally sought to preserve the status quo with respect to subsistence with a focus on its continuation. The better reading of the term “traditionally employed” under Section 811(b) is one that allows for the continuation of surface transportation means that were in use, for some decades, for subsistence purposes at the time of Gates' creation. This interpretation is bolstered by ANILCA's legislative history. The section-by-section analysis in the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources report for the bill that became ANILCA stated that the text of ANILCA Section 811 “recognize[d] the importance of” snowmobiles and motorboats. S. Rep. No. 96-413 at 275 (1979). Those means of access were not singled out as the exclusive means of subsistence access, but rather, as illustrative examples of “means of surface transportation traditionally employed.”
Applying the correct interpretation of ANILCA Section 811 within the greater context of ANILCA requires the conclusion that ORV use was “traditionally employed” by local rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass given the extensive factual record of that use as explained above. This proposed rule would codify the technical corrections to the GMP made by the Secretary's May 16, 2026, Memorandum in order to foster consistency and certainty for the residents of Anaktuvuk Pass who rely on subsistence uses for village life and well-being, consistent with the requirements of ANILCA.
In addition to codifying the proper interpretation of “traditionally employed” made by the Secretary's Memorandum, this rule allows the NPS to take reasonable mitigation measures consistent with ANILCA. Section 811(b) of ANILCA provides that “use for subsistence purposes of snowmobiles, motorboats, and other means of surface transportation traditionally employed for such purposes by local residents” is subject to “reasonable regulation.”
16 U.S.C. 3121(b)
. Such regulation should be narrowly tailored and minimally burdensome to accomplish ANILCA's statutory mandate, as stated in Section 811(a) of ANILCA, that the Secretary shall “ensure that rural residents engaged in subsistence uses have reasonable access to subsistence resources on the public lands.”
16 U.S.C. 3121(b)
. Specific to Gates, Section 201(4) of ANILCA expressly requires NPS to permit subsistence uses by local residents in Gates where such uses are traditional.
Regulations governing subsistence uses in National Park System units in Alaska are in
36 CFR part 13, subpart F
. These regulations authorize closure and restrictions of subsistence uses under certain conditions across all Alaska park areas, but specific System units have regulations tailored to the circumstances of subsistence use in those units. The management approach to implementing mitigation measures that is proposed in this rule is tailored to the specific statutory, factual, and geographic circumstances of Anaktuvuk Pass within Gates.
Consistent with the isolated location of Anaktuvuk Pass, the absence of road access, the community's reliance on subsistence resources, and the limited number of local residents engaged in such activities, the NPS has determined that the general regulatory framework found in
36 CFR 13.460
for prohibitions and closures on subsistence ORV use is not the management approach best suited to these circumstances. Rather, the NPS has determined that a narrowly tailored regulatory framework is appropriate here because it protects access required by ANILCA while preserving the agency's authority to address demonstrated adverse impacts when supported by specific facts and evidence.
This approach would allow the NPS and the residents of Anaktuvuk Pass to work together to manage the critical resources of Gates, combining local traditional knowledge and empirical science, for all of its purposes as directed by Congress in Section 201(4)(a) of ANILCA.
In developing this proposed rule, the NPS recognizes the importance of consultation with key stakeholders including the Nunamuit people, the community of Anaktuvuk Pass, and associated entities and has engaged with stakeholders accordingly. The current regulatory process reflects continued consultation, coordination, and cooperation with the local community and stakeholders that will persist through this regulator process and beyond. DOI is seeking comment on the proposed rule. In particular, DOI is interested in information about the number of ORVs in use annually in Gates for subsistence purposes and information about the expected change as a result of this proposed regulation. DOI also requests comments on the costs and benefits of the proposed rule.
Elements of the Rule
The rule adds a new section 13.1005 to
36 CFR part 13, subpart M
, Special
(
printed page 66038)
Regulations—Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve. The title of this section is “Off-road vehicle use for subsistence purposes in Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve.”
Paragraphs (a), (b), and (c) of § 13.1005 would codify the technical change made by the Secretary's May 16, 2026, Memorandum. Paragraph (a) would establish that operating a motor vehicle off road in Gates is prohibited except by authorized residents engaged in subsistence uses as already defined in
36 CFR 13.420
. “Authorized residents” would be defined as local rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass, reflecting the unique needs of this small, land-locked, rural community. Paragraph (b) would provide that ORVs constitute a means of surface transportation traditionally employed for subsistence purposes by authorized residents of Anaktuvuk Pass and that such use is permitted pursuant to section 811(b) of ANILCA. Paragraph (c) would address the scope of that use for subsistence purposes.
Paragraphs (d), (e), and (f) of § 13.1005 would establish specific requirements that must be met before the superintendent can establish reasonable mitigation measures to avoid adverse impacts from subsistence ORV use by local rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass.
Paragraph (d) would provide an operating standard, requiring that the authorized use be conducted in a manner that prevents waste or unnecessary damage to park resources, avoids the herding, harassment, hazing or driving of wildlife, and is reasonably related to lawful subsistence uses.
Paragraph (e) would place certain limitations on ORV use. It would establish a presumption in favor of ORV uses for subsistence purposes as defined in the rule and allow the implementation of reasonable mitigation measures (including closures) to address impacts of such use as long as that mitigation does not require authorized residents to incur unreasonable costs. This paragraph also would establish procedures for the imposition of mitigation measures. Paragraph (e)(1) would provide that the need for mitigation measures must be based on clear evidence that the use is causing or likely to cause an adverse impact. The rule would require the Superintendent to develop a written determination that articulates why the impact is an adverse impact and explains why the mitigation measures are the least restrictive measures capable of mitigating the identified adverse impact. The rule would require that the written determination be supported by specific and articulable facts in the administrative record. Paragraph (e)(2) would require the Superintendent to provide authorized residents notice of proposed mitigation measures 30 days in advance. The rule would require that the notice contain the information required in (e)(1), be published in the
Federal Register
and otherwise disseminated through means of notification reasonably expected to reach authorized residents, and invite authorized residents to consult with the Superintendent. Paragraph (e)(3) would require consultation with authorized residents and hold one public hearing before implementing the mitigation measures. Paragraph (e)(4) would provide that the Superintendent may issue a final written determination following the consultation and 30-day advance notice period providing that the final determination contains the information required in (e)(1) and explains why the findings have not changed since the initial notice. The rule also would require that the final determination address input from authorized residents and allow continuing reasonable access by ORV to subsistence resources during the mitigation period. Paragraph (e)(5) would allow mitigation measures to be imposed, with the concurrence of the Regional Director, to address an emergency situation without advance notice or consultation provided that such emergency mitigation measures must expire after 45 days. The rule would require that notice of an emergency mitigation measure be provided to authorized residents as soon as practicable after implementation of the mitigation measure.
Paragraph (f) of the rule would clarify that nothing in the new § 13.1005 authorizes recreational ORV use. Paragraph (g) would explain that the regulations in the rule would govern if there is a conflict with prior agency policy or park planning documents concerning whether the ORVs are traditionally employed for subsistence use in Gates. Paragraph (h) of the rule would define “adverse impact” as a direct significant impact to public health and safety, resources, historic or scientific values, subsistence uses, or endangered or threatened species. This paragraph also would require that adverse impacts be currently occurring or reasonably foreseeable.

Add § 13.1005 to subpart M as follows:
§ 13.1005
Off-road vehicle use for subsistence purposes in Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve.
(a)
General prohibition.
Operating a motor vehicle off road in Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve is prohibited except by authorized residents as defined in this section when engaged in subsistence uses as defined by § 13.420 of this part. For purposes of this subpart, “authorized residents” means local rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass.
(b)
Permitted use.
For purposes of implementing section 811(b) of ANILCA, off-road vehicles constitute a means of surface transportation traditionally employed for subsistence purposes by authorized residents. As a result, off-road vehicles are permitted to be used by authorized residents for subsistence purposes in Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve.
(c)
Scope of use.
Vehicles authorized under paragraph (b) of this section may be used for subsistence uses defined by § 13.420 of this part.
(d)
Operating standard.
Use authorized by this section must be conducted in a manner that:
(1) Prevents waste or unnecessary damage to park resources;
(2) Avoids the herding, harassment, hazing, or driving of wildlife; and
(3) Is reasonably related to lawful subsistence uses.
(e)
Limitations on off-road vehicle use.
The regulations contained in this section establish a presumption in favor of the subsistence uses described in this section. The Superintendent may require the implementation of reasonable mitigation measures (including closures) to address impacts of off-road vehicle use authorized by this section, which do not cause local authorized residents to incur unreasonable costs. Mitigation measures may only be required in compliance with the following procedures:
(1) The need for mitigation measures must be based upon clear evidence that such use is causing or is likely to cause an adverse impact as defined in paragraph (h) of this section. In support of any such measures, the Superintendent must develop a written determination that:
(i) Articulates why the impact supporting the need for mitigation measures constitutes an adverse impact as defined in paragraph (h) of this section;
(
printed page 66040)
(ii) Articulates why the mitigation measures are the least restrictive measures capable of mitigating the identified adverse impact; and
(iii) Is supported by specific, articulable facts in the administrative record.
(2) The Superintendent must provide authorized residents with notice of proposed mitigation measures at least 30 days prior to requiring such measures. The notice must:
(i) Contain the information required in paragraph (e)(1);
(ii) Be published in the
Federal Register
and disseminated through means of notification reasonably expected to reach authorized residents; and
(iii) Invite authorized residents to consult with the Superintendent consistent with paragraph (e)(3).
(3) Prior to implementing mitigation measures to address adverse impacts defined in paragraph (h), the Superintendent must participate in meaningful consultation with authorized residents, to include at least one public hearing.
(4) Following consultation and the 30-day notice period, the Superintendent may issue a final written determination requiring compliance with the proposed mitigation measures, provided that the final determination must:
(i) Contain the information required in paragraph (e)(1) and explain why the Superintendent's findings have not changed since issuance of the notice required by paragraph (e)(2);
(ii) Address input from authorized residents provided during the consultation process; and
(iii) Allow continuing reasonable use of off-road vehicles for subsistence purposes during the mitigation period.
(5) Mitigation measures may be imposed, with the concurrence of the Regional Director, to address an emergency situation without advance notice or consultation and shall expire after 45 days. Notice of a mitigation measure to address an emergency situation must be provided to authorized residents as soon as practicable after implementation of the mitigation measure.
(f)
No recreational authorization.
Nothing in this section authorizes recreational off-road vehicle use.
(g)
Relationship to other authorities.
This section implements sections 201(4)(a) and 811 of ANILCA for Gates of the Arctic National Park. In the event of a conflict between this section and prior agency policy or park planning documents concerning whether the vehicles described in paragraph (b) are traditionally employed for subsistence use in Gates, this section governs.
(h)
Definition of adverse impact.
For purposes of this section, “adverse impact” means a direct significant impact to public health and safety, resources, historic or scientific values, subsistence uses, or endangered or threatened species. For purposes of this section, adverse impacts to Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve must be currently occurring or reasonably foreseeable and cannot be based on impacts that are remote, speculative, dependent on uncertain future events, based on generalized climatic patterns, or derived from any type of modeling.
(i)
Applicability.
The regulations in this section apply notwithstanding any other provision contained in this chapter.

Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The National Park Service (NPS) amends its regulations for hunting, fishing, trapping, and other harvest-related activities in Alaska and the procedures used to restrict public use and access in Alaska park areas, including for subsistence. This rule restores the regulatory framework adopted to implement the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980 (ANILCA) in 1981 that guided management for more than three decades, with targeted updates to that framework in response to public comments and further agency review. The restored framework recognizes the complementary and distinct roles of the State of Alaska, the Federal Subsistence Management Program, and the NPS in managing public uses and resources in Alaska park areas. The rule removes regulatory changes made in 2015, 2017, and 2024 that departed from that framework. These amendments are consistent with Executive Orders 14153 and 14192 and Secretary of the Interior's Orders 3422 and 3447.
DATES:
This rule is effective November 18, 2026.

https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. NPS-2026-0034.

AKR_Regulations@nps.gov
.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This final rule updates and restores regulations for Alaska park areas to the framework in place from 1981 through amendments beginning in 2015. A table summarizing this restoration is included in the “Final Rule” section below. Detailed explanations are included in that section and in the “Background” and “Summary and Responses to Public Comments” sections below.
This rule does not alter the federal subsistence priority established in ANILCA. Federal Subsistence Management Program regulations and the rural preference for qualified users on federal public lands in ANILCA Title VIII are unchanged. What this rule means for subsistence users:
Permit requirements for collecting animal parts for handicrafts—removed. The 2017 changes added a mandatory permit for collecting antlers, bones, and similar materials to create handicrafts for barter and customary trade. This rule removes the permit requirement; collection for these purposes remains allowed.
Restrictions for harvesting bears over bait for subsistence uses—removed. Bait and other restrictions added in 2017, which limited subsistence users to using natural or legally harvested remains, are removed; regulations issued by state and federal boards govern these uses unless the statutory
(
printed page 65986)
criteria and procedures in ANILCA are met for a closure.
Public hearings before closures affecting fish and wildlife harvest—restored. The requirement to hold a hearing in the affected vicinity before closures affecting the harvest of fish and wildlife was removed in 2015. This rule restores that local hearing requirement.
Notice requirements for local rural residents—restored and updated. The requirement to post signs and/or provide notice in local newspapers, radio broadcasts, posted maps, and post office notifications was eliminated in 2015. The final rule restores these locally focused notice requirements, which remain essential tools for reaching remote communities with limited connectivity, and updates the regulatory text to ensure posted signs are required in addition to (not in the place of) published notice.
This rule does not expand or restrict NPS closure authorities beyond what Congress has provided for Alaska. It does not affect state management authority over Alaska's fish and wildlife resources or affect the authority of the Secretaries of the Interior and Agriculture under Title VIII of ANILCA, including the authority that the Secretaries delegated to the Federal Subsistence Board. The rule does not reopen areas closed to harvest by statute.
Background
In 1980, ANILCA established 10 national preserves, two national monuments, and eight new or expanded national parks across Alaska. Since enactment, the NPS has managed these units of the National Park System (System) under a regulatory framework that recognizes multiple, complementary state and federal authorities. The State of Alaska manages fish and wildlife populations on all lands under state regulations and requirements in the Alaska Constitution; the Secretaries of the Interior and Agriculture (through the Federal Subsistence Management Program) currently administer the subsistence taking and uses of fish and wildlife on federal public lands, as set forth in ANILCA Title VIII; and the NPS manages park areas in Alaska according to ANILCA provisions that expressly allow subsistence and sport hunting, fishing, and trapping in national preserves and subsistence harvest in certain specified parks and monuments according to applicable state and federal law. As part of its management of these areas, the NPS may close areas or restrict activities according to Alaska-specific criteria and procedures, including consultation and public participation requirements. See ANILCA Titles II, VIII, and XIII; see also
Alaska Dep't of Fish & Game
v.
Fed. Subsistence Bd.,
139 F.4th 773, 779, 783-84 (9th Cir. 2025).
These provisions reflect Congress's comprehensive and intentionally negotiated balance among competing uses, authorities, interests, and values. In enacting ANILCA, Congress affirmed the State of Alaska's existing authorities to manage Alaska's fish and wildlife resources and the NPS's authority to manage for specific unit purposes, with constraints on the discretion each manager has to close or restrict uses authorized in ANILCA.
Implementing regulations adopted in 1981 (
46 FR 31836
), 1983 (
48 FR 30252
), and 1986 (
51 FR 31619
) reflected this structure and governed Alaska park areas for more than three decades, recognizing state management authorities, the Secretary of the Interior's (Secretary) responsibilities in ANILCA Title VIII, including in parks and monuments that are closed to hunting except for subsistence, and NPS's authority to close areas and restrict activities in accordance with Alaska-specific criteria and procedures, one of numerous unique management directives for NPS in ANILCA. This final rule restores the regulatory framework that governed Alaska park areas from ANILCA's passage until the discretionary shift in 2015 to advance administration policy goals. The rule reinstates regulations that reflect ANILCA's balanced compromise and were designed to implement this unique, Alaska-specific approach.
Legal Authority
The proposed rule outlined the legal authorities supporting this action. See,
e.g.,
91 FR 11483
,
11484
(Mar. 10, 2026). In short, ANILCA established a clear, Alaska-specific framework in which national preserves are managed as units of the System while expressly allowing the harvest of fish and wildlife resources under applicable state and federal law. Congress affirmed the State of Alaska's responsibility for managing fish and wildlife resources except as provided in Title VIII, limited the NPS's involvement in regulations implementing Title VIII, and set out the statutory criteria and procedures for closures and restrictions in Alaska park areas, particularly for subsistence uses and other authorized harvest activities.
This framework guided the regulations adopted in the 1980s that successfully carried out ANILCA's unique requirements for more than three decades, until policy-driven interpretations in 2015 and 2017 departed from its balanced mandates for Alaska. This framework continues to guide NPS in restoring that proven regulatory approach and is the baseline for evaluating each of the amendments.
Regulatory Development
The proposed rule explores the history that led to this rule in significant detail. See,
e.g.,
91 FR 11484-87
. In short, ANILCA expanded or established park areas in Alaska within an overarching framework for managing federal lands and interests that differs from more general and nationwide frameworks in important respects. This means System units in Alaska have a unique management structure for preserving nationally significant natural, cultural, scenic, and wildlife resources as well as continuation of the Alaska way of life, including harvesting renewable natural resources for food, clothing, shelter, familial and cultural ties; access and transportation for traditional activities and connecting communities; long-term use, occupancy, and storage; and other uses Congress determined should continue in Alaska subject to the provisions in ANILCA.
Since ANILCA, the Department of the Interior (DOI) and NPS have implemented these provisions in regulations at
36 CFR part 13
,
43 CFR part 36
, and
43 CFR part 51
(formerly at
50 CFR part 100
) as follows.
1981-2014 (the established framework):
NPS regulations adopted shortly after ANILCA's passage included Alaska-specific provisions for hunting, fishing, trapping, subsistence, access, and public participation. Regulations recognized complementary state and federal authorities and provided transparent criteria and procedures for closures affecting authorized uses.
2015:
Starting with a proposed rule in 2014, NPS regulations for Alaska were amended to depart from the established framework. The 2015 amendments introduced narrower interpretations of ANILCA's provisions to support broader application of System-wide prohibitions; recharacterized statutory closure criteria as broader “factors”; reduced public engagement requirements; altered notice and consultation procedures; and removed cross-references to applicable state and DOI authorities. These changes marked a shift toward greater consistency with management practices outside Alaska and broader discretion for unit managers, rather than the Alaska-specific approach required by ANILCA.
Public comments on the 2015 changes included significant opposition from Alaska Native Tribes, villages,
(
printed page 65987)
corporations, and organizations. The Alaska Federation of Natives adopted Resolution 14-42 finding the rulemaking “overreaching, vague, and indiscrimina[te]” noting it “would further criminalize Alaska Native traditional resource management practices.” Tanana Chiefs Conference also opposed the rule for its potential impacts on subsistence, member Tribes, and traditional homelands. Many commenters observed there was no consultation or notice before publication and procedural amendments received sparse attention.
2017:
The NPS made additional revisions to its Alaska-specific regulations to address subsistence uses of renewable natural resources. Among other things, these changes added a permit requirement for collecting nonedible animal parts for handicrafts; restricted methods and types of bait used in harvesting bears for subsistence; and prohibited collection of live raptor chicks under a falconry permit (preempting state regulation at 5 AAC 92.037).
2020:
In a 2020 rulemaking, NPS removed most of the 2015 prohibitions on state-authorized activities including harvesting bears over bait, which was allowed from 2020 through 2024 after being prohibited in 2015; it has been limited for federally qualified subsistence users since 2017. In a lawsuit challenging the 2020 rulemaking, the U.S. District Court noted the 2020 rulemaking principally concerned the relationship between the federal and state management systems and the scope of NPS's regulatory authority, while the administrative record reflected limited evidence of population-level impacts under state management and the specific harvest practices at issue.
Alaska Wildlife Alliance
v.
Haaland,
632 F. Supp. 3d 974, 996-1002 (D. Alaska 2022). The court affirmed the NPS's conclusion that the practices reauthorized in 2020, including bear baiting, would not adversely impact populations or interfere with NPS's statutory obligations.
Id.
at 1002. The 2020 changes did not address the procedural, interpretive, and administrative changes made in 2015 and 2017.
2024:
NPS reinstated the prohibition on bear baiting in preserves, attempted to further define “trapping” in ways that are unnecessarily duplicative of the State's trapping regulations, and added an unnecessary severability provision.
Now:
Executive Order 14153
Sec. 3(b)(xix) directed rescission of the 2024 changes and restoration of the regulations adopted in 2020. This rule implements that direction and goes further to address the changes in 2015 and 2017 that the 2020 rulemaking did not consider.
This rule restores the established Alaska-specific framework, regulatory language, decision criteria, public procedures, and underlying interpretations that implemented Congress's direction for Alaska park areas from their establishment until the changes in 2015 and 2017. The NPS believes a return to this proven framework more closely reflects Congress's direction by preserving subsistence uses, local participation, and government coordination, and by providing greater consistency, clarity, and predictability in park administration.
Administrative Direction
As recognized in the proposed rule,
91 FR 11486
, this rule's comprehensive and updated restoration of the pre-2015 regulations is also consistent with current Executive and Departmental policy direction concerning Alaska, regulatory reform, public access, subsistence uses, hunting and fishing, and coordination with state and local partners in managing public lands.
Executive Order 14153
directs federal agencies to review and revise actions affecting Alaska and specifically directs DOI bureaus to consider the cultural significance of hunting and fishing in Alaska, the priority for subsistence in ANILCA, meaningful consultation with state resource agencies, and consistency between hunting and fishing opportunities on federal and state lands. Secretary's Order 3422 guides implementation through directed actions affecting Alaska and the administration of federal lands and resources.
Executive Order 14192
and Secretary's Order 3447 direct agencies to remove unnecessary regulatory burdens, improve regulatory clarity, and strengthen coordination with state, tribal, territorial, and local partners. The directives in Secretary's Order 3447 are specific to hunting and fishing on DOI-managed public lands. Restoring the established Alaska-specific framework directly advances all of these directives.
Requests for Action
The proposed rule details the history of requests for action related to the changes in the final rule. See
91 FR 11487
. In short, since the 2015 and 2017 changes, stakeholders have consistently raised concerns about those amendments affecting the closure process, public participation, consultation requirements, subsistence uses, permitting requirements, and the relationship between Alaska-specific regulations and System-wide regulations under ANILCA. Questions regarding the consistency of these amendments with ANILCA and its unique roles for federal and state managers have remained at the forefront of public comments, letters, petitions, and litigation since 2015.
The final rule responds to these concerns through a comprehensive review of the procedural, interpretive, and administrative amendments adopted in 2015 and 2017 that were not reconsidered in the 2020 or 2024 rulemakings. In addition to implementing the direction in
Executive Order 14153
to rescind the 2024 rule and restore the 2020 rule, NPS considered, among other things, the May 19, 2025, letter from Safari Club International and the October 10, 2025, Petition for Rulemaking submitted by the Alaska Outdoor Council, which both requested a broader review of the changes that began in 2015 and restoration of the established Alaska-specific provisions that endured for decades before those changes.
Consistent with NPS's review of ANILCA's requirements for Alaska, regulatory implementation from 1981 to 2015, the operation of NPS regulations under subsequent amendments, public comments on the proposed rule, and the potential environmental impacts from adopting it, the final rule restores the established regulatory provisions that implemented Congress's unique direction for Alaska park areas for more than three decades, addressing issues previous rulemakings left unresolved, with updates and clarifications in response to public comments and NPS's further review.

in effect before the changes made in 2015, which further restores alignments with the Alaska-specific procedures for access in
43 CFR part 36
. This rule removes the changes made through the 2015, 2017, and 2024 rulemakings that ultimately reduced public engagement, omitted required consultation with the State, and allowed for discretionary closures without the unique criteria and procedures previously established in the DOI and NPS regulations for Alaska park areas to comply with ANILCA. This rule maintains the NPS's authority to limit use, entry, and access through those criteria and procedures.

For the reasons stated above and in the proposed rule,
91 FR 11483
, the NPS rescinds the regulatory changes made in 2015 that were not rescinded in 2020; changes made in 2017, with the exception of the definitions for “customary trade” and “handicraft”, which are retained; and the changes made in 2024. to
