I. Hunting and Trapping—§ 13.40 (Restored) and § 13.42 (Removed)
The rule restores pre-2015 language governing the harvest of fish and wildlife in national preserves, including the requirement that non-emergency closures to non-subsistence uses become effective only after the superintendent consults with the appropriate state agency and representatives of affected users. Section 13.42, added in 2015 and amended in 2017 and 2024, is deleted in its entirety.
II. Harvesting Bears Over Bait—Restrictions Removed for All Users
NPS acknowledges this aspect of the rule represents a change in position from the 2015, 2017, and 2024 rules, which prohibited or limited using bait to harvest bears. Consistent with
FCC
v.
Fox Television Stations, Inc.,
556 at 515-16, NPS provides the following analysis.
(a)
Authority.
Allowing the harvest of bears over bait under state regulations in effect since 1982 is permissible under ANILCA and the NPS Organic Act. ANILCA expressly allows hunting in national preserves under applicable state and federal law. The district court confirmed NPS's conclusion that the 2020 allowance would not adversely impact wildlife populations or contravene NPS's statutory duties.
Alaska Wildlife Alliance,
632 F. Supp. 3d at 993. No new data has emerged since that decision indicating this regulated harvest activity will have population-level effects. The NPS maintains management authority, including closure authority under the Alaska-specific criteria and procedures restored in this rule, consistent with ANILCA to address any issues that might arise.
(b)
Improvements.
The 2015 and 2024 prohibitions were based primarily on public safety concerns and NPS policy favoring natural wildlife behaviors and ecosystem dynamics. On review, neither basis supports categorical prohibition. Regarding public safety, NPS estimates no more than 10 bears per year (2 black bears, up to 8 brown bears) will be harvested over bait across all national preserves, consistent with historical levels from 1982 through 2015 and from 2020 through 2024. State regulations require permits; minimum setbacks from roads, trails, dwellings, and public facilities; registration of bait stations with the State; and completion of a bear baiting clinic. 5 AAC 92.044. The Alaska Board of Game has stated it has no information on bear baiting causing public safety concerns and found no fact-based support for that concern in any state that allows the practice. The one study cited in the 2024 rule (Herrero 2018) is, on further review, relevant only to human-bear conflicts at campgrounds and other congregation points, not remote bait stations. NPS is not aware of safety incidents from bait stations established in unauthorized locations within Wrangell-St. Elias National Preserve. NPS Management Policies § 8.2.5 recognizes that not all hazards in areas managed as natural environments can be eliminated; a categorical prohibition is not required to manage residual risk. Regarding natural conditions, the district court's 2022 decision confirmed that bear baiting does not contravene NPS's statutory duties. The Alaska Board of Game has stated that bear baiting tends to focus harvest on mature bears while avoiding female and immature bears, making it compatible with sustainable population management.
(c)
Reliance interests.
The 2015 prohibition was in effect from 2015 to 2020, lifted from 2020 to 2024, and reimposed from 2024 to the present. This demonstrates that reliance on any particular rule was limited after 2015. Conservation interests supporting the 2015 and 2024 prohibitions do not have a sufficient reliance interest to override the analysis above. The NPS will continue to monitor harvest and visitor safety and retains full authority to, among other things, close specific areas if a documented concern arises meeting the criteria in § 13.50 and § 13.490.
(d)
Factual findings.
To the extent the 2015 amendments expressed concern that state regulations do not adequately
(
printed page 65989)
address public safety risks from bear baiting, state requirements for permits, setbacks, and educational clinics partially mitigate those risks. To the extent the 2024 rule relied on the Herrero study and an informal survey of bear biologists, the NPS does not rely on those findings because: (1) the study is inapplicable to remote bait stations; (2) the biologist survey addressed theoretical risks without reference to actual documented incidents in Alaska; and (3) the State of Alaska's decades of operational experience without documented public safety incidents are more probative than speculation without context or data.
III. Definition of Trapping—§ 13.1 (Restored)
The definition of “trapping” in § 13.1 was amended in 2024 to define the circumstances where individuals may use firearms to take similarly redefined “furbearers” under a state trapping license. State regulations at 5 AAC 92.075(d) and 92.095(a)(8) already address these circumstances and no basis exists for NPS to impose a duplicative and unnecessary regulation. The rule restores the former definition for “trapping” and removes the definition of “furbearer” as unnecessary under the restoration. This change eliminates a regulatory burden that lacks a corresponding management benefit, and is consistent with direction in
Executive Order 14192
to remove unnecessary regulations and in
Executive Order 14153
to maximize consistency in harvest opportunities across public lands.
IV. Live Wildlife Collection/Falconry—§ 13.42(j) (Removed)
The 2017 rule added § 13.42(j) which prohibited the regulated collection of live raptor chicks in national preserves on the basis that such activities are not “hunting or trapping” and are therefore subject to System-wide prohibition at
36 CFR 2.2(a)(2)
. This conclusion is not consistent with Congress's direction for national preserves in Alaska. The State of Alaska manages falconry under 5 AAC 92.037, which requires permits and applies on all public lands in Alaska. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service manages migratory raptors under
50 CFR 21.82
and
21.85
, which authorize chick collection under state permits. Removing § 13.42(j) restores the pre-2017 framework and recognizes the adequate management of falconry activities by the State and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The NPS requested input on any documented management need for this prohibition, and public comments did not identify impacts or concerns to justify retaining it.
V. Subsistence Collection—§ 13.482 (Removed) and § 13.485 (Revised)
As noted before and elsewhere, this rule does not alter the federal subsistence priority established in ANILCA, Federal Subsistence Management Program regulations, or ANILCA's rural preference for qualified users on federal public lands. The 2017 rule added § 13.482, which created a mandatory permit system for collecting nonedible animal parts for use in handicrafts for barter and customary trade. This permit requirement was opposed by nearly every commenter representing subsistence users and Alaska Native organizations in the 2017 rulemaking, who noted the activity was already authorized under ANILCA, the permit added burdens for subsistence users who already must hold federally qualified status, the most common collection method is opportunistic gathering and is incompatible with a permit system requiring advance authorization, and subsistence users had been engaged for nearly a decade in good faith in the regulatory process only to receive additional restrictions rather than the clarification they sought.
Removing § 13.482 does not prohibit the uses it addressed; collection of animal parts for handicrafts remains authorized under ANILCA Title VIII and applicable federal regulations. The permit requirement and any conditions attached to it are removed. The removal of this permit requirement is a deregulatory action that will benefit subsistence users by removing unnecessary administrative burdens. The definition of “animal parts” in § 13.420 is likewise removed as unnecessary, while the definitions of “customary trade” and “handicraft” are retained with minor technical edits to align with federal regulations at
43 CFR part 51
, with NPS-specific modifications including products made from plant materials and excluding trophies or European mounts of horns or antlers. Section 13.485(b) is revised to restore pre-2017 language authorizing noncommercial gathering of plant materials and dead or downed timber for firewood without a permit.
VI. Closure and Restriction Procedures—§ 13.50 (Restored)
The 2015 rule significantly revised closure procedures in ways that reduced public engagement, eliminated durational requirements, removed specific notice methods essential to local rural residents, and recharacterized statutory “criteria” as discretionary “factors.” This rule restores the pre-2015 procedures, as follows.
(a)
Emergency closures:
30-day maximum; may not be extended. Emergency closures affecting harvest of fish and wildlife resources require notice and hearing before taking effect. Other emergency closures take effect on notice.
(b)
Temporary closures:
affecting fish or wildlife harvest requires notice and hearing in the affected vicinity and other appropriate locations before taking effect. Other temporary closures take effect on notice. Maximum duration of 12 months may not be extended.
(c)
Permanent closures:
published as rulemaking in the
Federal Register
with a minimum 60-day public comment period and public hearings in the affected area and other appropriate locations.
(d)
Notice requirements:
all closures and restrictions shall be published in at least one newspaper of general circulation in the state and at least one local newspaper where available; posted at community post offices in the affected vicinity; made available for broadcast on local radio stations in a manner reasonably calculated to inform residents in the affected vicinity; and designated on a map available for public inspection at the superintendent's office and other convenient locations. The proposed rule language has been revised slightly (replacing an “or” with “and') to confirm that all of these notice methods must be utilized in addition to the posting of appropriate signs.
(e)
Openings:
Federal Register
notice required with hearings on request in the affected vicinity and other appropriate locations before a final determination.
(f)
Facility closures and restrictions:
restored as a distinct category with defined criteria (public health, safety, and protection of public property), duration (limited to the circumstance requiring closure), and notice requirements.
These restorations directly respond to concerns from rural Alaska residents and communities that the changes in 2015 to rely on website postings and discretionary notice were inadequate to inform residents of changes affecting subsistence and harvest activities in remote areas. Fixed durations and defined criteria provide predictability, consultation requirements restore meaningful government engagement, and hearing requirements restore opportunities to engage decision-makers before closures take effect.

On March 10, 2026, the NPS published the proposed rule in the

91 FR 18340

The NPS received 5,172 comments on the proposed rule, including submissions from organizations representing more than 48,000 collective signatories. A summary of the pertinent issues raised in the comments received and NPS responses are provided below.
Statutory Consistency and Priorities
1. Comment:
Several commenters stated the proposed rule and its approach to management are inconsistent with NPS's obligations under the law, including the NPS Organic Act, Wilderness Act, and ANILCA, arguing that National Park System units must be managed to prioritize conservation and natural processes over consumptive uses.
NPS Response:
Through ANILCA, Congress mandated that consumptive uses such as subsistence and sport hunting, fishing, and trapping be allowed in Alaska's national preserves under applicable state and federal law and that certain parks and monuments be available for subsistence uses. ANILCA §§ 203, 1313, and 1314. The continuation of these activities is one of the intrinsic values Congress saw in establishing preserves in Alaska as distinct from parks and monuments, where hunting would only continue for federally qualified users in specified areas. In its report on the language that became ANILCA through a negotiated compromise with the U.S. House of Representatives, the U.S. Senate Committee for Energy and Natural Resources explained this intentional approach:
Like the House-passed bill, the Committee amendment directs that a preserve be managed as a national park except that all forms of hunting be permitted to continue. This includes sport, subsistence, and guided hunting . . . . The Committee also adopted an amendment clarifying that trapping shall be allowed in national preserves and that the statutory requirement that the taking of fish and wildlife be allowed does not deprive the Secretary of his traditional authority to close public lands located within conservation system units to the taking of fish and wildlife under statutory criteria. In allowing trapping to continue within preserves, it was not the intent of the Committee to allow exploitative forms of commercial trapping to occur. The intent of the committee is to allow individual Alaskans to continue to operate their own trap lines within the preserves, even though those individuals might not qualify as subsistence users . . . . The Secretary, through the National Park Service, is expected to monitor trapping operations within the preserves and the associated wildlife populations and issue appropriate regulations to insure that exploitative forms of trapping do not take place and that there is no substantial or permanent harm to the wildlife populations. S. Rep. 96-413, 96th Cong. 1st Sess. 1979, at 307-308.
Some concerns with accommodating these and other consumptive use mandates rest on the premise that managing for natural processes under the NPS Organic Act and Wilderness Act is an exclusive, independent standard from other applicable laws. That premise does not hold for the areas established and expanded under ANILCA, which referenced both laws in specifying which uses are allowed, grounds for restricting them, and procedures to enact those restrictions. Regulatory expectations discussed by the committee, such as allowing activities necessary to conduct consumptive uses and limits only where monitoring shows exploitation or substantial harm, are the ways Congress defined resource protection for these areas given the unique Alaska context. In implementing those expectations, the final rule is not deprioritizing a natural processes standard in favor of consumptive uses, it is applying the standards Congress wrote for Alaska park areas.
2. Comment:
In Title VIII of ANILCA, Congress established a federal priority for customary and traditional uses of fish and wildlife resources by rural residents on federal public lands and
(
printed page 65992)
certain waters in Alaska. Commenters raised concerns that proposed changes would diminish the federal subsistence priority by allowing state-regulated harvest activities in national preserves, potentially increasing competition for subsistence resources with insufficient attention to subsistence users and their expertise, perspective, and needs.
NPS Response:
The federal subsistence priority for rural Alaska residents cannot be diminished or overridden by state law or NPS regulation. ANILCA Title VIII and Federal Subsistence Board regulations are unchanged and addressed in this rulemaking through the restored and updated language. The final rule acknowledges subsistence opportunities and preferences are available in certain Alaska park areas under both federal and state regulations, and that NPS's authority is contingent on the Alaska-specific criteria and procedures in ANILCA.
While the State cannot implement ANILCA's rural preference under the state constitution, it remains an important manager of Alaska's fish and wildlife resources on federal lands, including harvest seasons, methods, means, limits, and other regulations. This authority was affirmed in the Alaska Statehood Act, again in section 1314 of ANILCA, and is recognized in implementing regulations for wildlife refuges at
50 CFR 36.11
. On all lands, Alaska law requires that, if a portion of a stock or population can be harvested consistent with sustained yield principles, a reasonable opportunity will be provided with a preference for subsistence uses that applies to all Alaska residents.
The Federal Subsistence Board, in cooperation with Subsistence Regional Advisory Councils, Subsistence Resource Commissions, the NPS, the public, local experts, Tribes, other federal land managers, and the State of Alaska carries out the Secretary's responsibilities under Title VIII of ANILCA, which include ensuring: the continuation of subsistence uses by rural residents on federal public lands; rural residents with personal knowledge of local conditions and requirements have a meaningful role in the management of fish and wildlife and of subsistence uses on the public lands in Alaska; and rural residents engaged in subsistence uses have reasonable access to subsistence resources on the public lands. The NPS has the authority to preempt state law where necessary to implement the NPS Organic Act, Wilderness Act, ANILCA, and other statutory direction. The NPS has not found it necessary to exercise that authority in issuing this rule.
The Secretary's delegation of authority to the Federal Subsistence Board is to administer the subsistence taking and uses of fish and wildlife on public lands and the related promulgation and signature authority for regulations in subparts C and D of
43 CFR part 51
and
36 CFR part 242
. The Board is empowered, to the extent necessary, to implement Title VIII of ANILCA, to undertake various actions as set forth in
43 CFR 51.10(d)(4)
and
36 CFR 242.10(d)(4)
, including the following:
issue regulations for the management of subsistence taking and uses of fish and wildlife on public lands;
allocate subsistence uses of fish and wildlife populations on public lands;
ensure that the taking on public lands of fish and wildlife for nonwasteful subsistence uses shall be accorded priority over the taking on such lands of fish and wildlife for other purposes;
restrict the taking of fish and wildlife on public lands for nonsubsistence uses or closing public lands to the take of fish and wildlife for nonsubsistence uses when necessary for the conservation of healthy populations of fish or wildlife, to continue subsistence uses of fish or wildlife, or for reasons of public safety or administration;
restrict the taking of a particular fish or wildlife population on public lands for subsistence uses, closing public lands to the take of fish and wildlife for subsistence uses, or otherwise modifying the requirements for take from a particular fish or wildlife population on public lands for subsistence uses when necessary to ensure the continued viability of a fish or wildlife population, or for reasons of public safety or administration;
establish priorities for the subsistence taking of fish and wildlife on public lands among rural Alaska residents;
restrict or eliminate taking of fish and wildlife on public lands; and
determine what types and forms of trade of fish and wildlife taken for subsistence uses constitute allowable customary trade.
Of note, however, the Federal Subsistence Board's regulations do not authorize subsistence uses in Glacier Bay National Park, Kenai Fjords National Park, Katmai National Park, and that portion of Denali National Park established as Mt. McKinley National Park prior to passage of ANILCA, where subsistence taking and uses are prohibited.
43 CFR 51.3(a)
;
36 CFR 242.3(a)
. Also, the subsistence regulations in
43 CFR part 51
do not supersede agency-specific regulations.
Id.
State and federal regulations can be in effect in the same area unless the Federal Subsistence Board or the NPS have closed or restricted use of the area by non-federally qualified users or to all harvest or entry.
Changes made to NPS regulations in 2015 to support the preemption of state law in national preserves removed language recognizing this unique partnership of authorities and procedures. The restored and updated language in the final rule clarifies that federally qualified users can continue subsistence uses of fish and wildlife regulated by state and federal boards consistent with NPS regulations, including Alaska-specific procedures for area closures and user restrictions. Under the final rule, Alaskans and others can continue making board proposals and guide the management of customary and traditional uses without encountering the discretionary permissions and automatic preemptions added for certain park areas in 2015 and 2017. Public use will continue to be managed in Alaska park areas in accordance with federal law and, under the final rule, more specifically in accordance with the criteria and procedures in ANILCA.
To ensure federally qualified subsistence users are unaffected or benefited by these changes, the final rule adds clarifying revisions to
36 CFR 13.35
and
13.400
. These revisions confirm general limitations for park visitors do not apply to federally qualified users engaged in subsistence, including those defined as “local rural residents” in § 13.420 and other authorized users (
e.g.,
those with a federal harvest permit from another bureau or agency). The rule restores the regulatory framework adopted immediately after ANILCA's passage, when, as now, the State did not have a program to implement the mandates in Title VIII, see
46 FR 31836
,
31839
,
31860-62
(June 17, 1981). The text is updated as needed to reflect the development of a federal program to carry out those mandates.
3. Comment:
A number of commenters opposed deferring to the State of Alaska in managing fish and wildlife resources, noting authorized practices may conflict with federal mandates for the NPS. Conversely, comments were received asserting the State is the appropriate and legal administrator of fish and wildlife resources on all lands in Alaska, with exceptions that do not apply in this
(
printed page 65993)
rulemaking, and that direction to align federal and state regulations will have positive effects.
NPS Response:
The NPS does not “defer” to the State of Alaska in implementing federal mandates. As explained above, the State manages fish and wildlife on all lands in Alaska except as specifically modified by Congress, and the NPS manages System units consistent with the Alaska-specific criteria, procedures, and priorities outlined in ANILCA. In adopting the clarifying amendment that became ANILCA § 1314, the Senate Committee stated:
This Section, adopted as a Committee Amendment, preserves the status quo with regard to the responsibility and authority of the State to manage fish and wildlife, and reconciles this authority with the Act, including the subsistence title. At the same time, the Section confirms the status quo with regard to the authority of the Secretary to manage the wildlife habitat on federal lands. The Section also clarifies that fishing shall be permitted in national parks and monuments and that subsistence uses shall be permitted where specifically provided by the Act. S. Rep. 96-413, at 308.
The “status quo” division of state-federal authorities in § 1314 is primarily about resource management and not about implementing Title VIII. It was in effect when the final rule language was initially adopted in 1981, a few months after ANILCA's passage; in 1982, when the Secretary approved the State's program to administer the federal subsistence priority; in 1985, when the Secretary intervened during the program's compliance issues (outside of parks and monuments); in 1989, when a state court found the State's program violated the Alaska Constitution; and in 1990, when the Federal Subsistence Management Program was established to administer the priority. Despite these shifts, the state-federal authorities Congress established for Alaska did not change, including NPS's limited role and responsibilities under ANILCA. The final rule acknowledges establishment of the federal program, updates references to its newly relocated regulations in
43 CFR part 51
, and restores the “status quo” language that provided decades of stability for all park users.
The final rule also improves consistency for hunting and fishing across DOI-administered lands in Alaska, as directed in Secretary's Order 3447 § 4(b)(3), while preserving the distinctions for National Park System units outlined in ANILCA and other laws. In enacting a single, comprehensive law governing all the federal lands in one state, Congress was able to build consistencies into jurisdictional landscapes in Alaska, and, shortly after ANILCA's passage, similar regulatory language was adopted for managing public uses in Alaska's national preserves and wildlife refuges based on similar or the same provisions. See
46 FR 31818
,
31819
(June 17, 1981);
46 FR 31836
. With the Congressionally directed restoration of regulations for wildlife refuges in 2017, this final rule solidifies the long-standing alignments in Congress' design. Revisions in the final rule will simplify compliance and enforcement by making it easier for eligible users to cross jurisdictional boundaries while harvesting under state or federal regulations in Alaska's wildlife refuges and preserves and under federal regulations in other park areas (as noted above, Klondike Gold Rush and Sitka national historical parks, Katmai and Kenai Fjords national parks, and parts of Denali National Park are closed to harvest by law).
Conservation and Public Use
4. Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern the proposed rule would harm tourism, asserting that hunting and trapping can reduce opportunities for non-consumptive uses and damage Alaska's reputation as a destination for wildlife viewing and photography.
NPS Response:
Section 1313 of ANILCA recognizes that, for national preserves in Alaska, “the Secretary may designate zones where and periods when no hunting, fishing, trapping, or entry may be permitted for reasons of public safety, administration, floral and faunal protection, or public use and enjoyment.” Understanding that all of these reasons have implications for tourism, and using the best available information, including diverse and meaningful experiences shared by park users in their comments on the proposed rule, the NPS has not found evidence that regulated harvest impairs or is likely to impair opportunities for non-consumptive uses in Alaska's park areas.
Most areas where harvest occurs are highly remote, with few if any overlapping uses. A number of factors affect successful wildlife viewing for all user groups in all areas where animals largely dictate the encounter. Populations in Alaska park areas have been targeted by hunters and trappers for millennia and demonstrate significant variations in tolerance levels for humans regardless of their activity. Environmental analyses prepared for the 2015, 2020, and 2024 Alaska-specific rulemakings did not identify a correlation between harvest activities addressed in those rules and measurable impacts in wildlife viewing opportunities across Alaska park areas. To the extent harvest activities affect visitor experiences, those effects are more likely to be location-specific rather than indicative of a broader reduction in non-consumptive recreational opportunities across Alaska park areas. Limiting one user group without impacting other user experiences could contribute to the problem those limits are looking to resolve (
e.g.,
reducing user conflicts and barriers for allowed uses). The final rule maintains ANILCA's balanced mandates for federal public lands in Alaska.
5. Comment:
Commenters expressed concerns that harvest methods authorized by the State of Alaska and available under state law will impact natural ecosystem dynamics, like predator-prey relationships and pack formations. A smaller number of commenters opposed all state-regulated harvest opportunities as potentially incompatible with or a violation of conservation purposes and values.
NPS Response:
As explained in the response to Comment 3, Congress restricted the NPS's general management authority over hunting, fishing, or trapping in Alaska park areas; it affirmed the State's existing authority; and it provided that, when NPS uses its management authority to close areas to allowed uses, it must meet certain requirements, including “consultation with the appropriate State agency having responsibility over hunting, fishing, and trapping activities.” ANILCA § 1313 (cross-referencing § 816, where unit manager discretion to restrict regulated harvest by federally qualified subsistence users is further restricted).
State and federal managers have defined roles and enforcement obligations that work together for the safe, responsible management of Alaska's public lands. Under the final rule, NPS continues to steward habitats, protect resources, and implement closures when statutory criteria and procedures are met, in consultation with the State, which continues to establish harvest methods and other regulations in managing populations for sustainability under the Alaska Constitution. When the State and NPS work together to meet these interconnected obligations, the Federal Subsistence Management Program is more effective in exercising its delegated authority to regulate subsistence uses under ANILCA Title VIII, including necessary closures. Directing comments, proposals, and information on harvest activities to state
(
printed page 65994)
officials and established processes, including the Alaska Boards of Fisheries and Game, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, and the Alaska State Legislature, or to the Federal Subsistence Board, will ensure that input is considered in the venues where population management decisions and policies are made for Alaska.
Some commenters view this intersectional management collaboration using each organization's respective authorities as a prohibited form of deference, as noted in Comment 3, or as an abdication of NPS's duty to allow for natural processes and ecosystem dynamics and to protect fish and wildlife resources for future generations, as noted in Comment 1. Many argued NPS should take a stronger position in shaping harvest regulations that affect Alaska park areas, including through discretionary preemption based on administrative criteria and values, which the restored and updated language in the final rule would not support. The NPS has the authority to preempt state law where necessary to implement the NPS Organic Act, Wilderness Act, ANILCA, and other statutory direction. The NPS has not found it necessary to exercise that authority in issuing this rule.
As explained in the detailed preamble for changes to NPS regulations in 2020,
85 FR 35181
(June 9, 2020), regulated harvest in Alaska cannot legally function as a predator control program, which can only be conducted under specific requirements in federal and state law and have not been authorized in Alaska park areas. The NPS believes the final rule language is more consistent with balanced statutory mandates for Alaska, for the reasons explained in this rulemaking and based on decades of proven workability and cooperation toward science-based, user-informed conservation objectives.
6. Comment:
Regarding the NPS's closure authorities, a large number of comments specifically opposed the use of bait in harvesting bears, sharing ethical concerns and potential risks to wildlife populations and public safety.
NPS Response:
Harvest methods are established under applicable state and federal regulations that are continuously refined through regional input and monitoring. These regulations, and the publicly accountable processes that create and rigorously maintain them, define ethical practices from a management standpoint. The NPS is committed to its ongoing participation in these defined regulatory processes, as a stakeholder and a resource manager with independent authorities, and to continuing to work collaboratively with the public, subsistence users, gateway communities, Alaska Native Tribes and corporations, other federal agencies, and the State in executing distinct and shared responsibilities in a transparent and consistent manner based on our respective authorities.
Harvesting bears over bait has been regulated across Alaska since 1982 with no evidence of notable public safety incidents or population-level impacts. To the contrary, this harvest method can be effective at targeting animals with an established tolerance for human activities, which are more likely to be involved in an incident, and to close the distance and expand the time available for targeting a particular sex or age class, which is a key consideration in managing populations for sustainability. Analysis supporting the rule's determinations is set out in detail in Section II of the “Finalized Changes” section above. The NPS will continue to monitor and may close areas if a specific concern arises using the appropriate criteria and procedures in ANILCA. Comments submitted on the proposed rule and in previous rulemakings provide detailed data and analyses that support NPS's conclusion this state-authorized activity is not detrimental to wildlife conservation and public safety at current levels.
Procedural Issues
7. Comment:
Commenters questioned whether the rulemaking process meets the procedural requirements in the Administrative Procedure Act, National Environmental Policy Act, and section 810 of ANILCA, sharing concerns about sufficiency, rationale, and transparency.
NPS Response:
With this final rule and associated decision-making materials, including an environmental assessment and section 810 of ANILCA analysis, the NPS has fully complied with all applicable procedural requirements. The rule is supported by a detailed administrative record, including the above-referenced analyses, public notice and comment and consultations with state officials, tribal governments, and Alaska Native corporations. This is not to imply that input provided during the comment period and consultations is uniformly supportive of the final rule, from a substantive perspective, only that, from a procedural perspective, that input was fully considered in developing the final rule.
8. Comment:
Some commenters found the proposed rule unclear and potentially misleading without more information, with recurring concerns that certain provisions could lead to unintentional loopholes, inconsistent application in the field, and challenges in determining where rules apply. Commenters did not find the proposed rule made it clear what is changing for Alaska park areas.
NPS Response:
The NPS recognizes that confusion can occur in any rulemaking process and has endeavored in its outreach efforts to focus on providing accurate and detailed information in open dialogue, and comments expressing confusion have influenced NPS's approach to modifications and explanations in this final rule.
One area of confusion revolves around the amount of language being changed, with a rulemaking format that makes it hard to compare versions of the regulation, and which appears to be inconsistent with NPS's statement it is making minor changes. Although the proposed and final rules contain substantial text showing edits, much of this language is not new, not all of it represents a change to current language and most of it reflects long-standing regulations in place for more than 30 years. The main goal is to make a single change across multiple provisions: a return to the framework that more closely adheres to ANILCA's requirements in implementing its mandates for Alaska park areas. Changes to the restored regulations reflect changes in the governing situation, like the creation of the Federal Subsistence Board and its relocation into the Office of the Secretary, or respond to comments on the proposed rule, which made several requests for specific information and ideas for reform. See
91 FR 11483
,
11486
,
11488
,
11491
, and
11492
.
Another identified area of confusion relates to changes in definitions, specifically modifying established terms like “subsistence uses” and “customary trade” and more recent terms like “handicraft”, leading to questions about what activities are allowed, who qualifies, and how enforcement will work. Clear definitions can help public land users and enforcement officials better understand compliance with unique laws like ANILCA.
One of the requests made in the proposed rule for specific reform ideas involves NPS's definition of “customary trade”.
91 FR 11483
,
11491
. Reverting to the pre-2015 language does not seem to cover the breadth of activities implicated by this term, and if the current definition does or could do that better, retaining or reforming it would be an improvement over pre-2015 regulations. One alternative to retention would be to adopt the definition used by the Federal Subsistence Management
(
printed page 65995)
Program at
43 CFR 51.4
, which is very similar to the current NPS definition, or to include a cross-reference to that definition in
36 CFR 13.420
along with any differences, similar to the definition for “handicraft”. Without a clear expression of a need for reform in the comments, the final rule retains the current definitions of “customary trade” and “handicraft” (a term used in NPS's definition of “customary trade”) to provide consistency for subsistence users and law enforcement. This change from the proposed rule also reduces the amount of edited text in the final rule, addressing the source of confusion described earlier.
The final rule does not retain the recently added definition for “animal parts”. As noted above and in the proposed rule,
91 FR 11491
, this does not mean subsistence use and gathering of animal parts is not allowed in Alaska park areas. This definition was added when NPS began regulating these activities, primarily due to concerns that general rules and policies prohibiting visitors from removing natural objects may be interpreted to prohibit subsistence uses. See
82 FR 3626
,
3627
(January 12, 2017). Reflecting on these stated concerns, the definition's decade in use addressing them, comments encouraging removal of unnecessary barriers to subsistence, and statutory direction and guidance in ANILCA Title VIII, NPS does not see the same value in retaining the definition for “animal parts” as it does for “customary trade” and “handicraft”. A basic understanding of the term should suffice for compliance and enforcement purposes.
To make the relationship between nationwide rules, administrative policies, and ANILCA easier to understand in practice moving forward, the final rule adds minor wording changes in
36 CFR 13.35
and
13.400
. These adjustments are intended to reduce confusion about how System-wide prohibitions apply to local residents and others authorized to conduct subsistence activities. They also clarify that subsistence uses are not treated or managed the same way as general public uses, and that Alaska park areas operate under ANILCA's balanced mandates rather than System-wide direction alone, unless Congress states otherwise. These edits and the final rule's restoration of Alaska-specific closure procedures in the sections they address (
36 CFR part 13, subparts B
and
F
) also respond to comments expressing confusion about which authorities apply in a given situation and concerns about how closures are administered and communicated.
Several commenters cautioned that greater alignment between state and federal regulations in Alaska park areas could unintentionally give state managers too much authority over subsistence uses on federal public lands. Many expressed frustration about the overlapping state and federal systems in park areas and conflicting priorities, even with specific roles assigned to each manager. As in Comment 2, commenters noted state management actions do not always support customary and traditional uses by prioritizing opportunities for all Alaskans, marginalizing regional input, and increasing competition and harvest pressure on struggling stocks and populations, and that obscure phrasing in the proposed rule could expand the reach of those actions. Comments frequently referred to direction in ANILCA to ensure rural residents are advising in management decisions and prioritized among consumptive users of Alaska's fish and wildlife resources.
Alaska's system of “dual management” is a measured and complex approach to these overlapping systems to meet constitutional and statutory mandates, and commenters are correct that federal and state priorities are not always aligned, an issue of particular concern for communities that rely heavily on wild food resources. To be clear, this rule does not change ANILCA's rural subsistence priority or the intent, priorities, or structure of the Federal Subsistence Management Program. Under dual management, the State manages fish and wildlife populations according to sustained yield principles on all lands and waters unless Congress modifies that authority, like in ANILCA Title VIII, and federal agencies have their own responsibilities and authorities on federal lands to protect public safety, meet statutory purposes, and fulfill federal mandates, like the rural subsistence priority. This structure is explicitly recognized in ANILCA and the rules and land use plans that guide managers and decision-makers in Alaska. As discussed in the response to Comment 2, this rule does not change that division of authorities. State law will continue to govern harvest activities on all lands to the extent permissible under federal law. However, so long as the State cannot implement the rural subsistence priority required in ANILCA, the Secretaries of the Interior and Agriculture are responsible for administering ANILCA's framework for the subsistence taking and uses of fish and wildlife on public lands and have delegated most of their responsibilities to the Federal Subsistence Board. The NPS will carry out its respective duties to manage park areas, including consultation with the Federal Subsistence Board under the 2015 revisions to § 13.490, which is retained in the final rule. State and federal managers will carry out their respective duties, and the revisions in this rulemaking will better equip unit managers in Alaska to meet NPS's obligations within this shared system consistent with the balanced mandates in ANILCA. The NPS has the authority to preempt state law where necessary to implement the NPS Organic Act, Wilderness Act, ANILCA, and other statutory direction. The NPS has not found it necessary to exercise that authority in issuing this rule.
To help limit the potential for other misunderstandings, now or in the future, a table is included in the section entitled “Final Rule” above to show which regulations are changing in a substantive way with a short summary explaining the change.
9. Comment:
Some comments supported or opposed changes beyond those in the proposed rule. Several urged the NPS to expand the scope of the rule by reinstating restrictions removed in 2020, by adding more restrictions, or by adding more harvest opportunities and improved access. Commenters also requested more definitions (
e.g.,
“sport” hunting) and expanded policy-based explanations on the circumstances where regulated harvest might conflict with National Park System purposes and values.
NPS Response:
The NPS has decided that the final rule should closely adhere to the proposed rule and the framework that implemented ANILCA's balanced mandates for more than three decades. Many comments advocating broader changes, whether to restrict or expand harvest opportunities and access, reflect competing interests similar to those Congress weighed in enacting ANILCA's balanced compromise, where the type of protected area and scope of permitted uses were calibrated to accommodate Alaska-specific needs and interests within a single comprehensive statute. See,
e.g.,
126 Cong. Rec. S11052, S11116, (Aug. 18, 1980) (statement of Sen. Tsongas) (describing the “compromise worked out during many hours of debate and discussions on these issues” in “trying to protect in a balanced way the legitimate concerns of numerous interest groups”, including the State of Alaska, noting “91.4 percent of Alaska is open to sport hunting” under the compromise); S. Rep. 95-64, pt. 2, 95th Cong. 2d Sess. 1978, 487 (statement of Sen. Andrus) (“We have designated national park preserves
(
printed page 65996)
where hunting would still be permitted; we don't do that in the lower 48. Subsistence hunting would be permitted in areas where it would not in the lower 48.”); S. Rep. 96-413, at 145 (describing the amendment to designate Cape Krusenstern “as a national monument rather than a preserve” to reduce the potential for user conflicts, noting “there is little sport hunting in the area at this time while this is one of the most important and concentrated subsistence use areas in the State”). Given the purpose of this rulemaking, NPS has concluded that revisiting these broader policy questions would not be warranted without a substantial basis for departing from the time-honored, Alaska-specific framework the final rule restores, addressed through a separate rulemaking process with that objective.
Adhering closely to the proposed rule, and its close adherence to the regulations that guided management of Alaska park areas from ANILCA's passage until 2015, will minimize disruption for users and managers and restore the Alaska-specific procedures they long relied on for responsible and cooperative resource management. The NPS has considered the comments encouraging additional or different action and determined that changes in the final rule must meet an exacting standard with a compelling reason, like the creation of the Federal Subsistence Management Program, or make important clarifications, like the definition for “customary trade” and other reforms to facilitate allowed uses and the continuation of subsistence uses. Many comments included valuable recommendations for improvements to the framework beyond the scope of this rulemaking, which would require or benefit from consultation, notice and comment, and environmental analysis in a separate rulemaking process.
In the final rule, definitions are aligned with state and federal regulations to the greatest extent practicable to promote consistency across jurisdictional boundaries and simplify compliance in the places where people hunt, fish, and trap in Alaska. Congress intended for all forms of regulated hunting to be allowed in national preserves under applicable state and federal law, where relevant distinctions between subsistence and “sport” hunting are made and enforced in Alaska park areas. Consistent with that direction, this rule restores the roles, responsibilities, and limitations that governed wildlife management in Alaska park areas for decades following their establishment in ANILCA. While commenters expressed differing views regarding wildlife conservation and access to harvest opportunities, the restored regulations reflect the balance Congress directed for Alaska and the framework that successfully implemented that balance for decades. The NPS has concluded that departures from this long-standing framework, whether to expand or restrict authorities, should be supported by substantial justification, thoughtful analysis, meaningful public engagement, and a demonstrated basis in law for improving upon this proven management approach for Alaska park areas.
10. Comment:
Community leaders, tribal governments, Alaska-based organizations, and others shared concerns and frustration with the rulemaking process, public engagement, and government-to-government consultation, highlighting the limited amount of time for outreach and meaningful contributions.
NPS Response:
The NPS takes these concerns seriously and acknowledges that 46 days is a shorter comment period than some stakeholders requested for this rule. A 15-day extension was provided in direct response to requests for more time, recognizing that extension did not fully address the concerns from affected communities. As noted above, the NPS received 5,172 comments during the public comment period for the proposed rule, including submissions from organizations representing more than 48,000 collective signatories. The NPS carefully considered all of these comments in finalizing this rule.
The NPS undertook the following steps to engage on this rulemaking. In April and May 2025, NPS sent letters to federally recognized Tribes and Alaska Native corporations with interests in Alaska park areas inviting pre-consultation on the proposed rule, following up on each letter with direct calls and emails. The letter described the proposed action at that time as recission of the 2024 Rule and reinstatement of the 2020 Rule. The NPS met in person or virtually, as indicated in the request, with every Tribal entity that requested a meeting. Following publication of the proposed rule on March 10, 2026, with an expanded proposed action, NPS presented the rule at Alaska Board of Game meetings, Subsistence Resource Commission meetings, and Subsistence Regional Advisory Council meetings across the state. A second consultation letter sent in April 2026 included information on the expanded proposed action. Formal consultation commenced following publication of the proposed rule for public comment and continued for the life of the project. The NPS followed these letters with calls and emails, and met with every entity that requested a meeting in the venue and format of their choosing to best facilitate their meaningful engagement. DOI and NPS leadership met with the Alaska Federation of Natives on April 8, 2026. NPS leadership met with the Alaska Congressional Delegation on multiple occasions during the comment period. NPS consulted directly with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game at the staff and leadership level.
NPS acknowledges some affected communities, particularly in rural areas with limited connectivity and without a regular NPS presence, may have had less opportunity to engage than those in more accessible locations. Federal Subsistence Regional Advisory Councils formally requested an extension to the public comment period, stating the initial 30-day window was unreasonably short and insufficient to analyze the complex proposed changes encompassing four separate rulemakings over the last decade. Comments noted the timing prevented most advisory bodies from reviewing and convening to discuss the rule during their scheduled meetings and emphasized the importance of meaningful and informed participation from the communities represented on the councils. The Gates of the Arctic Subsistence Resource Commission was the only commission with a scheduled meeting during the comment period that had time to review the proposed rule and prepare recommendations and was the only commission that commented on the proposed rule.
NPS has attempted to account for this in its review of the record, giving particular weight to comments from advisory bodies and entities whose mandates are specifically designed to represent the interests of rural communities. The concerns those groups have expressed, including opposition to permits, support for the rural subsistence priority, and requests for clear and accessible procedures, are reflected in the final rule.
The NPS is committed to improving government-to-government consultation processes for Alaska-specific rulemakings, including providing earlier notice of proposed actions, meaningful accommodation of advisory body meeting schedules whenever practicable, and more time for intergovernmental review prior to the publication of a proposal.

Changes From the Proposed Rule
Based on public comments received and NPS's further review, the final rule makes the following changes to the proposed rule:
1. The title of this rule has been changed to reflect its scope that addresses hunting and trapping in national preserves, but also subsistence harvest of live wildlife and plant materials, and procedures used to restrict public use and access to Alaska park areas, including for subsistence.
2. § 13.50(f),
notice methods:
The proposed rule and pre-2015 regulations could be interpreted to allow for public notice through the posting of appropriate signs, instead of or in addition to newspaper publications, radio broadcasts, post office flyers, available maps, and other methods likely to inform affected users. The final rule replaces “or” with “and” to confirm that all the listed notice methods are required, where available, rather than having an option to close areas to harvest through the posting of signs alone.
3. §§ 13.35(g) and 13.400(e),
authorized users:
In response to comments and further agency review, the final rule adds language to clarify that generally applicable limitations on park visitors do not generally apply to those authorized to harvest renewable resources for subsistence uses in park areas in Alaska, including local rural residents, as defined in § 13.420, and other federally qualified users engaged in authorized harvest activities (
e.g.,
subsistence permits issued by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service pursuant to the Migratory Bird Treaty Act).
4. § 13.400(e),
new citation:
A cross-reference to the Federal Subsistence Board regulations at
43 CFR part 51
was added in response to comments, including from the Alaska Federation of Natives, seeking greater specificity for subsistence users than a general reference to ANILCA as applicable federal law.
5. § 13.420,
definitions:
The proposed rule solicited comment on revising the definition of “customary trade.” No submissions included specific reforms that would improve upon any particular definition. Rather than reverting to the pre-2015 language, the final rule retains the current definitions of “customary trade” and “handicraft” to provide continuity and reduce confusion for subsistence users and enforcement personnel.
6. § 13.420,
revised citation:
The final rule updates the cross-reference in the definition of “handicraft” to Federal Subsistence Board regulations formerly located at
50 CFR part 100
which were transferred to
43 CFR part 51
to align with the transfer of the Office of Subsistence Management to the Office of the Secretary of the Interior. See
90 FR 34142
(July 18, 2025).
7. § 13.490,
consultation:
In response to comments and agency review, the requirement to consult with the Federal Subsistence Board before temporarily closing a park area to harvest for subsistence uses is retained in the final rule as an important update for ensuring rural Alaska residents have a meaningful role in the management of fish and wildlife and subsistence uses on all public lands in Alaska.

This rule has been determined to be significant for purposes of
Executive Order 12866
and has been submitted for review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). This rule is a deregulatory action under
Executive Order 14192
. It removes the 2017 permit requirement for collecting animal parks for handicrafts, removes restrictions for all user groups on hunting bears over bait, and removes the 2024 firearm-related definition of “trapping” and its associated compliance burdens, without imposing any new permit, reporting, or recordkeeping requirements on regulated entities. The rule also restores fixed procedural requirements (
e.g.,
durational limits, consultation obligations, and notice requirements) that constrain agency discretion and reduce regulatory uncertainty for the public, which the 2015 and 2017 rules had displaced with greater focus on System-wide standards and less focus on affected areas and users. Because this rule aligns federal and state requirements, rather than adding or maintaining conflicting layers of regulation, NPS does not consider it a new regulatory burden for purposes of this classification.
Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
)
This final rule will not have a significant economic effect on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act. This certification is based on information contained in the economic analyses found in the report entitled “Benefit-Cost and Regulatory Flexibility Analyses: Alaska Wildlife, Harvest, and Access Regulations (RIN 1024-AE96).” The report may be viewed in the docket for this rulemaking action by visiting
https://www.regulations.gov/​
and searching for “RIN 1024-AE96”.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (
2 U.S.C. 1501
et seq.
)
This rule does not impose an unfunded mandate on State, local, or Tribal governments or the private sector of more than $100 million per year. The rule does not have a significant or unique effect on State, local or Tribal governments or the private sector. It addresses public use of lands and waters administered by the NPS and imposes no requirements on other agencies or governments. A statement containing the information required by the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (
2 U.S.C. 1531
et seq.
) is not required.
Takings—
Executive Order 12630
This rule will not affect a taking of private property or otherwise have takings implications under
Executive Order 12630
. A takings implication assessment is not required.
Federalism—
Executive Order 13132
Under the criteria in section 1 of
Executive Order 13132
, this rule does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement. This rule only affects use of federally administered lands and waters. It has no direct effects on other areas. A federalism summary impact statement is not required.
Civil Justice Reform—
Executive Order 12988
This rule complies with the requirements of
Executive Order 12988
. This rule:
(a) Meets the criteria of section 3(a) requiring that all regulations be reviewed to eliminate errors and ambiguity and be written to minimize litigation; and
(b) Meets the criteria of section 3(b)(2) requiring that all regulations be written in clear language and contain clear legal standards.
Consultation With Indian Tribes and ANCSA Corporations—
Executive Order 13175
and Department Policy
The DOI strives to strengthen its government-to-government relationship with Indian Tribes through a commitment to consultation with Indian Tribes and recognition of their right to self-governance and Tribal sovereignty. This rule was informed by feedback from Tribal entities. In April 2025, the NPS invited Alaska Native Tribes and
(
printed page 65998)
corporations organized under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) to participate in pre-consultation regarding NPS's wildlife management practices in Alaska. The NPS incorporated feedback received and met with all Tribal entities that requested a meeting. The NPS has evaluated this rule under the criteria in
Executive Order 13175
and under the Department's Tribal consultation and ANCSA Corporation policies. Because the rule does not restrict Title VIII subsistence harvest, the rule will not have a substantial direct effect on federally recognized Tribes or ANCSA Corporation lands, water areas, or resources. Consultation and communication with Tribes and ANCSA Corporations was considered by the NPS throughout the rulemaking process.
Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
)
This rule does not contain information collection requirements, and a submission to the OMB under the Paperwork Reduction Act is not required. The NPS may not conduct or sponsor, and you are not required to respond, to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA;
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
)
The NPS has prepared a Wildlife, Harvest, and Access in National Parks and Preserves in Alaska Environmental Assessment (EA) to determine whether this rule will have a significant impact on the quality of the human environment under the NEPA. The EA included appropriate available information and an analysis of impacts for public safety, wildlife, federal subsistence use, and public use and experience resource issues. The EA incorporated feedback received during the public comment period on the proposed rule and during consultation with Tribes and ANCSA Corporations and with the State of Alaska. On September 28, 2026, the Regional Director, Alaska Region, signed a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) that identified the preferred alternative in the EA as the selected action. This rule is not a major Federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment. A detailed statement under the NEPA is not required because of the FONSI. A copy of the EA and FONSI are available online at
https://parkplanning.nps.gov/​akro
by clicking the link entitled “
https://parkplanning.nps.gov/​AlaskaWildlifeRule2026
”
and then clicking the link entitled “Document List.”
Energy Supply, Distribution or Use—
Executive Order 13211
This rule is not a significant energy action under the definition in
Executive Order 13211
; the rule is not likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution, or use of energy, and the rule has not otherwise been designated by the Administrator of OIRA as a significant energy action. A statement of energy effects is not required.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-09-02, which applies to certain Pratt & Whitney RTX Corporation (PW) Model PW4074, PW4074D, PW4077, PW4077D, PW4084D, PW4090, and PW4090-3 engines. AD 2026-09-02 requires repetitive angle ultrasonic scan inspections (AUSIs) of the high-pressure compressor (HPC) 15th-stage disks, front turbine hubs, high-pressure turbine (HPT) 1st-stage air seals, and HPT 2nd-stage hubs for crack indications, and removal from service and replacement if necessary, and for certain serial numbers, removal from service and replacement of the HPT 1st-stage air seal. Since the FAA issued AD 2026-09-02, the FAA was notified that a certain part number was omitted from AD 2026-09-02 and the applicability of the optional terminating action was matched to an unrelated requirement. This proposed AD would require repetitive AUSIs of the HPC 15th-stage disks, front turbine hubs, HPT 1st-stage air seals, and HPT 2nd-stage hubs for crack indications, and removal from service and replacement if necessary, and for certain serial numbers, removal from service and replacement of the HPT 1st-stage air seal. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Molly Sturgis, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th Street, Des Moines, WA 98198. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2026-09-02, Amendment 39-23322 (
91 FR 30191
, May 22, 2026) (AD 2026-09-02), for PW Model PW4074, PW4074D, PW4077, PW4077D, PW4084D, PW4090, and PW4090-3 engines. AD 2026-09-02 was prompted by an analysis of an event involving an International Aero Engines, LLC (IAE LLC) Model PW1127GA-JM engine, which experienced an HPC 7th-stage integrally bladed rotor (IBR-7) separation that resulted in an aborted takeoff. Following this event, the manufacturer analysis found that the failure of the HPC IBR-7 was caused by a nickel powdered metal anomaly,
(
printed page 66013)
similar in nature to an anomaly previously observed. The analysis also concluded that there is an increased risk of failure for additional nickel powdered metal parts in certain nickel powdered metal production campaigns, and these parts are susceptible to failure much earlier than previously determined. AD 2026-09-02 requires repetitive AUSIs of the HPC 15th-stage disks, front turbine hubs, HPT 1st-stage air seals, and HPT 2nd-stage hubs for crack indications, and removal from service and replacement if necessary, and for certain serial numbers, removal from service and replacement of the HPT 1st-stage air seal. The FAA issued AD 2026-09-02 to prevent failure of the HPC 15th-stage disk, front turbine hub, HPT 1st-stage air seal, and HPT 2nd-stage hub. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in uncontained disk failure, release of high energy debris, damage to the engine, damage to the airplane, and possible loss of the airplane.
Actions Since AD 2026-09-02 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2026-09-02, the FAA has become aware that the manufacturer revised PW Alert Service Bulletin (ASB) PW4G-112-A72-368, dated June 20, 2024 (PW ASB PW4G-112-A72-368) to include HPT 2nd-stage hub part number (P/N) 53L402, which was not identified in PW ASB PW4G-112-A72-368 and inadvertently omitted from AD 2026-09-02. Additionally, the applicability of the optional terminating action was matched to paragraph (g)(1) of AD 2026-09-02, which is an unrelated requirement.
FAA's Determination
The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed PW ASB PW4G-112-A72-368, Revision No. 1, dated September 20, 2024, which specifies procedures for performing repetitive AUSIs on affected HPT 2nd-stage hubs.
This proposed AD would also require the following material, which the Director of the Federal Register approved for incorporation by reference as of June 26, 2026 (
91 FR 30191
, May 22, 2026).
PW ASB PW4G-112-A72-365, Revision No. 1, dated June 20, 2024, which specifies procedures for performing repetitive AUSIs on affected HPC 15th-stage disks.
PW ASB PW4G-112-A72-366, dated June 20, 2024, which specifies procedures for performing repetitive AUSIs on affected HPT 1st-stage air seals.
PW ASB PW4G-112-A72-367, dated June 20, 2024, which specifies procedures for performing repetitive AUSIs on affected front turbine hubs.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require repetitive AUSIs of the HPC 15th-stage disks, front turbine hubs, HPT 1st-stage air seals, and HPT 2nd-stage hubs for crack indications, and removal from service and replacement if necessary. This proposed AD would also require, for certain serial numbers, removal from service and replacement of the HPT 1st-stage air seal.
Costs of Compliance
The FAA estimates that this AD, if adopted as proposed, would affect 124 engines installed on airplanes of U.S. registry. The FAA estimates that 124 engines will need AUSIs of the HPC 15th-stage disk, front turbine hub, HPT 2nd-stage hub, and HPT 1st-stage air seal; and 6 engines will need replacement of the HPT 1st-stage air seals.

Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.

(d) Subject

(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by an analysis of an event involving an International Aero Engines, LLC Model PW1127GA-JM engine, which experienced a high-pressure compressor (HPC) 7th-stage integrally bladed rotor separation that resulted in an aborted takeoff. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent failure of the HPC 15th-stage disk, front turbine hub, high-pressure turbine (HPT) 1st-stage air seal, and HPT 2nd-stage hub. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in uncontained disk failure, release of high energy debris, damage to the engine, damage to the airplane, and possible loss of the airplane.

Abstract:
Authority for this information collection is found in
Title 38 Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) Part 51, “Per Diem for Nursing Home, Domiciliary or Adult Day Health Care of Veterans in State Veterans Homes.” Specifically, the legal requirements that necessitate this collection of information are found in
Title 38 CFR
Parts § 51.31, § 51.43 and § 51.210 for all three levels of care: nursing home, domiciliary, and adult day health care. VA requires State Veterans Homes (SVHs) to be recognized by the Under Secretary for Health as providing safe, high-quality programs in these areas.
The six forms in this collection (10-0143, 10-0143A, 10-0144, 10-0144A, 10-0460 and 10-3567) are completed by SVH management as part of the VA survey process and ongoing compliance. This information collection falls under the auspices of the Office of Geriatrics and Extended Care in VA Central Office (12GEC). The information is assessed in accordance with the applicable regulations by VA contracted vendors during a VA survey at each SVH.
a. VA Form 10-0143 is used for annual certification pursuant to the Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988.
b. VA Form 10-0143A is used for annual certification of compliance with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Pub. L. 93-112).
c. VA Form 10-0144 is used for annual certification regarding lobbying, in compliance with Public Law 101-121.
d. VA Form 10-0144A is used for annual certification of compliance with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as incorporated in
Title 38 CFR
18.1-18.3.
e. VA Form 10-0460 is used for the SVH to submit to the VA medical center of jurisdiction a monthly itemization of the corresponding prescription(s) for each eligible Veteran.
f. VA Form 10-3567 is completed by SVH management for the annual VA survey and is used by VA to record and then assess the following: operating beds versus recognized beds, total full-time employee equivalent (FTEE) authorized and total FTEE available, and resident census.

Background
Commerce published the

Partial Rescission of Administrative Review
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
, Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if the party that requested a review withdraws its request within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation. Requests were timely withdrawn within 90 days of the publication of the initiation notice for this review for 93 companies.

As a result, Commerce is rescinding this review with respect to these companies, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
.

9

Additionally, pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(3)
, Commerce will rescind an administrative review when there are no entries of subject merchandise during the POR for which liquidation is suspended. Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the AD assessment rate calculated for the review period.
[
10
]
Therefore, for an administrative review of a company to be conducted, there must be a suspended entry that Commerce can instruct and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the AD assessment rate calculated for the POR.
[

In the absence of any suspended entries of subject merchandise from 12 companies that were initiated upon, we are rescinding the administrative review for these companies, in accordance with

.

12

Analysis of Comments Received
All issues raised in the case briefs filed in this administrative review are addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum. A list of the topics discussed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum is included in Appendix I of this notice. The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is available electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Services System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at

.

Changes Since the Preliminary Results
Based on our review of the record and comments received from interested parties, we have rescinded this review with regard to 105 companies, as we stated in the Intent to Rescind Memorandum.
[
13
]
In addition, we revised the names of certain respondents as identified in the
Preliminary Results
and made certain changes to the dumping margin calculations for the mandatory respondents. For a discussion of these changes,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
Rate for Non-Selected Companies
The Act does not address the establishment of a rate to apply to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(e)(2) of the Act. However, Commerce's regulation at
19 CFR 351.109(g)
states that Commerce will determine the rate for non-selected companies by following the process set forth in
19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)-(2)
, which generally parallels the process for determining the all-others rate in an investigation under section 735(c)(5) of the Act.
Under section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.109(f)
, the all-others rate is normally an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any rates that are zero,
de minimis
(
i.e.,
less than 0.5 percent), or determined entirely on the basis of facts available. Where the weighted-average dumping margin for each of the individually examined companies is zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available, section 735(c)(5)(B) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.109(f)(2)(iii)
provide that Commerce may use “any reasonable method” to establish the estimated all-others rate for exporters and producers not individually investigated, including averaging the estimated weighted-average dumping margins determined for the exporters and producers individually investigated.
In this review, we calculated above-
de minimis
weighted-average dumping margins for Canfor, Resolute, and West Fraser that were not determined entirely on the basis of facts available. Therefore, consistent with section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act, we are assigning the weighted average of the three mandatory
(
